Chapter 1 Strain

1.17 Strain in space

In section 1.1 we announced that three normal and three shear strains together describe completely how the material close to a point is deformed, as long as the deformation is small. At the end of section 1.6.2 we found what we need to derive this: derivatives of functions of three variables, and a way of writing that gives the strain of a fibre for every direction. We now have both. By theorem 1.88 on the change of a field over a short step, the difference of the displacements of the ends of a short fibre is almost exactly a sum of products of partial derivatives with the components of the fibre. In section 1.16 we wrote such sums as the product of a matrix and a vector.

The goal of this section is to calculate, from the displacement field, the strain of a short fibre in any direction through any interior point of a body. First we calculate it exactly, without assuming that the strains are small. Then we look at what remains when the partial derivatives of the displacements are small, as in steel structures. This gives the six promised numbers, and we say what each of them measures. At the end we separate the part of the change in which the material only turns, and we show with an example when the simplified measure fails. Finally we meet a measure that compares the change of the length of a fibre with its length after loading.

The physical model is the same as before. A body is a continuum (definition 1.1), its change of shape is described by the displacement field (definition 1.23), and we measure the stretching of the material close to a point with short fibres (definition 1.24), which we shorten towards zero, just as we shortened a piece of the bar. We make two assumptions.

  1. The displacement field is continuously differentiable (definition 1.90). Physically this means that the body has no cracks, that no layer slides along its neighbour and that the strain nowhere jumps, as it would at the joint of two different materials (section 1.15.6). We need the assumption because without it we may not use the theorem on the change of a field over a short step. At a crack, or at a glued joint that gives way, the results of this section do not hold. In a body made of two materials we use them in each material separately.
  2. The point \(P\) at which we calculate is an interior point of the body: there is still material around it in all directions, up to some distance \(r > 0\). In this way every fibre from \(P\) shorter than \(r\) stays in the body.

We do not need the assumption that the strains are small in the first part of the section. We introduce it only in section 1.17.3, and there we say how small they must be.

We will test everything on two bodies we already know (figure 1.342).

Let us first draw the bar, on the left of the figure. The upright rectangle is the steel bar with a diameter of 10 mm, seen from the side in the plane \(z = 0\). It is drawn much thicker than it is, so that we can see where the point \(P\) lies. The grey dashed vertical line is its axis. The point \(O\) is the centre of the top end. Only this point is fixed. The five arrows above the top end are the force that holds the bar. The arrows point up because the force carries the weight, and they are spread over the whole top face because the force is distributed evenly over it, which is an idealization. The axis \(x\) and the axis \(y\) are drawn at the side: \(x\) points down and \(y\) to the right, while the axis \(z\) points towards the reader. The dimension \(L\) says that the bar is \(10\) m long. The point \(P\) lies at the middle of the bar, so the dimension \(x_{\mathrm{P}}\) from \(O\) to it is half the length, \(5\) m. The point is to the right of the axis, by the dimension \(y_{\mathrm{P}}\), which is \(4\) mm, while the radius of the bar is \(5\) mm. So in the figure it is near the right edge of the bar.

The first body is the hanging bar from the figure (figure 1.342, left), \(L = 10\) m long and round. It is held in the idealized way of section 1.7.1, with the axis \(x\) from the point \(O\) downwards, and the displacement field is ((1.18))

\[\begin{aligned} u_{\mathrm{x}} &= a\,(2Lx - x^2) - 0{,}3\,a\,(y^2 + z^2) , \\ u_{\mathrm{y}} &= -0{,}6\,a\,(L - x)\,y , \\ u_{\mathrm{z}} &= -0{,}6\,a\,(L - x)\,z , \end{aligned}\]

where \(L = 10\) m and \(a = 1{,}952 \cdot 10^{-7}\ \text{m}^{-1}\). We will calculate at the point \(P\) with \(x_{\mathrm{P}} = 5\) m, \(y_{\mathrm{P}} = 4\) mm and \(z_{\mathrm{P}} = 0\), which lies 5 m below the point \(O\) and 4 mm from the axis of the bar.

Now the cube, on the right of the figure. The hatched line is the table to which the cube is glued. The axes at the side show \(x\) to the right, in the direction of the push, and \(z\) upwards. We draw the front face, first before the push. The bottom edge \(AB\) and the vertical edge \(AD\) are thickened because we will follow them, the right and top edge are thinner and blackwhite. The corners are \(A\) bottom left, \(B\) bottom right, \(C\) top right and \(D\) top left. The dimension \(h\) is the height of the cube, \(10\) mm. Then we draw the face after the push, in orange. The orange edge is such that the bottom edge stays on the table and the top edge moves to the right. The corner \(C\) goes to \(C_1\), the corner \(D\) to \(D_1\) on the orange part of the edge \(AD\). The dimension \(s\) is the shift of the top face, \(10\) µm. It is greatly magnified, in the figure it is \(0{,}15\) of the height instead of \(0{,}001\). The diagonal \(AC\) and the diagonal \(BD\) are drawn grey before the push and orange after it. The first gets longer and the second shorter, because the top edge moves to the right.

The second body is the sheared cube of section 1.6.2 (figure 1.342, right): a steel cube with an edge of 10 mm, glued to a table by its bottom face, whose top face we pushed sideways by 10 µm. The axis \(x\) points in the direction of the push, the axis \(z\) up, and the displacement field is \(u_{\mathrm{x}} = 0{,}001\,z\), \(u_{\mathrm{y}} = 0\), \(u_{\mathrm{z}} = 0\) ((1.16)). On the front face we will follow the same fibres as in section 1.6.2: the bottom edge \(AB\), the vertical edge \(AD\) and the diagonals \(AC\) and \(BD\).

1.17.1 The displacement gradient and the deformation gradient

We start with a fibre. Let a fibre from the interior point \(P\) have the direction of the unit vector \(\vek n = (n_{\mathrm{x}}, n_{\mathrm{y}}, n_{\mathrm{z}})\) and reach to the point \(Q\) with \(\overrightarrow{PQ} = h\,\vek n\), as in section 1.7.3. The number \(h\) may be positive or negative, the length of the fibre is \(|h|\), and we take \(0 < |h| < r\), so that the fibre stays in the body. After loading the fibre has, by (1.15), the vector

\[\overrightarrow{P_1 Q_1} = h\,\vek n + \big(\vek u(Q) - \vek u(P)\big) .\]

In section 1.7.3 we wrote the difference of displacements component by component. For the component \(x\), by (1.24) with the components of the step \(\Delta x = h\,n_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(\Delta y = h\,n_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(\Delta z = h\,n_{\mathrm{z}}\),

\[u_{\mathrm{x}}(Q) - u_{\mathrm{x}}(P) = \frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{x}}}{\partial x}(P)\,h\,n_{\mathrm{x}} + \frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{x}}}{\partial y}(P)\,h\,n_{\mathrm{y}} + \frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{x}}}{\partial z}(P)\,h\,n_{\mathrm{z}} + R_{\mathrm{x}} ,\]

and the same for \(u_{\mathrm{y}}\) with the remainder \(R_{\mathrm{y}}\) and for \(u_{\mathrm{z}}\) with the remainder \(R_{\mathrm{z}}\). Theorem 1.88 on the change of a field over a short step tells us that for a continuously differentiable field each of the three remainders is small compared with the length of the fibre: for every allowed error \(\eta > 0\) there is a \(\delta > 0\) such that \(|R_{\mathrm{x}}| \le \eta\,|h|\) for every \(h\) with \(0 < |h| < \delta\), and the same for \(R_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(R_{\mathrm{z}}\).

The three sums contain nine partial derivatives at the point \(P\). Each sum is the product of one row of partial derivatives with the components of the vector \(h\,\vek n\), so it is exactly one component of the product of a matrix and a vector ((1.38)). So we arrange the partial derivatives in a matrix in which the row says which component of the displacement we take, and the column the coordinate with respect to which we differentiate. This is the table of section 1.7.2, written as a matrix.

Let us arrange the derivatives in a table, as we will write it. Top left is the table of nine partial derivatives, all at the point \(P\). We name the rows after the component of the displacement, \(u_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(u_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(u_{\mathrm{z}}\), because each row says how this component changes. We name the columns after the coordinate with respect to which we differentiate, \(x\), \(y\) and \(z\). The grey fields on the diagonal are the derivatives of a component with respect to its own coordinate, for example \(\partial u_{\mathrm{x}} / \partial x\). The blue field is \(\partial u_{\mathrm{x}} / \partial z\), in the row \(x\) and column \(z\): how the component \(x\) of the displacement changes as we go in the direction of the axis \(z\). Top right is the same table for the shifted cube, in which the only nonzero entry is \(0{,}001\), because \(u_{\mathrm{x}} = 0{,}001\,z\). Below are the identity matrix, the displacement gradient of the cube and their sum, to which we will give a name below. The signs \(+\) and \(=\) say that we add entry by entry. The grey ones on the diagonal stay ones, because in \(\mat H\) there is zero there, and the entry \(0{,}001\) of \(\mat H\) is copied into \(\mat F\).

Definition 1.109 Displacement gradient (gradient pomikov)

Let the displacement field \(\vek u = (u_{\mathrm{x}}, u_{\mathrm{y}}, u_{\mathrm{z}})\) have all nine partial derivatives at an interior point \(P\) of a body. The displacement gradient at the point \(P\) (gradient pomikov) is the matrix

\[\mat H = \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{\partial u_{\mathrm{x}}}{\partial x} & \dfrac{\partial u_{\mathrm{x}}}{\partial y} & \dfrac{\partial u_{\mathrm{x}}}{\partial z} \\[3mm] \dfrac{\partial u_{\mathrm{y}}}{\partial x} & \dfrac{\partial u_{\mathrm{y}}}{\partial y} & \dfrac{\partial u_{\mathrm{y}}}{\partial z} \\[3mm] \dfrac{\partial u_{\mathrm{z}}}{\partial x} & \dfrac{\partial u_{\mathrm{z}}}{\partial y} & \dfrac{\partial u_{\mathrm{z}}}{\partial z} \end{bmatrix} , \tag{1.44}\]

in which all partial derivatives are taken at the point \(P\). Its entry in row \(\ix{i}\) and column \(\ix{j}\) is \(H_{\mathrm{ij}} = \dfrac{\partial u_{\mathrm{i}}}{\partial x_{\mathrm{j}}}(P)\). The indices \(\ix{i}\) and \(\ix{j}\) run over \(x\), \(y\), \(z\), and \(x_{\mathrm{j}}\) means the coordinate named \(\ix{j}\): \(x_{\mathrm{x}} = x\), \(x_{\mathrm{y}} = y\), \(x_{\mathrm{z}} = z\).

Source: BOWER §2.1.2 (PDF p. 41), SADD (2.1.5) (PDF p. 40). CM (3.3.8) (PDF p. 120) writes \(\nabla_0\vek u\), which is the transpose of the matrix \(\mat H\).

Let us try the definition on both bodies. For the hanging bar we calculated all nine partial derivatives at the point \(P\) in section 1.7.2. We arrange them in a matrix:

\[\mat H = \begin{bmatrix} 1{,}952 \cdot 10^{-6} & -4{,}685 \cdot 10^{-10} & 0 \\ 4{,}685 \cdot 10^{-10} & -5{,}856 \cdot 10^{-7} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -5{,}856 \cdot 10^{-7} \end{bmatrix} .\]

For the sheared cube \(u_{\mathrm{x}} = 0{,}001\,z\) depends only on \(z\), and the components \(u_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(u_{\mathrm{z}}\) are zero everywhere. So the only partial derivative different from zero is \(\partial u_{\mathrm{x}} / \partial z = 0{,}001\), in row \(x\) and column \(z\), and this at every point of the cube:

\[\mat H = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 & 0{,}001 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix} .\]

With the displacement gradient the three equations for the components of the difference of displacements become one. By (1.38) the component \(\ix{i}\) of the product \(\mat H\,(h\,\vek n)\) is the sum \(\sum_{\mathrm{j}} H_{\mathrm{ij}}\,h\,n_{\mathrm{j}}\), and this is exactly the sum in the equation for \(u_{\mathrm{i}}\). So

\[\vek u(Q) - \vek u(P) = \mat H\,(h\,\vek n) + (R_{\mathrm{x}}, R_{\mathrm{y}}, R_{\mathrm{z}}) ,\]

and the vector of the fibre after loading is

\[\overrightarrow{P_1 Q_1} = h\,\vek n + \mat H\,(h\,\vek n) + (R_{\mathrm{x}}, R_{\mathrm{y}}, R_{\mathrm{z}}) .\]

We can combine the first two terms. The identity matrix \(\mat I\) leaves every vector as it is (lemma 1.106 on multiplication by the identity matrix), so \(h\,\vek n = \mat I\,(h\,\vek n)\). By point 3 of lemma 1.99 on the properties of the matrix product, the sum \(\mat I\,(h\,\vek n) + \mat H\,(h\,\vek n)\) is the product of the matrix \(\mat I + \mat H\) with the vector \(h\,\vek n\). So the matrix \(\mat I + \mat H\) gets its own name.

Definition 1.110 Deformation gradient (gradient deformacije)

Let \(\mat H\) be the displacement gradient at an interior point \(P\) of a body and \(\mat I\) the identity matrix. The deformation gradient at the point \(P\) (gradient deformacije) is the matrix

\[\mat F = \mat I + \mat H = \begin{bmatrix} 1 + \dfrac{\partial u_{\mathrm{x}}}{\partial x} & \dfrac{\partial u_{\mathrm{x}}}{\partial y} & \dfrac{\partial u_{\mathrm{x}}}{\partial z} \\[3mm] \dfrac{\partial u_{\mathrm{y}}}{\partial x} & 1 + \dfrac{\partial u_{\mathrm{y}}}{\partial y} & \dfrac{\partial u_{\mathrm{y}}}{\partial z} \\[3mm] \dfrac{\partial u_{\mathrm{z}}}{\partial x} & \dfrac{\partial u_{\mathrm{z}}}{\partial y} & 1 + \dfrac{\partial u_{\mathrm{z}}}{\partial z} \end{bmatrix} , \tag{1.45}\]

with the entries \(F_{\mathrm{ij}} = I_{\mathrm{ij}} + H_{\mathrm{ij}}\), where \(I_{\mathrm{ij}} = 1\) for \(\ix{i} = \ix{j}\) and \(I_{\mathrm{ij}} = 0\) for \(\ix{i} \neq \ix{j}\).

Source: CM (3.3.1) (PDF p. 118), (3.3.4) (PDF p. 119) and (3.3.8) (PDF p. 120), BOWER §2.1.2 (PDF p. 41).

Why the name deformation gradient? In the books the gradient of a function means all its partial derivatives at a point, collected together (CM (2.4.26), PDF p. 74). The matrix \(\mat H\) collects the partial derivatives of the displacement, so it is the displacement gradient. The matrix \(\mat F\) collects the partial derivatives of the position of a point after loading, whose coordinates are \(x + u_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(y + u_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(z + u_{\mathrm{z}}\). For example \(F_{\mathrm{xx}} = \partial(x + u_{\mathrm{x}})/\partial x = 1 + \partial u_{\mathrm{x}}/\partial x\), because the coordinate \(x\) changes with \(x\) at the rate \(1\), and \(F_{\mathrm{xy}} = \partial(x + u_{\mathrm{x}})/\partial y = \partial u_{\mathrm{x}}/\partial y\), because \(x\) does not change when we change only \(y\) (CM (3.3.8), PDF p. 120). The positions of the points after loading describe the deformed body, hence the name. What \(\mat F\) tells us about a short fibre is the content of the next lemma, and figure 1.344 shows it in advance.

Let us draw the fibre. The point \(P\) and the point \(Q\) are the end points of the fibre before loading, the blackwhite segment between them is the fibre with the vector \(h\,\vek n\). After loading both end points move. The grey dimension \(\vek u(P)\) and the grey dimension \(\vek u(Q)\) show by how much, and lead to the point \(P_1\) and the point \(Q_1\). The orange line between them is the fibre after loading. It is drawn only approximately straight, since we are interested only in the vector from \(P_1\) to \(Q_1\). Everything is greatly magnified so that it can be seen. The blue arrow from \(P_1\) is the vector \(\mat F\,(h\,\vek n)\), that is, the vector of the fibre after loading without the remainder. It ends near \(Q_1\), not in it. The grey dimension between the end of the arrow and \(Q_1\) is the missing remainder \((R_{\mathrm{x}}, R_{\mathrm{y}}, R_{\mathrm{z}})\). For ever shorter fibres it gets ever smaller compared with the length of the fibre.

Let us draw what the bound for the remainders means, with made-up numbers. The axes show the length of the fibre \(|h|\) and the size of the remainder \(|R_{\mathrm{x}}|\). The blue line is the bound \(\eta\,|h|\) and grows in proportion to the length of the fibre. The orange curve is the remainder \(|R_{\mathrm{x}}|\). It grows faster than the length, so for small \(|h|\) it is below the line and for large ones above it. The dot and the measure show where the curve and the line cross. Up to there the bound holds, this is \(\delta_{\mathrm{x}}\). The same holds for the remainders \(R_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(R_{\mathrm{z}}\), where the bound is satisfied on the interval up to \(\delta_{\mathrm{y}}\) and on the interval up to \(\delta_{\mathrm{z}}\). The fibre stays in the body on the interval up to \(r\). All four conditions hold at once on the shortest of these intervals, up to the number \(\delta\). It is drawn thick, and the dashed vertical line shows where it ends.

Lemma 1.111 A short fibre after loading (kratko vlakno po obremenitvi)

Let the displacement field of a body be continuously differentiable, \(P\) an interior point of the body, \(r > 0\) a number such that all points closer to \(P\) than \(r\) are interior points of the body (such an \(r\) exists by lemma 1.89 on the neighbourhood of an interior point), \(\mat F\) the deformation gradient at \(P\) and \(\vek n\) a unit vector. For a number \(h\) with \(0 < |h| < r\) let a fibre reach from \(P\) to the point \(Q\) with \(\overrightarrow{PQ} = h\,\vek n\). Then the vector of the fibre after loading is

\[\overrightarrow{P_1 Q_1} = \mat F\,(h\,\vek n) + (R_{\mathrm{x}}, R_{\mathrm{y}}, R_{\mathrm{z}}) , \tag{1.46}\]

where \(R_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(R_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(R_{\mathrm{z}}\) are the remainders of (1.24) for the step \(h\,\vek n\). For every \(\eta > 0\) there is a \(\delta > 0\) such that \(|R_{\mathrm{x}}| \le \eta\,|h|\), \(|R_{\mathrm{y}}| \le \eta\,|h|\) and \(|R_{\mathrm{z}}| \le \eta\,|h|\) for every \(h\) with \(0 < |h| < \delta\).

Proof

We must show the equation (1.46) and the bounds for the remainders.

  1. By (1.15), \(\overrightarrow{P_1 Q_1}\) \(= \overrightarrow{PQ} + \big(\vek u(Q) - \vek u(P)\big) = h\,\vek n + \big(\vek u(Q) - \vek u(P)\big)\).
  2. By (1.24), written for the step with the components \(h\,n_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(h\,n_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(h\,n_{\mathrm{z}}\), the component \(\ix{i}\) of the difference of displacements is \(\sum_{\mathrm{j}} H_{\mathrm{ij}}\,h\,n_{\mathrm{j}} + R_{\mathrm{i}}\), where \(R_{\mathrm{i}}\) is the remainder \(R_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(R_{\mathrm{y}}\) or \(R_{\mathrm{z}}\).
  3. By (1.38) the sum \(\sum_{\mathrm{j}} H_{\mathrm{ij}}\,h\,n_{\mathrm{j}}\) is the component \(\ix{i}\) of the product \(\mat H\,(h\,\vek n)\). So \(\vek u(Q) - \vek u(P) = \mat H\,(h\,\vek n) + (R_{\mathrm{x}}, R_{\mathrm{y}}, R_{\mathrm{z}})\).
  4. By lemma 1.106 on multiplication by the identity matrix, \(h\,\vek n\) \(= \mat I\,(h\,\vek n)\).
  5. By point 3 of lemma 1.99 on the properties of the matrix product, used for the column \(h\,\vek n\), \(\mat I\,(h\,\vek n) + \mat H\,(h\,\vek n) = (\mat I + \mat H)(h\,\vek n) =\) \(\mat F\,(h\,\vek n)\).
  6. Steps 1, 3, 4 and 5 give (1.46).
  7. The field is continuously differentiable, so each component of the displacement has partial derivatives at all points closer to \(P\) than \(r\), and they are continuous at \(P\). By theorem 1.88 on the change of a field over a short step, for a given \(\eta > 0\) there are numbers \(\delta_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(\delta_{\mathrm{y}}\), \(\delta_{\mathrm{z}} > 0\) such that \(|R_{\mathrm{x}}| \le \eta\,|h|\) for \(0 < |h| < \delta_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(|R_{\mathrm{y}}| \le \eta\,|h|\) for \(0 < |h| < \delta_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(|R_{\mathrm{z}}| \le \eta\,|h|\) for \(0 < |h| < \delta_{\mathrm{z}}\). The step \(h\,\vek n\) has the length \(|h|\), so \(|h|\) here is exactly the length of the step in the theorem.
  8. For \(\delta\) we take the smallest of the numbers \(\delta_{\mathrm{x}}\), \(\delta_{\mathrm{y}}\), \(\delta_{\mathrm{z}}\) and \(r\). For every \(h\) with \(0 < |h| < \delta\) all three bounds hold at once.

Source: CM (3.3.1) (PDF p. 118) and BOWER §2.1.5 (PDF p. 48) write the equation for an infinitesimally short fibre, without a remainder. The remainders and their bounds are not from a source, they follow from the theorem on the change of a field over a short step.

The lemma tells us what the deformation gradient means. The vector of a short fibre after loading is almost exactly \(\mat F\) times the vector of the same fibre before loading, the blue vector \(\mat F\,(h\,\vek n)\) in figure 1.344. The difference is the remainders, which for a short fibre are small compared with its length. For the bar it was the same with a single number. A piece of length \(\Delta x\) was, after loading, about \((1 + u'(x))\,\Delta x\) long, because it got longer by \(u(x + \Delta x) - u(x) \approx u'(x)\,\Delta x\). In space the number \(1 + u'(x)\) is replaced by the matrix \(\mat I + \mat H\), because a fibre can not only get longer but also tilt.

What does a single entry of the matrix \(\mat F\) tell us? Take a fibre in the direction of the axis \(x\), with \(\vek n = \vek e_{\mathrm{x}} = (1, 0, 0)\). By (1.38), \(\mat F\,\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\) is the first column of the matrix \(\mat F\):

\[\mat F\,\vek e_{\mathrm{x}} = \Big(1 + \frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{x}}}{\partial x},\ \frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{y}}}{\partial x},\ \frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{z}}}{\partial x}\Big) .\]

The axes on the left show \(x\) to the right and \(y\) upwards. The point \(P\) is the corner of a small square. The blackwhite square has an edge \(h\) in the direction of the axis \(x\) and an edge \(h\) in the direction of the axis \(y\), these are the fibres \(h\,\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\) and \(h\,\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\) before loading. It is drawn relative to \(P\), that is, without the common displacement \(\vek u(P)\), which would only move the square. In orange is the same square after loading, and the deformation is made up and greatly magnified so that it can be seen. The bottom orange edge is the fibre \(h\,\mat F\,\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\) after loading, and the left orange edge is the fibre \(h\,\mat F\,\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\). The other two orange edges complete the parallelogram, so that the whole square after loading is visible. The end points of both fibres have moved, and the grey dimensions beside them, which the next paragraph mentions, show piece by piece by how much.

The end of a fibre of length \(h\) along the axis \(x\) therefore moves relative to \(P\), up to the remainder, by \(h\,\partial u_{\mathrm{x}} / \partial x\) in the direction of the fibre and by \(h\,\partial u_{\mathrm{y}} / \partial x\) in the direction of the axis \(y\) and by \(h\,\partial u_{\mathrm{z}} / \partial x\) in the direction of the axis \(z\), that is, sideways. The first displacement lengthens the fibre, the other two tilt it, as the edge along the axis \(x\) lengthened and tilted. The second and the third column say the same for fibres in the directions of the axes \(y\) and \(z\). The second column moves the end of the edge along the axis \(y\) sideways by \(h\,\partial u_{\mathrm{x}} / \partial y\) and along the edge by \(h\,\partial u_{\mathrm{y}} / \partial y\). The figure does not show the third column, because it lies in the plane \(x\)-\(y\), while the fibre along the axis \(z\) points out of it. So the entries on the diagonal of the matrix \(\mat H\) describe how fibres along the axes lengthen, and the entries off the diagonal how they tilt. We will need this when we explain what the components of the strain mean.

For the sheared cube the deformation gradient is

\[\mat F = \mat I + \mat H = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0{,}001 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} .\]

The first column is \((1, 0, 0)\): the fibres along the axis \(x\) do not change, just as the bottom edge \(AB\) did not change. The third column has the entries \(0{,}001\), \(0\) and \(1\): the fibres along the axis \(z\) tilt towards the axis \(x\), their end moves sideways by a thousandth of the length of the fibre, as for the vertical edge \(AD\), which tilts into \(AD_1\). The field of the cube has one more special feature. The difference of the displacements of two points of the cube has the components \(0{,}001\,(z_{\mathrm{Q}} - z_{\mathrm{P}})\), \(0\) and \(0\), which is exactly \(\mat H\,\overrightarrow{PQ}\). So there are no remainders, and every fibre of the cube, not only a short one, has the vector \(\mat F\,\overrightarrow{PQ}\) after loading. For the vertical edge \(AD\) with \(\overrightarrow{AD} = (0, 0, 10\,000)\) in micrometres,

\[\mat F\,\overrightarrow{AD} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0{,}001 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \\ 10\,000 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 0{,}001 \cdot 10\,000 \\ 0 \\ 10\,000 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 10 \\ 0 \\ 10\,000 \end{bmatrix} ,\]

which is the vector after loading in the table of section 1.6.2.

CM also writes the deformation gradient as \(\mat F\), denotes the positions of points before loading by \(\vek X\) and writes \(d\vek x = \mat F\cdot d\vek X\) (CM (3.3.1), PDF p. 118).

1.17.2 The exact strain of a fibre

From the vector of a fibre after loading we want to calculate its length and its strain. For the sheared cube the square root in the length was in the way, and we got rid of it by comparing the squares of the lengths instead of the lengths ((1.17)). We do the same here. The square of the length of a vector is the sum of the squares of its components ((1.10)) and contains no root.

First let us see what we get if we leave out the remainders in (1.46). That we may do so for ever shorter fibres we will show in the theorem below. Without the remainders the fibre has the vector \(\mat F\,(h\,\vek n) = h\,\mat F\,\vek n\) after loading (lemma 1.97 on the linearity of the product with a matrix).

Let us start with a fibre along the axis \(x\), with \(\vek n = \vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\). Then \(\mat F\,\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\) is the first column of the matrix \(\mat F\) (the edge \(h\,\mat F\,\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\) in figure 1.346, divided by \(h\)), and the square of its length is the sum of the squares of the entries of this column:

\[|\mat F\,\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}|^2 = F_{\mathrm{xx}}^2 + F_{\mathrm{yx}}^2 + F_{\mathrm{zx}}^2 .\]

For the vertical edge \(AD\) of the sheared cube, with \(\vek n = \vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\), this is the third column, and \(|\mat F\,\vek e_{\mathrm{z}}|^2 = 0{,}001^2 + 0^2 + 1^2 = 1{,}000001\). For an oblique direction \(\vek n\) all three columns contribute, each multiplied by its own component of the vector \(\vek n\). So we write the square of the length with a double sum, in steps.

Let us draw how such sums add up. Above is the entry \((x, y)\) of the product \(\mat F^\T\mat F\). The row \(x\) of the matrix \(\mat F^\T\) is the column \(x\) of the matrix \(\mat F\), so we multiply the column \(x\) and the column \(y\) of the matrix \(\mat F\) place by place and add the three products. The letters \(x\) and \(y\) are here an example for \(\ix{j}\) and \(\ix{k}\) in the steps below. Below is the entry \((y, z)\) of the product \(\mat I\mat H\). The column \(y\) of the identity matrix has a single \(1\), in the row \(y\), and zeros elsewhere. We multiply it by the column \(z\) of the matrix \(\mat H\). So only the product remains \(1 \cdot H_{\mathrm{yz}}\) and the sum equals \(H_{\mathrm{yz}}\).

  1. The square of the length after loading is \(L_1^2 \approx |h\,\mat F\,\vek n|^2 = h^2\,|\mat F\,\vek n|^2\). This is because every component of the vector \(h\,\mat F\,\vek n\) is \(h\) times a component of the vector \(\mat F\,\vek n\), so its square is \(h^2\) times the square.

  2. The component \(\ix{i}\) of the vector \(\mat F\,\vek n\) is, by (1.38), the sum \(\sum_{\mathrm{j}} F_{\mathrm{ij}}\,n_{\mathrm{j}}\), the row \(\ix{i}\) of the matrix \(\mat F\) times the column \(\vek n\). So by (1.10)

    \[|\mat F\,\vek n|^2 = \sum_{\mathrm{i}} \Big(\sum_{\mathrm{j}} F_{\mathrm{ij}}\,n_{\mathrm{j}}\Big)^2 .\]

  3. We write each square of a component of the vector \(\mat F\,\vek n\) as the product of two equal sums. In the second sum we write the letter \(\ix{k}\) instead of \(\ix{j}\), to tell the terms of the two sums apart. We multiply every term of the first sum by every term of the second, just as in section 1.6.2 we multiplied out the product \((1 + \varepsilon)(1 + \varepsilon)\):

    \[\Big(\sum_{\mathrm{j}} F_{\mathrm{ij}}\,n_{\mathrm{j}}\Big)^2 = \Big(\sum_{\mathrm{j}} F_{\mathrm{ij}}\,n_{\mathrm{j}}\Big)\Big(\sum_{\mathrm{k}} F_{\mathrm{ik}}\,n_{\mathrm{k}}\Big) = \sum_{\mathrm{j}} \sum_{\mathrm{k}} F_{\mathrm{ij}}\,F_{\mathrm{ik}}\,n_{\mathrm{j}}\,n_{\mathrm{k}} .\]

  4. We sum over \(\ix{i}\). The sum has finitely many terms, so we may rearrange them as we like. We collect the terms with the same \(\ix{j}\) and \(\ix{k}\) and take the factors \(n_{\mathrm{j}}\) and \(n_{\mathrm{k}}\) out. This gives the square of the length of the vector \(\mat F\,\vek n\):

    \[|\mat F\,\vek n|^2 = \sum_{\mathrm{j}} \sum_{\mathrm{k}} n_{\mathrm{j}} \Big(\sum_{\mathrm{i}} F_{\mathrm{ij}}\,F_{\mathrm{ik}}\Big) n_{\mathrm{k}} .\]

  5. In the transposed matrix \(\mat F^\T\) the entry in row \(\ix{j}\) and column \(\ix{i}\) is \(F_{\mathrm{ij}}\) (definition 1.100). So the sum \(\sum_{\mathrm{i}} F_{\mathrm{ij}}\,F_{\mathrm{ik}} = \sum_{\mathrm{i}} (\mat F^\T)_{\mathrm{ji}}\,F_{\mathrm{ik}}\) is, by the definition of the matrix product 1.98, the entry in row \(\ix{j}\) and column \(\ix{k}\) of the matrix \(\mat F^\T\mat F\):

    \[|\mat F\,\vek n|^2 = \sum_{\mathrm{j}} \sum_{\mathrm{k}} n_{\mathrm{j}}\,(\mat F^\T\mat F)_{\mathrm{jk}}\,n_{\mathrm{k}} = \vek n^\T\,\mat F^\T\mat F\,\vek n .\]

    The last expression is short for the double sum, as in section 1.16: the row \(\vek n^\T\), multiplied by the matrix and then by the column \(\vek n\), gives one number.

  6. The square of the length before loading is \(L_0^2 = h^2\). The number \(1 = n_{\mathrm{x}}^2 + n_{\mathrm{y}}^2 + n_{\mathrm{z}}^2\), the square of the length of the unit vector, we write in the same way with the identity matrix, \(1 = \sum_{\mathrm{j}} \sum_{\mathrm{k}} n_{\mathrm{j}}\,I_{\mathrm{jk}}\,n_{\mathrm{k}} = \vek n^\T\mat I\,\vek n\). In the double sum only the terms with \(\ix{j} = \ix{k}\) remain, because \(I_{\mathrm{jk}} = 0\) for \(\ix{j} \neq \ix{k}\).

  7. We divide the relative change of the square of the length by \(2\), as in section 1.6.2, and subtract the two double sums term by term:

    \[\frac{L_1^2 - L_0^2}{2L_0^2} \approx \frac{h^2\,\vek n^\T\mat F^\T\mat F\,\vek n - h^2\,\vek n^\T\mat I\,\vek n}{2h^2} = \vek n^\T\,\tfrac12\big(\mat F^\T\mat F - \mat I\big)\,\vek n .\]

On the right stands a single matrix, which depends only on the displacement field at the point \(P\). The direction of the fibre appears only in the vector \(\vek n\). This matrix has its own name.

Let us draw the table that we will name, and compute its entries for the cube. Top left is the table \(\mat E\) with nine entries. The grey fields on the diagonal are \(E_{\mathrm{xx}}\), \(E_{\mathrm{yy}}\) and \(E_{\mathrm{zz}}\). The blue fields above the diagonal are \(E_{\mathrm{xy}}\), \(E_{\mathrm{xz}}\) and \(E_{\mathrm{yz}}\), and the blue fields below it hold the same three numbers, because the table is symmetric with respect to the diagonal. Top right is the same table for the shifted cube, with the numbers that we compute below. Below are the matrix \(\mat H\) of the cube, the transposed matrix, in which each entry is mirrored across the diagonal, and the product \(\mat H^\T\mat H\), which has a single nonzero entry. The signs \(+\) and \(=\) say that we add entry by entry. The sum of the three matrices, divided by \(2\), is the matrix \(\mat E\) of the cube.

Definition 1.112 Green-Lagrange strain tensor (Green-Lagrangeov tenzor deformacij)

Let \(\mat F\) be the deformation gradient at an interior point \(P\) of a body. The Green-Lagrange strain tensor at the point \(P\) (Green-Lagrangeov tenzor deformacij) is the matrix

\[\mat E = \tfrac12\big(\mat F^\T\mat F - \mat I\big) . \tag{1.47}\]

Source: CM (3.4.10), (3.4.11) (PDF p. 129), BOWER §2.1.5 (PDF p. 47).

What kind of object is \(\mat E\)? It is a \(3 \times 3\) matrix, calculated from the deformation gradient at one point. It is symmetric (definition 1.102). This is because the entry \((\mat F^\T\mat F)_{\mathrm{jk}} = \sum_{\mathrm{i}} F_{\mathrm{ij}}\,F_{\mathrm{ik}}\) equals the entry \((\mat F^\T\mat F)_{\mathrm{kj}} = \sum_{\mathrm{i}} F_{\mathrm{ik}}\,F_{\mathrm{ij}}\), since the order of the factors in a product does not matter, and the identity matrix is symmetric too. So \(\mat E\) has at most six different entries: three on the diagonal, \(E_{\mathrm{xx}}\), \(E_{\mathrm{yy}}\) and \(E_{\mathrm{zz}}\), and three above it, \(E_{\mathrm{xy}}\), \(E_{\mathrm{xz}}\) and \(E_{\mathrm{yz}}\), which equal the entries below it. Books call such a matrix a tensor (tenzor). What this word means we will say in chapter 2, when we see how the components change when we turn the axes. Until then the Green-Lagrange strain tensor is for us a matrix of six numbers in a chosen coordinate system. CM also calls it the Green strain tensor (CM, PDF p. 129).

The six numbers are arranged in the matrix symmetrically with respect to the main diagonal:

\[\mat E = \begin{bmatrix} E_{\mathrm{xx}} & E_{\mathrm{xy}} & E_{\mathrm{xz}} \\ E_{\mathrm{xy}} & E_{\mathrm{yy}} & E_{\mathrm{yz}} \\ E_{\mathrm{xz}} & E_{\mathrm{yz}} & E_{\mathrm{zz}} \end{bmatrix} .\]

In practice we do not know \(\mat F\) directly, but the displacement field, and from it the matrix \(\mat H\). Let us write \(\mat E\) with \(\mat H\).

Lemma 1.113 Green-Lagrange strain from the displacement gradient (Green-Lagrangeov tenzor iz gradienta pomikov)

Let \(\mat H\) be the displacement gradient and \(\mat E\) the Green-Lagrange strain tensor at an interior point \(P\) of a body. Then

\[\mat E = \tfrac12\big(\mat H + \mat H^\T + \mat H^\T\mat H\big) , \qquad E_{\mathrm{ij}} = \frac12\Big(H_{\mathrm{ij}} + H_{\mathrm{ji}} + \sum_{\mathrm{k}} H_{\mathrm{ki}}\,H_{\mathrm{kj}}\Big) ,\]

written out, with all partial derivatives at the point \(P\),

\[\begin{aligned} E_{\mathrm{xx}} &= \frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{x}}}{\partial x} + \frac12\bigg[\Big(\frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{x}}}{\partial x}\Big)^2 + \Big(\frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{y}}}{\partial x}\Big)^2 + \Big(\frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{z}}}{\partial x}\Big)^2\bigg] , \\ E_{\mathrm{xy}} &= \frac12\bigg[\frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{x}}}{\partial y} + \frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{y}}}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{x}}}{\partial x}\,\frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{x}}}{\partial y} + \frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{y}}}{\partial x}\,\frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{y}}}{\partial y} + \frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{z}}}{\partial x}\,\frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{z}}}{\partial y}\bigg] . \end{aligned} \tag{1.48}\]

The entries \(E_{\mathrm{yy}}\) and \(E_{\mathrm{zz}}\) follow from \(E_{\mathrm{xx}}\), and the entries \(E_{\mathrm{xz}}\) and \(E_{\mathrm{yz}}\) from \(E_{\mathrm{xy}}\), when we rename the axes. The remaining three are \(E_{\mathrm{yx}} = E_{\mathrm{xy}}\), \(E_{\mathrm{zx}} = E_{\mathrm{xz}}\) and \(E_{\mathrm{zy}} = E_{\mathrm{yz}}\).

Proof

We must show the form with entries, from which the other two follow.

  1. By the definitions of the transposed matrix and of the matrix product, \((\mat F^\T\mat F)_{\mathrm{ij}} = \sum_{\mathrm{k}} F_{\mathrm{ki}}\,F_{\mathrm{kj}}\), the column \(\ix{i}\) times the column \(\ix{j}\) of the matrix \(\mat F\).
  2. We substitute \(F_{\mathrm{ki}} = I_{\mathrm{ki}} + H_{\mathrm{ki}}\) and \(F_{\mathrm{kj}} = I_{\mathrm{kj}} + H_{\mathrm{kj}}\) ((1.45)) and multiply out the brackets term by term:
    \[(\mat F^\T\mat F)_{\mathrm{ij}} = \sum_{\mathrm{k}} I_{\mathrm{ki}}\,I_{\mathrm{kj}} + \sum_{\mathrm{k}} I_{\mathrm{ki}}\,H_{\mathrm{kj}} + \sum_{\mathrm{k}} H_{\mathrm{ki}}\,I_{\mathrm{kj}} + \sum_{\mathrm{k}} H_{\mathrm{ki}}\,H_{\mathrm{kj}} .\]
  3. In the first sum \(I_{\mathrm{ki}}\) is different from zero only for \(\ix{k} = \ix{i}\), so the sum equals \(I_{\mathrm{ii}}\,I_{\mathrm{ij}} = I_{\mathrm{ij}}\). In the second sum only the term with \(\ix{k} = \ix{i}\) remains, which is \(H_{\mathrm{ij}}\). In the third sum only the term with \(\ix{k} = \ix{j}\) remains, which is \(H_{\mathrm{ji}}\).
  4. So \((\mat F^\T\mat F)_{\mathrm{ij}} - I_{\mathrm{ij}} = H_{\mathrm{ij}} + H_{\mathrm{ji}} + \sum_{\mathrm{k}} H_{\mathrm{ki}}\,H_{\mathrm{kj}}\), and by (1.47) \(E_{\mathrm{ij}}\) is half of this. This is the form with entries.
  5. The entry \(H_{\mathrm{ji}}\) is the entry \((\mat H^\T)_{\mathrm{ij}}\), and the sum \(\sum_{\mathrm{k}} H_{\mathrm{ki}}\,H_{\mathrm{kj}}\) is, by step 1 written for \(\mat H\), the entry \((\mat H^\T\mat H)_{\mathrm{ij}}\). Since the matrices agree in all entries, \(\mat E = \tfrac12(\mat H + \mat H^\T + \mat H^\T\mat H)\).
  6. For \(\ix{i} = \ix{j} = x\) we have \(H_{\mathrm{xx}} + H_{\mathrm{xx}} = 2\,\partial u_{\mathrm{x}} / \partial x\), and the sum is \(H_{\mathrm{xx}}^2 + H_{\mathrm{yx}}^2 + H_{\mathrm{zx}}^2\). Substituting \(H_{\mathrm{xx}} = \partial u_{\mathrm{x}} / \partial x\), \(H_{\mathrm{yx}} = \partial u_{\mathrm{y}} / \partial x\) and \(H_{\mathrm{zx}} = \partial u_{\mathrm{z}} / \partial x\) gives \(E_{\mathrm{xx}}\).
  7. For \(\ix{i} = x\) and \(\ix{j} = y\) the sum is \(H_{\mathrm{xx}}\,H_{\mathrm{xy}} + H_{\mathrm{yx}}\,H_{\mathrm{yy}} + H_{\mathrm{zx}}\,H_{\mathrm{zy}}\). With the partial derivatives substituted we get \(E_{\mathrm{xy}}\).
  8. The formula for \(E_{\mathrm{ij}}\) is the same for all pairs of indices, so we get the other entries by renaming the axes. Step 4 shows that \(E_{\mathrm{ij}}\) does not change when \(\ix{i}\) and \(\ix{j}\) are swapped.

Source: CM (3.4.11) (PDF p. 129), (3.4.12) and (3.4.13) (PDF p. 130), BOWER §2.1.5 (PDF p. 47). CM writes the displacement gradient transposed and the coordinates before loading as \(X_1\), \(X_2\), \(X_3\).

The entry \(E_{\mathrm{xx}}\) contains only the first column of the matrix \(\mat H\), that is, only the displacements of the end of the edge along the axis \(x\), as it should, since it measures this fibre.

So far we have left out the remainders. Let us show that this is justified for ever shorter fibres. The relative change of the square of the length approaches the number \(\vek n^\T\mat E\,\vek n\), and the strain of the fibre approaches a number calculated from it.

Let us see how the strain is expressed with \(G = \vek n^\T\mat E\,\vek n\). On the left is the graph of the strain \(\varepsilon = \sqrt{1 + 2G} - 1\) as a function of \(G\), drawn in the axes \(G\) and \(\varepsilon\). The grey dashed line is \(\varepsilon = G\), which the curve follows for small \(G\). The dot is a made-up example \(G = 0{,}3\), in reality the numbers are much smaller. On the right is the same example as lengths. The top segment is the length \(1\) of the unit vector \(\vek n\) before loading. The next one is the length \(|\vek v|\) of the vector \(\vek v = \mat F\,\vek n\), which after loading is \(\sqrt{1 + 2G}\). Their difference is the strain \(\varepsilon = |\vek v| - 1\). The bottom row places \(|\vek v|\) and \(L_1/L_0\) one after the other, because in the proof we will divide by their sum, and this is not shorter than \(|\vek v|\).

Let us draw what we are proving, on the example of the hanging bar. On the left is the graph of the difference \(g(h) - G\) as a function of the length of the fibre \(h\), where \(G = \vek n^\T\mat E\,\vek n\) is the limit. The axes show \(h\) and the difference. The difference approaches zero as \(h \to 0\). The blue band is the allowed error, from \(-\eta\) to \(\eta\). We look for the lengths up to \(\delta\) at which the graph is still in the band. On the top right the difference is split into two pieces. The pieces \(V\mu\) and \(\tfrac32\mu\) lie together in the length \((V + \tfrac32)\mu\), which is shorter than the error \(\eta\), since a reserve \(\tfrac12\mu\) remains. For the bar \(V\) is close to \(\tfrac53\). On the bottom right is the band for \(g(h) - G\) with the half-width \(\eta\,|\vek v|/2\). The factor \(2/|\vek v|\) widens it into the band for the strain with the half-width \(\eta\), for the bar \(|\vek v|\) is close to \(1\).

Theorem 1.114 Strain of a short fibre (deformacija kratkega vlakna)

Let the displacement field of a body be continuously differentiable, \(P\) an interior point of the body, \(r > 0\) a number such that all points closer to \(P\) than \(r\) are interior points of the body (such an \(r\) exists by lemma 1.89 on the neighbourhood of an interior point), \(\mat F\) the deformation gradient and \(\mat E\) the Green-Lagrange strain tensor at \(P\), and \(\vek n\) a unit vector. For a number \(h\) with \(0 < |h| < r\) let a fibre reach from \(P\) to the point \(Q\) with \(\overrightarrow{PQ} = h\,\vek n\). Its length before loading is \(L_0 = |h|\), and after loading \(L_1 = |\overrightarrow{P_1 Q_1}|\). Then:

  1. the relative change of the square of the length, divided by \(2\), approaches the number \(\vek n^\T\mat E\,\vek n\),
    \[\lim_{\mathrm{h} \to 0} \frac{L_1^2 - L_0^2}{2L_0^2} = \vek n^\T\mat E\,\vek n , \tag{1.49}\]
  2. if \(\mat F\,\vek n\) is not the zero vector, the strain of the fibre approaches the number
    \[\lim_{\mathrm{h} \to 0} \frac{L_1 - L_0}{L_0} = \sqrt{1 + 2\,\vek n^\T\mat E\,\vek n} - 1 . \tag{1.50}\]
Proof

We first prove item 1, then item 2 from it.

1. The square of the length. We write the definition of the limit 1.5 for the function \(g(h) = (L_1^2 - L_0^2)/(2L_0^2)\), which is defined for \(0 < |h| < r\), and for the number \(\vek n^\T\mat E\,\vek n\). We must show: for every \(\eta > 0\) there is a \(\delta > 0\) such that \(|g(h) - \vek n^\T\mat E\,\vek n| < \eta\) for every \(h\) with \(0 < |h| < \delta\).

  1. By lemma 1.111 on a short fibre after loading, \(\overrightarrow{P_1 Q_1} = h\,\mat F\,\vek n + (R_{\mathrm{x}}, R_{\mathrm{y}}, R_{\mathrm{z}})\), where we wrote \(\mat F\,(h\,\vek n) = h\,\mat F\,\vek n\) by lemma 1.97 on the linearity of the product with a matrix. We write \(\vek v = \mat F\,\vek n\) and \(\vek q = (R_{\mathrm{x}}/h,\ R_{\mathrm{y}}/h,\ R_{\mathrm{z}}/h)\). The vector \(h\,\vek v\) is the blue vector, and the vector \(h\,\vek q\) is the remainder up to \(Q_1\). The vector \(\vek v\) does not depend on \(h\), the vector \(\vek q\) does. Then \(\overrightarrow{P_1 Q_1} = h\,(\vek v + \vek q)\).
  2. The squares of the lengths of the vector after loading and of the vector before it are \(L_1^2 = h^2\,|\vek v + \vek q|^2\) and \(L_0^2 = h^2\), so \(L_1^2/L_0^2 = |\vek v + \vek q|^2\).
  3. We write the square of the length of the sum of the vectors \(\vek v\) and \(\vek q\) component by component ((1.10)), and each square of a sum as \((v_{\mathrm{i}} + q_{\mathrm{i}})^2 = v_{\mathrm{i}}^2 + 2v_{\mathrm{i}}\,q_{\mathrm{i}} + q_{\mathrm{i}}^2\):
    \[|\vek v + \vek q|^2 = \sum_{\mathrm{i}} v_{\mathrm{i}}^2 + 2\sum_{\mathrm{i}} v_{\mathrm{i}}\,q_{\mathrm{i}} + \sum_{\mathrm{i}} q_{\mathrm{i}}^2 .\]
  4. The first sum is \(|\mat F\,\vek n|^2 = \vek n^\T\mat F^\T\mat F\,\vek n\), as we calculated before definition 1.112, and \(1 = \vek n^\T\mat I\,\vek n\). So \(\tfrac12\big(|\vek v|^2 - 1\big) = \vek n^\T\,\tfrac12(\mat F^\T\mat F - \mat I)\,\vek n = \vek n^\T\mat E\,\vek n\), and the first sum is the square of the length of the blue vector.
  5. From steps 2 to 4,
    \[g(h) = \frac12\Big(\frac{L_1^2}{L_0^2} - 1\Big) = \vek n^\T\mat E\,\vek n + \sum_{\mathrm{i}} v_{\mathrm{i}}\,q_{\mathrm{i}} + \frac12\sum_{\mathrm{i}} q_{\mathrm{i}}^2 .\]
    So we must bound the difference \(g(h) - \vek n^\T\mat E\,\vek n = \sum_{\mathrm{i}} v_{\mathrm{i}}\,q_{\mathrm{i}} + \tfrac12\sum_{\mathrm{i}} q_{\mathrm{i}}^2\), which is a sum of two pieces.
  6. Let \(V = |v_{\mathrm{x}}| + |v_{\mathrm{y}}| + |v_{\mathrm{z}}|\). Suppose that every component of the vector \(\vek q\) is at most \(\mu\) in absolute value, where \(0 < \mu \le 1\). The absolute value of a product is the product of the absolute values, and by the triangle inequality for numbers, used twice (lemma 1.6, items 2 and 1), \(\big|\sum_{\mathrm{i}} v_{\mathrm{i}}\,q_{\mathrm{i}}\big| \le \sum_{\mathrm{i}} |v_{\mathrm{i}}|\,|q_{\mathrm{i}}| \le V\,\mu\). Each \(q_{\mathrm{i}}^2\) is at most \(\mu^2\), and this is at most \(\mu\), because \(\mu \le 1\). So \(\tfrac12\sum_{\mathrm{i}} q_{\mathrm{i}}^2 \le \tfrac32\,\mu\). Altogether \(|g(h) - \vek n^\T\mat E\,\vek n| \le (V + \tfrac32)\,\mu\).
  7. We choose any error \(\eta > 0\). For \(\mu\) we take the smaller of the numbers \(1\) and \(\eta/(V + 2)\). The number \(\mu\) is positive.
  8. By the lemma on a short fibre after loading there is a \(\delta > 0\) such that \(|R_{\mathrm{x}}| \le \mu\,|h|\), \(|R_{\mathrm{y}}| \le \mu\,|h|\) and \(|R_{\mathrm{z}}| \le \mu\,|h|\) for every \(h\) with \(0 < |h| < \delta\). For such \(h\) every component of the vector \(\vek q\) has the absolute value \(|R_{\mathrm{i}}|/|h| \le \mu\).
  9. By step 6, for these \(h\) the difference is \(|g(h) - \vek n^\T\mat E\,\vek n| \le (V + \tfrac32)\,\mu < (V + 2)\,\mu \le \eta\). We chose the error \(\eta\) arbitrarily, so the condition of the definition of the limit is satisfied.

2. The strain. By step 4, \(|\vek v|^2 = 1 + 2\,\vek n^\T\mat E\,\vek n\), so \(|\vek v| = \sqrt{1 + 2\,\vek n^\T\mat E\,\vek n}\), and by assumption \(|\vek v| > 0\). We write the definition of the limit for the function \((L_1 - L_0)/L_0\) and the number \(|\vek v| - 1\).

  1. We rearrange the difference we must bound: \(\dfrac{L_1 - L_0}{L_0} - \big(|\vek v| - 1\big) = \dfrac{L_1}{L_0} - |\vek v|\).
  2. We multiply and divide by the positive number \(L_1/L_0 + |\vek v|\), as for (1.17). A difference of squares appears in the numerator:
    \[\frac{L_1}{L_0} - |\vek v| = \frac{L_1^2/L_0^2 - |\vek v|^2}{L_1/L_0 + |\vek v|} .\]
  3. The numerator is \((1 + 2g(h)) - (1 + 2\,\vek n^\T\mat E\,\vek n) = 2\big(g(h) - \vek n^\T\mat E\,\vek n\big)\), because \(L_1^2/L_0^2 = 1 + 2g(h)\). The denominator is not smaller than \(|\vek v|\), because \(L_1/L_0\) is not negative. So
    \[\Big|\frac{L_1}{L_0} - |\vek v|\Big| \le \frac{2\,|g(h) - \vek n^\T\mat E\,\vek n|}{|\vek v|} .\]
  4. We choose \(\eta > 0\). By item 1 there is a \(\delta > 0\) such that \(|g(h) - \vek n^\T\mat E\,\vek n| < \eta\,|\vek v|/2\) for every \(h\) with \(0 < |h| < \delta\). For these \(h\), by step 3, the difference is smaller than \(\eta\), which means that the limit equals \(|\vek v| - 1\).

Source: BOWER §2.1.5 (PDF pp. 47-48) and CM (3.4.8), (3.4.10) (PDF p. 129) write item 1 for an infinitesimally short fibre, without a limit. The proof with remainders is not from a source.

This is the main result of the section, so let us remember it. The nine partial derivatives of the displacement at the point \(P\) determine, through the matrix \(\mat E\), the strain of a short fibre in every direction through \(P\). For the direction we need only the unit vector \(\vek n\), and for the state of the material near the point only the six numbers of the matrix \(\mat E\). We assumed nothing about the size of the strains, so the theorem also holds for rubber stretched by half. The proof showed why it holds. After loading the vector of a short fibre differs from \(h\,\mat F\,\vek n\) only by the remainders, which become ever smaller after division by \(h\), and the square of the length of the vector \(h\,\mat F\,\vek n\) is \(h^2\) times a double sum with the matrix \(\mat F^\T\mat F\). The theorem does not hold where the field is not continuously differentiable, for example at a crack, and not on the surface of a body, where in some directions there is no fibre.

The theorem is also the Green-Lagrange strain of section 1.1, written in space. There, for a bar of length \(L\) that gets longer by \(\Delta L\), we wrote the quotient \(\big((L + \Delta L)^2 - L^2\big)/(2L^2)\). The left side of (1.49) is the same quotient for a short fibre. For a fibre along the axis \(x\), with \(\vek n = \vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\), only the term with \(\ix{j} = \ix{k} = x\) remains in the double sum \(\vek n^\T\mat E\,\vek n\), and it is \(E_{\mathrm{xx}}\). So the entry \(E_{\mathrm{xx}}\) is the Green-Lagrange strain of a short fibre along the axis \(x\) (CM (3.4.15), PDF p. 131). Where does the root in item 2 come from? From \(L_1 = L_0\,(1 + \varepsilon)\) we get \(L_1^2 / L_0^2 = (1 + \varepsilon)^2\), so \(1 + \varepsilon\) is the square root of \(L_1^2 / L_0^2\), which approaches \(1 + 2\,\vek n^\T\mat E\,\vek n\). We take the positive root because \(1 + \varepsilon = L_1 / L_0\) is positive.

What does the assumption that \(\mat F\,\vek n\) is not the zero vector mean? By lemma 1.111 on a short fibre after loading, a short fibre in the direction \(\vek n\) would otherwise be squeezed almost into a point: its length after loading would be small even compared with its original length \(|h|\). Matter cannot be squeezed so that a fibre disappears (CM, PDF pp. 119-120), so the assumption holds for every real body. It does not follow from the displacement field alone, so the theorem requires it. In the proof we need it in step 3 of item 2, where we divide by \(|\vek v|\). When all partial derivatives of the displacements are small, though, we get it by computation, as we will see in section 1.17.3 (step 8).

Let us test the theorem on the sheared cube. From its deformation gradient we get

\[\mat F^\T = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0{,}001 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} , \qquad \mat F^\T\mat F = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0{,}001 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0{,}001 & 0 & 1{,}000001 \end{bmatrix} .\]

For example, the entry in row \(z\) and column \(z\) is the product of row \(z\) of the matrix \(\mat F^\T\) with column \(z\) of the matrix \(\mat F\), that is, \(0{,}001 \cdot 0{,}001 + 0 \cdot 0 + 1 \cdot 1 = 1{,}000001\). So

\[\mat E = \tfrac12\big(\mat F^\T\mat F - \mat I\big) = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 & 0{,}0005 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0{,}0005 & 0 & 0{,}0000005 \end{bmatrix} .\]

The field of the cube is linear, so the remainders are zero, as we saw above, and in the proof \(\vek q\) is the zero vector. So for the cube the equalities (1.49) and (1.50) hold for every fibre, whatever its length, without a limit. Let us compare them with the table of exactly calculated strains in section 1.6.2. For the diagonal \(AC\) we have \(n_{\mathrm{x}} = n_{\mathrm{z}} = 1/\sqrt2\) and \(n_{\mathrm{y}} = 0\), so only the terms with the indices \(x\) and \(z\) remain in the double sum:

\[\begin{aligned} \vek n^\T\mat E\,\vek n &= E_{\mathrm{xx}}\,n_{\mathrm{x}}^2 + E_{\mathrm{xz}}\,n_{\mathrm{x}} n_{\mathrm{z}} + E_{\mathrm{zx}}\,n_{\mathrm{z}} n_{\mathrm{x}} + E_{\mathrm{zz}}\,n_{\mathrm{z}}^2 \\ &= 0 + 0{,}0005 \cdot \tfrac12 + 0{,}0005 \cdot \tfrac12 + 0{,}0000005 \cdot \tfrac12 = 0{,}00050025 . \end{aligned}\]

We calculate the other fibres in the same way.

fibre \(\vek n\) \(\vek n^\T\mat E\,\vek n\) \(\sqrt{1 + 2\,\vek n^\T\mat E\,\vek n} - 1\) calculated before
bottom edge \(AB\) \((1, 0, 0)\) \(0\) \(0\) \(0\)
vertical edge \(AD\) \((0, 0, 1)\) \(5 \cdot 10^{-7}\) \(5{,}0 \cdot 10^{-7}\) \(5{,}0 \cdot 10^{-7}\)
diagonal \(AC\) \((1, 0, 1)/\sqrt2\) \(5{,}0025 \cdot 10^{-4}\) \(+5{,}001 \cdot 10^{-4}\) \(+5{,}001 \cdot 10^{-4}\)
diagonal \(BD\) \((-1, 0, 1)/\sqrt2\) \(-4{,}9975 \cdot 10^{-4}\) \(-4{,}999 \cdot 10^{-4}\) \(-4{,}999 \cdot 10^{-4}\)

Everything agrees. This time, though, we did not calculate two lengths for each fibre separately, we only put its direction \(\vek n\) into the same matrix \(\mat E\).

For the hanging bar the remainders are not zero, and the theorem speaks about a limit. Take the fibre from the point \(P\) in the direction \(\vek n = (\tfrac13, \tfrac23, \tfrac23)\) of section 1.7.3. From the matrix \(\mat H\) at the point \(P\), lemma 1.113 gives

\[\mat E = \begin{bmatrix} 1{,}952002 \cdot 10^{-6} & -5{,}94 \cdot 10^{-16} & 0 \\ -5{,}94 \cdot 10^{-16} & -5{,}855998 \cdot 10^{-7} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -5{,}855998 \cdot 10^{-7} \end{bmatrix} .\]

The entries on the diagonal we get from (1.48), with \(H_{\mathrm{zx}} = H_{\mathrm{zy}} = 0\):

\[\begin{aligned} E_{\mathrm{xx}} &= H_{\mathrm{xx}} + \tfrac12\big(H_{\mathrm{xx}}^2 + H_{\mathrm{yx}}^2\big) = 1{,}952 \cdot 10^{-6} + 1{,}905 \cdot 10^{-12} = 1{,}952002 \cdot 10^{-6} , \\ E_{\mathrm{yy}} &= H_{\mathrm{yy}} + \tfrac12\big(H_{\mathrm{xy}}^2 + H_{\mathrm{yy}}^2\big) = -5{,}856 \cdot 10^{-7} + 1{,}715 \cdot 10^{-13} = -5{,}855998 \cdot 10^{-7} , \end{aligned}\]

the entry \(E_{\mathrm{zz}}\) in the same way, and in the digits shown it equals \(E_{\mathrm{yy}}\). The entry \(E_{\mathrm{xy}}\) we compute in section 1.17.3. In the double sum with \(n_{\mathrm{x}}^2 = \tfrac19\), \(n_{\mathrm{y}}^2 = n_{\mathrm{z}}^2 = \tfrac49\) and \(n_{\mathrm{x}} n_{\mathrm{y}} = \tfrac29\) four terms remain, because \(E_{\mathrm{xz}}\) and \(E_{\mathrm{yz}}\) are zero:

\[\begin{aligned} \vek n^\T\mat E\,\vek n &= \tfrac19\,E_{\mathrm{xx}} + \tfrac49\,E_{\mathrm{yy}} + \tfrac49\,E_{\mathrm{zz}} + 2 \cdot \tfrac29\,E_{\mathrm{xy}} \\ &= 2{,}168891 \cdot 10^{-7} - 2{,}602666 \cdot 10^{-7} - 2{,}602666 \cdot 10^{-7} - 2{,}6 \cdot 10^{-16} \\ &= -3{,}036441 \cdot 10^{-7} . \end{aligned}\]

For fibres of length 1 mm and 0.1 mm let us calculate the quotient \(g(h) = (L_1^2 - L_0^2)/(2L_0^2)\) exactly, from the field (1.18):

fibre length \(h\) \(g(h)\) difference from \(\vek n^\T\mat E\,\vek n\)
1 mm \(-3{,}036340 \cdot 10^{-7}\) \(1{,}01 \cdot 10^{-11}\)
0,1 mm \(-3{,}036431 \cdot 10^{-7}\) \(1{,}01 \cdot 10^{-12}\)

The quotient approaches \(\vek n^\T\mat E\,\vek n\), as the theorem says (figure 1.351). For a fibre ten times shorter the difference is ten times smaller, so the dot at 0.1 mm lies on the same line through the origin as the dot at 1 mm, only ten times lower. Why? For this field the remainders are proportional to \(h^2\) (section 1.7.3). The components of the vector \(\vek q\) of the proof are \(q_{\mathrm{i}} = R_{\mathrm{i}}/h\), so they are proportional to \(h\), and so is the main part of the difference, the sum \(\sum_{\mathrm{i}} v_{\mathrm{i}}\,q_{\mathrm{i}}\).

Let us draw the graph. The horizontal axis is the length of the fibre \(h\) in millimetres, from \(0\) to \(1\) mm. The vertical axis is the difference between the quotient \(g(h)\) and its limit \(\vek n^\T\mat E\,\vek n\), that is, how far the quotient still is from the limit. The dot at \(h = 1\) is the fibre of length 1 mm. The grey dashed guides from it point to the axes, saying that the difference is \(1{,}01 \cdot 10^{-11}\). The dot at \(h = 0{,}1\) is the fibre of length 0.1 mm and has the difference \(1{,}01 \cdot 10^{-12}\), ten times smaller. The thick line from the origin joins the two dots and is drawn through both dots and the origin, because the differences are in the ratio \(10 : 1\), like the lengths of the fibres, so the difference is proportional to the length of the fibre. The empty circle at the origin says that a fibre of length zero does not exist, so the point \(h = 0\) is not on the graph.

The strain of this fibre is negative, the fibre gets shorter, although its end moves down more than \(P\). Why, figure 1.352 below shows, where the fibre before loading is blackwhite. The fibre lies mostly across the bar: its part along the bar is \(h/3\), while the transverse part is \(\tfrac{\sqrt8}{3}\,h \approx 0{,}94\,h\), almost three times longer. Along the bar the material stretches, but across it the bar gets thinner, as we saw in section 1.6, and for this fibre the thinning prevails. We show this by computation in section 1.17.4.

Let us draw the fibre in the plane spanned by the axis of the bar and the transverse direction. The arrow \(x\) on the left points down, in the direction of the axis of the bar. The point \(P\) is the start of the fibre. The thin grey lines through \(P\) are the vertical axis of the bar and the horizontal transverse direction, from which we measure. The blackwhite segment to the point \(Q\) is the fibre before loading. It is slanted because the fibre has a part along the bar and a part across it. The grey dimension \(h/3\) is its part along the bar. The grey dimension at the top is the transverse part, \(\tfrac{\sqrt8}{3}\,h\), almost three times longer. The orange segment to the point \(Q_1\) is the fibre after loading. The orange dimension on the left is the longitudinal part after loading, longer by the factor \(1 + \varepsilon\), where \(\varepsilon = 1{,}952 \cdot 10^{-6}\) is the strain of the bar along its axis at the depth of the point \(P\), because the material stretches along the bar. The orange dimension at the bottom is the transverse part after loading, shorter by the factor \(1 - 0{,}3\,\varepsilon\), because the bar gets thinner, and the number \(0{,}3\) is the thinning ratio of steel. The deformation is greatly magnified: \(\varepsilon\) is drawn as \(0{,}4\) instead of \(1{,}952 \cdot 10^{-6}\). Since the transverse part prevails, the orange fibre is shorter than the blackwhite one.

The Green-Lagrange strain tensor is exact but awkward to compute, because each of its entries contains products of partial derivatives. For the hanging bar these products are extremely small. This leads us to a simplification.

1.17.3 Small deformations

Let us look at how large each part of the Green-Lagrange tensor is. By lemma 1.113, \(\mat E = \tfrac12(\mat H + \mat H^\T) + \tfrac12\,\mat H^\T\mat H\). The first part is linear in the partial derivatives: each of its entries is half the sum of two partial derivatives. The second part is quadratic: each of its entries is half the sum of three products of two partial derivatives. For the hanging bar at the point \(P\), \(E_{\mathrm{xx}}\) is the sum of the linear part \(1{,}952 \cdot 10^{-6}\) and the quadratic part

\[\tfrac12\big((1{,}952 \cdot 10^{-6})^2 + (4{,}685 \cdot 10^{-10})^2 + 0^2\big) = 1{,}905 \cdot 10^{-12} ,\]

which is a million times smaller. The entry \(E_{\mathrm{xy}}\) has no linear part, because the sum of the partial derivatives is \(-4{,}685 \cdot 10^{-10} + 4{,}685 \cdot 10^{-10} = 0\). Only the quadratic part remains,

\[\begin{aligned} &\tfrac12\big(1{,}952 \cdot 10^{-6} \cdot (-4{,}685 \cdot 10^{-10}) + 4{,}685 \cdot 10^{-10} \cdot (-5{,}856 \cdot 10^{-7}) + 0 \cdot 0\big) \\ &\qquad = -5{,}94 \cdot 10^{-16} . \end{aligned}\]

Since \(\partial u_{\mathrm{x}} / \partial y = -\partial u_{\mathrm{y}} / \partial x\) and the last product is zero, the sum in the bracket equals \(-\dfrac{\partial u_{\mathrm{y}}}{\partial x}\Big(\dfrac{\partial u_{\mathrm{x}}}{\partial x} - \dfrac{\partial u_{\mathrm{y}}}{\partial y}\Big)\). This is, with the opposite sign, the product that we mentioned in section 1.7.2 as the difference between the tilts of two fibres, about \(1{,}2 \cdot 10^{-15}\), and \(E_{\mathrm{xy}}\) is half of it. For the sheared cube the linear part of the entry \(E_{\mathrm{xz}}\) is \(0{,}0005\), and the quadratic part of the entry \(E_{\mathrm{zz}}\), which belongs to the vertical edge \(AD\), is \(\tfrac12 \cdot 0{,}001^2 = 5 \cdot 10^{-7}\), a thousand times less.

The horizontal axis shows values, each mark is ten times larger than the previous one, so the gap between powers always means the same factor \(10\). The number \(m\) is an upper bound of the absolute value of every partial derivative of the displacement, and we derive both bounds below from it. The three rows are three sizes of \(m\): at the top \(m = 10^{-1}\), in the middle \(m = 10^{-2}\) and at the bottom \(m = 10^{-3}\). In each row the blue dot \(m\) is the bound of the linear part, which can be as large as \(m\). The orange dot \(\tfrac32 m^2\) is the bound of the quadratic part. The grey dimension between them is the gap between the bounds. The empty orange circle \(\tfrac92\,m^2\) is the bound of the error of the formula that keeps only the linear part, which we use below. For a smaller \(m\) the gap is larger. At \(m = 10^{-3}\) the bound of the quadratic part is one and a half thousandths of the bound of the linear part.

This is the rule we met with the sheared cube: next to a small number, its square is smaller by about a factor of that small number. Let us write it precisely. Suppose that every partial derivative of the displacement at the point \(P\) is at most \(m\) in absolute value. Then each of the three products in the entry \((\mat H^\T\mat H)_{\mathrm{ij}} = \sum_{\mathrm{k}} H_{\mathrm{ki}}\,H_{\mathrm{kj}}\) is at most \(m \cdot m\) in absolute value, their sum at most \(3m^2\), and the quadratic part of the entry \(E_{\mathrm{ij}}\) at most \(\tfrac32 m^2\). The linear part can be as large as \(m\). For \(m = 0{,}001\) the quadratic part of every entry is at most \(1{,}5 \cdot 10^{-6}\), one and a half thousandths of the largest size of the linear part. For the hanging bar \(m = 1{,}952 \cdot 10^{-6}\), and the calculated quadratic part \(1{,}905 \cdot 10^{-12}\) is indeed below the bound \(\tfrac32 m^2 = 5{,}7 \cdot 10^{-12}\).

From history

In the autumn of 1822 Cauchy showed how to calculate the elongation of every short line through a point from the derivatives of the displacements (LOVE, PDF p. 25). In an article on the condensation and dilatation of solid bodies, published in 1827, he described the change of shape by six numbers and three perpendicular directions, as we saw in section 1.1 (LOVE, PDF p. 25). In 1847 Saint-Venant treated the question of when a body is at rest if the displacements are not very small (LOVE, PDF p. 78). Exact deformation that is not limited to small displacements, such as the Green-Lagrange tensor of section 1.17, was treated by Love only in an appendix to the first chapter of his book. He regarded it as an interesting branch of kinematics and remarked that the rest of his book does not need it (LOVE, PDF p. 78).

From the estimate that the quadratic part of the entry \(E_{\mathrm{ij}}\) is much smaller than the linear part when the partial derivatives of the displacement are small follows the assumption that we will use throughout the book unless we say otherwise.

  • Small deformation assumption (predpostavka majhnih deformacij): all partial derivatives of the displacements at the point \(P\) are at most \(m\) in absolute value, where the number \(m\) is small compared with \(1\).

How small \(m\) must be, we show below in steps 5 to 9: for \(m < \tfrac13\) the strain of a short fibre in any direction differs from the formula that keeps only the linear part by at most \(4{,}5\,m^2\). Compared with \(m\), the bound for the partial derivatives, this is at most \(4{,}5\,m\):

\(m\) error bound \(4{,}5\,m^2\) compared with \(m\)
\(0{,}001\) \(4{,}5 \cdot 10^{-6}\) \(0{,}45\) %
\(0{,}01\) \(4{,}5 \cdot 10^{-4}\) \(4{,}5\) %
\(0{,}1\) \(0{,}045\) \(45\) %

Let us draw the ruler. The hatched line on the left is the wall to which the ruler is fixed at the left end. The grey dashed rectangle is the ruler before bending, \(L = 300\) mm long, as the dimension \(L\) at the bottom shows. The dimension \(t\) at the wall is its thickness, \(1\) mm. The thickness is drawn about 25 times too large so that it can be seen. The orange arc is the ruler after bending: a circular arc that starts horizontally at the wall. The end of the arc is the free end of the ruler. The grey lines from its middle show the horizontal direction and the direction of the end, the angle between them is the turn \(\varphi = 30^\circ\). The middle line of the ruler stays \(L\) long, so \(L = R\varphi\) and the radius of the arc is \(R = L/\varphi \approx 573\) mm. The outer surface is farther from the centre of the arc by \(t/2\), so its arc is longer by the factor \((R + t/2)/R\) and the strain of the surface is \(t/(2R) \approx 0{,}00087\), less than \(0{,}001\).

In steel structures the assumption for the strains is justified by section 1.1: the strains of steel are almost always smaller than \(0{,}001\), because at larger strains steel deforms permanently. The name of the assumption is somewhat misleading, though, because it asks for more than small strains. The partial derivatives also describe how the material turns, and in section 1.17.6 we will see a body that does not deform at all, while its partial derivatives are not small. For the turns there is no such reason. We can bend a thin steel ruler into an arc, and when we let go it straightens again. So its strains stayed below about \(0{,}001\), while its end turned visibly. The smallness of the turns therefore has to be checked separately for every structure. We now use the assumption by leaving out the quadratic part.

Definition 1.115 Small strain tensor (tenzor malih deformacij)

Let \(\mat H\) be the displacement gradient at an interior point \(P\) of a body. The small strain tensor at the point \(P\) (tenzor malih deformacij) is the matrix

\[\ten\varepsilon = \tfrac12\big(\mat H + \mat H^\T\big) , \tag{1.51}\]

with the entries \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}} = \tfrac12(H_{\mathrm{ij}} + H_{\mathrm{ji}})\), written out, with all partial derivatives at the point \(P\),

\[\begin{aligned} \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} &= \frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{x}}}{\partial x} , \qquad \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} = \frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{y}}}{\partial y} , \qquad \varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}} = \frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{z}}}{\partial z} , \\ \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}} &= \frac12\Big(\frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{x}}}{\partial y} + \frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{y}}}{\partial x}\Big) , \\ \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}} &= \frac12\Big(\frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{x}}}{\partial z} + \frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{z}}}{\partial x}\Big) , \\ \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yz}} &= \frac12\Big(\frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{y}}}{\partial z} + \frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{z}}}{\partial y}\Big) , \end{aligned} \tag{1.52}\]

and \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yx}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}\), \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{zx}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}}\) and \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{zy}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yz}}\).

Source: CM (3.5.3)-(3.5.5) (PDF p. 141), SADD (2.1.7) (PDF p. 40) and (2.2.5) (PDF p. 43), BOWER §2.1.7 (PDF pp. 49-50).

The small strain tensor is a symmetric matrix, since \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\) does not change when the indices are swapped. It is the symmetric part of the matrix \(\mat H\) (lemma 1.103 on the split into symmetric and antisymmetric parts) and has six different entries. The Green-Lagrange tensor differs from it only by the quadratic part, \(\mat E = \ten\varepsilon + \tfrac12\,\mat H^\T\mat H\). CM calls it the infinitesimal strain tensor (tenzor infinitezimalnih deformacij) (CM §3.5.1, PDF pp. 140-141), SADD simply the strain tensor, written \(e_{\mathrm{ij}}\) (SADD (2.1.7), PDF p. 40). For the hanging bar at the point \(P\),

\[\ten\varepsilon = \begin{bmatrix} 1{,}952 \cdot 10^{-6} & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -5{,}856 \cdot 10^{-7} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -5{,}856 \cdot 10^{-7} \end{bmatrix} ,\]

and for the sheared cube

\[\ten\varepsilon = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 & 0{,}0005 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0{,}0005 & 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix} .\]

What remains of theorem 1.114 on the strain of a short fibre? We denote the strain of a short fibre in the direction \(\vek n\), that is, the limit (1.50), by \(\varepsilon(\vek n)\). The vector in the brackets reminds us that this is a strain in a direction, not the strain \(\varepsilon(x)\) of a bar at the point \(x\). The theorem gives it when \(\mat F\,\vek n\) is not the zero vector, and for small partial derivatives this always holds, as we show in step 8. Let us show in steps how \(\varepsilon(\vek n)\) differs from the double sum with the matrix \(\ten\varepsilon\).

  1. From (1.50), \(1 + \varepsilon(\vek n) = \sqrt{1 + 2\,\vek n^\T\mat E\,\vek n}\). We square and multiply out \((1 + \varepsilon(\vek n))^2 = 1 + 2\varepsilon(\vek n) + \varepsilon(\vek n)^2\). Subtracting \(1\) and dividing by \(2\) gives exactly
    \[\vek n^\T\mat E\,\vek n = \varepsilon(\vek n) + \tfrac12\,\varepsilon(\vek n)^2 .\]
  2. We substitute \(\mat E = \ten\varepsilon + \tfrac12\,\mat H^\T\mat H\). A double sum with a sum of matrices is the sum of the double sums, because every term \(n_{\mathrm{j}}\,(A_{\mathrm{jk}} + B_{\mathrm{jk}})\,n_{\mathrm{k}}\) splits into two. So \(\vek n^\T\mat E\,\vek n = \vek n^\T\ten\varepsilon\,\vek n + \tfrac12\,\vek n^\T\mat H^\T\mat H\,\vek n\).
  3. The double sum \(\vek n^\T\mat H^\T\mat H\,\vek n\) is the square of the length of the vector \(\mat H\,\vek n\), \(|\mat H\,\vek n|^2\). The same steps 2 to 5 as for \(|\mat F\,\vek n|^2\) before definition 1.112 show this, only with \(\mat H\) instead of \(\mat F\).
  4. Steps 1 to 3 give the exact equality
    \[\varepsilon(\vek n) = \vek n^\T\ten\varepsilon\,\vek n + \tfrac12\,|\mat H\,\vek n|^2 - \tfrac12\,\varepsilon(\vek n)^2 .\]
  5. The two corrections on the right are halves of squares of two numbers, the strain \(\varepsilon(\vek n)\) and the length \(|\mat H\,\vek n|\). What does the vector \(\mat H\,\vek n\) measure? By lemma 1.111 on a short fibre after loading, the difference of the displacements of the ends of the fibre equals, up to the remainders, \(\mat H\,(h\,\vek n) = h\,\mat H\,\vek n\). So the vector \(\mat H\,\vek n\) is the displacement of the end \(Q\) relative to the start \(P\), divided by \(h\). We denote it by \(\vek w = \mat H\,\vek n\). In figure 1.355, \(h\,\vek w\) is the blue displacement of the end. We will bound the length \(|\vek w|\) by the number \(m\) from the small deformation assumption (step 7). We will not bound the strain \(\varepsilon(\vek n)\): in step 8 we compare it with the number \(t\), and in step 9 the correction \(-\tfrac12\,\varepsilon(\vek n)^2\) drops out, because it is not positive.

The point \(P\) is the start of the fibre, drawn relative to \(P\), that is, without the common displacement \(\vek u(P)\). The blackwhite segment to \(Q\) is the fibre \(h\,\vek n\) before loading. The orange segment from \(P\) to \(Q_1\) is the same fibre after loading, of length \(L_1\). We do not draw the remainders and everything is greatly magnified. The blue dimension from \(Q\) to \(Q_1\) is the displacement of the end, \(h\,\vek w\). We split it into two perpendicular parts. The part along the fibre has length \(h\,t\) and shows the lengthening of the fibre. The part across it has length \(h\,p\), and the right angle between them shows that they are perpendicular. The bottom dimension has length \((1 + t)\,h\), that is, the fibre together with the longitudinal part of the displacement. This dimension and the transverse part are the legs of a right triangle, and the fibre after loading is its hypotenuse. So it is never shorter than \((1 + t)\,h\).

Let us draw why this holds, on the made-up numbers \(b = 0{,}7\) and \(d = 0{,}3\). The large square has the side \(b + d\), which is made of the length \(b\) and the length \(d\). The two blue squares in opposite corners have the areas \(b^2\) and \(d^2\). The two grey rectangles each have the area \(b\,d\), together \(2bd\). The two blue squares together cover more area than the two grey rectangles, by \((b - d)^2\), which is not negative.

  1. First we bound the sum of the absolute values of the components of the unit vector \(\vek n\). For nonnegative numbers \(b\) and \(d\) we have \(2bd \le b^2 + d^2\), because the difference \(b^2 + d^2 - 2bd = (b - d)^2\) is a square and therefore not negative. We use this for all three pairs of numbers \(|n_{\mathrm{x}}|\), \(|n_{\mathrm{y}}|\) and \(|n_{\mathrm{z}}|\), whose squares are \(n_{\mathrm{x}}^2\), \(n_{\mathrm{y}}^2\) and \(n_{\mathrm{z}}^2\):
    \[\begin{aligned} \big(|n_{\mathrm{x}}| + |n_{\mathrm{y}}| + |n_{\mathrm{z}}|\big)^2 &= n_{\mathrm{x}}^2 + n_{\mathrm{y}}^2 + n_{\mathrm{z}}^2 + 2|n_{\mathrm{x}}|\,|n_{\mathrm{y}}| + 2|n_{\mathrm{x}}|\,|n_{\mathrm{z}}| + 2|n_{\mathrm{y}}|\,|n_{\mathrm{z}}| \\ &\le 1 + (n_{\mathrm{x}}^2 + n_{\mathrm{y}}^2) + (n_{\mathrm{x}}^2 + n_{\mathrm{z}}^2) + (n_{\mathrm{y}}^2 + n_{\mathrm{z}}^2) = 1 + 2 = 3 . \end{aligned}\]
    By lemma 1.28, that a larger nonnegative number has a larger square, it follows that \(|n_{\mathrm{x}}| + |n_{\mathrm{y}}| + |n_{\mathrm{z}}| \le \sqrt3\).
  2. The length of the vector \(\vek w\). Its component \(\ix{i}\) is \(w_{\mathrm{i}} = \sum_{\mathrm{j}} H_{\mathrm{ij}}\,n_{\mathrm{j}}\). By the triangle inequality for numbers and the rule for the absolute value of a product (lemma 1.6) and by step 6,
    \[|w_{\mathrm{i}}| \le \sum_{\mathrm{j}} |H_{\mathrm{ij}}|\,|n_{\mathrm{j}}| \le m\,\big(|n_{\mathrm{x}}| + |n_{\mathrm{y}}| + |n_{\mathrm{z}}|\big) \le \sqrt3\,m .\]
    So \(|\vek w|^2 = w_{\mathrm{x}}^2 + w_{\mathrm{y}}^2 + w_{\mathrm{z}}^2 \le 3 \cdot 3m^2 = 9m^2\), by lemma 1.28 \(|\vek w| \le 3m\), and the first correction is at most \(\tfrac12 \cdot 9m^2 = 4{,}5\,m^2\). The factor \(3\) cannot be reduced. If all entries of the matrix \(\mat H\) equal \(m\) and \(\vek n = (1, 1, 1)/\sqrt3\), each component of the vector \(\vek w\) is a sum of three equal products, \(3 \cdot m/\sqrt3 = \sqrt3\,m\), and \(|\vek w| = \sqrt{3 \cdot 3m^2} = 3m\). For \(m = 0{,}001\) the end of the fibre can therefore move relative to \(P\) by \(0{,}003\) of the length of the fibre, three times the largest partial derivative.
  3. The strain of the fibre. We write the vector \(\vek w\) as the sum \(t\,\vek n + (\vek w - t\,\vek n)\), where \(t = \sum_{\mathrm{i}} n_{\mathrm{i}}\,w_{\mathrm{i}}\). The first part is the part of the displacement along the fibre, the second the part across it, and we denote the square of the length of the second part by \(p^2\). Since \(\sum_{\mathrm{i}} n_{\mathrm{i}}^2 = 1\),
    \[p^2 = \sum_{\mathrm{i}} (w_{\mathrm{i}} - t\,n_{\mathrm{i}})^2 = \sum_{\mathrm{i}} w_{\mathrm{i}}^2 - 2t \sum_{\mathrm{i}} n_{\mathrm{i}}\,w_{\mathrm{i}} + t^2 \sum_{\mathrm{i}} n_{\mathrm{i}}^2 = |\vek w|^2 - t^2 .\]
    The sum of squares \(p^2\) is not negative, so \(t^2 \le |\vek w|^2\) and by lemma 1.28 \(|t| \le |\vek w| \le 3m\). We write the square of the length of the vector \(\mat F\,\vek n = \vek n + \vek w\) component by component, as in step 3 of the proof of theorem 1.114:
    \[|\mat F\,\vek n|^2 = 1 + 2t + |\vek w|^2 = 1 + 2t + t^2 + p^2 = (1 + t)^2 + p^2 .\]
    So the fibre after loading is the hypotenuse of a right triangle with the leg \((1 + t)\,h\) along the original direction and the transverse leg \(p\,h\). For \(m < \tfrac13\) we have \(1 + t \ge 1 - 3m > 0\). So \(\mat F\,\vek n\) is not the zero vector, item 2 of the theorem holds, and by its proof \(1 + \varepsilon(\vek n) = |\mat F\,\vek n|\). Since \(|\mat F\,\vek n|^2 \ge (1 + t)^2\) and the numbers \(|\mat F\,\vek n|\) and \(1 + t\) are positive, by lemma 1.28 \(1 + \varepsilon(\vek n) \ge 1 + t\), so \(\varepsilon(\vek n) \ge t\).
  4. The number \(t\) is the double sum with the matrix \(\ten\varepsilon\). We have \(t = \sum_{\mathrm{i}} n_{\mathrm{i}} \sum_{\mathrm{j}} H_{\mathrm{ij}}\,n_{\mathrm{j}} = \sum_{\mathrm{i}} \sum_{\mathrm{j}} n_{\mathrm{i}}\,H_{\mathrm{ij}}\,n_{\mathrm{j}}\), and this sum does not change if we replace \(H_{\mathrm{ij}}\) by \(H_{\mathrm{ji}}\), because that only renames the indices. So \(t = \sum_{\mathrm{i}} \sum_{\mathrm{j}} n_{\mathrm{i}}\,\tfrac12(H_{\mathrm{ij}} + H_{\mathrm{ji}})\,n_{\mathrm{j}} = \vek n^\T\ten\varepsilon\,\vek n\). The formula with the small strain tensor therefore takes only the part of the displacement of the end along the fibre. From step 8 and the equality in step 4 it follows that
    \[0 \le \varepsilon(\vek n) - \vek n^\T\ten\varepsilon\,\vek n = \tfrac12\,|\vek w|^2 - \tfrac12\,\varepsilon(\vek n)^2 \le \tfrac12\,|\vek w|^2 \le 4{,}5\,m^2 .\]
    So the small strain tensor never overestimates the strain of a fibre, and underestimates it by at most \(4{,}5\,m^2\). It underestimates it because the transverse part of the displacement tilts the fibre and lengthens it a little in doing so, as the hypotenuse is longer than the leg. In the example of step 7 there is no transverse part, because \(\vek w = 3m\,\vek n\), and there is no error. The error is large when the displacement of the end is mostly transverse, as for the vertical edge \(AD\) below. The estimate needs exactly the small deformation assumption with \(m < \tfrac13\). When the partial derivatives are not small, the error can be large, as we will see in section 1.17.6. We leave out the corrections:
    \[\varepsilon(\vek n) \approx \vek n^\T\ten\varepsilon\,\vek n = \sum_{\mathrm{i}} \sum_{\mathrm{j}} \varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}\,n_{\mathrm{i}}\,n_{\mathrm{j}} .\]
  5. We write out the double sum. The terms with \(\ix{i} = \ix{j}\) give \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\,n_{\mathrm{x}}^2 + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}}\,n_{\mathrm{y}}^2 + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}}\,n_{\mathrm{z}}^2\). The terms with \(\ix{i} \neq \ix{j}\) come in pairs, for example \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}\,n_{\mathrm{x}} n_{\mathrm{y}}\) and \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yx}}\,n_{\mathrm{y}} n_{\mathrm{x}}\), which are equal because \(\ten\varepsilon\) is symmetric. Each pair gives twice one term:
    \[\begin{aligned} \varepsilon(\vek n) &\approx \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\,n_{\mathrm{x}}^2 + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}}\,n_{\mathrm{y}}^2 + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}}\,n_{\mathrm{z}}^2 \\ &\quad + 2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}\,n_{\mathrm{x}} n_{\mathrm{y}} + 2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}}\,n_{\mathrm{x}} n_{\mathrm{z}} + 2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yz}}\,n_{\mathrm{y}} n_{\mathrm{z}} . \end{aligned} \tag{1.53}\]

This is the formula we will use most often. We need it whenever we care about stretching in a direction that is not an axis, for example along the diagonal of a cube or along a slanted fibre of a bar. From six numbers at the point \(P\) it gives the strain of a short fibre in every direction through \(P\), with no roots and no products of partial derivatives (CM (3.5.6), PDF p. 142, BOWER, PDF p. 50, SADD (2.3.3), PDF p. 47). Let us test it on our fibres.

  • The diagonal \(AC\) of the sheared cube, \(\vek n = (1, 0, 1)/\sqrt2\): the formula gives \(2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}}\,n_{\mathrm{x}} n_{\mathrm{z}} = 2 \cdot 0{,}0005 \cdot \tfrac12 = 0{,}0005\), the exact strain is \(5{,}0012 \cdot 10^{-4}\). The corrections of step 4 are \(\tfrac12|\mat H\,\vek n|^2 = 2{,}5 \cdot 10^{-7}\) and \(-\tfrac12\,\varepsilon(\vek n)^2 = -1{,}25 \cdot 10^{-7}\), and their sum \(1{,}25 \cdot 10^{-7}\) is exactly the difference.
  • The fibre from the point \(P\) of the hanging bar in the direction \(\vek n = (\tfrac13, \tfrac23, \tfrac23)\): the formula gives
    \[\begin{aligned} &1{,}952 \cdot 10^{-6} \cdot \tfrac19 - 5{,}856 \cdot 10^{-7} \cdot \tfrac49 - 5{,}856 \cdot 10^{-7} \cdot \tfrac49 \\ &\qquad = 2{,}168889 \cdot 10^{-7} - 5{,}205333 \cdot 10^{-7} = -3{,}036444 \cdot 10^{-7} , \end{aligned}\]
    the exact strain \(\varepsilon(\vek n) = \sqrt{1 + 2\,\vek n^\T\mat E\,\vek n} - 1\) is \(-3{,}036441 \cdot 10^{-7}\). On the digits shown they differ by \(3 \cdot 10^{-13}\). We get the difference more precisely from the corrections of step 4. We computed the vector \(\mat H\,\vek n = (6{,}5035 \cdot 10^{-7},\ -3{,}9024 \cdot 10^{-7},\ -3{,}9040 \cdot 10^{-7})\) in section 1.16.2, so
    \[\tfrac12\,|\mat H\,\vek n|^2 - \tfrac12\,\varepsilon(\vek n)^2 = 3{,}638 \cdot 10^{-13} - 0{,}461 \cdot 10^{-13} = 3{,}2 \cdot 10^{-13} ,\]
    almost a million times less than the strain.
  • The vertical edge \(AD\) of the sheared cube, \(\vek n = (0, 0, 1)\): the formula gives \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}} = 0\), but the exact strain is \(5{,}0 \cdot 10^{-7}\). Here the whole shift of the end is transverse: \(\mat H\,\vek n = (0{,}001, 0, 0)\), so \(t = 0\) and \(p = 0{,}001\). The term we keep vanishes, and only the correction \(\tfrac12|\mat H\,\vek n|^2 = \tfrac12 \cdot 0{,}001^2\) remains.
