After loading the edge is the hypotenuse with the vertical leg \(h\) and the horizontal leg \(s = 0{,}001\,h\):
    \[L_1 = \sqrt{h^2 + (0{,}001\,h)^2} = h\,\sqrt{1 + 10^{-6}} \approx h\,(1 + 5 \cdot 10^{-7}) .\]
    This is the vertical edge of section 1.6.2, which only tilts and whose strain grows with the square of the shift. The error \(5 \cdot 10^{-7}\) is small compared with the strains we care about, but it is not small compared with zero. The small strain tensor says that the edge does not get longer, while in fact it gets longer by a thousand times less than the diagonals.

Figure 1.357 shows \(\varepsilon(\vek n)\) for all directions in one plane, on the left for the cube, on the right for the bar.

For the cube take the directions in the plane \(x\)-\(z\), \(\vek n = (n_{\mathrm{x}}, 0, n_{\mathrm{z}})\), where \(n_{\mathrm{z}} = \sqrt{1 - n_{\mathrm{x}}^2}\). A fibre and the opposite fibre have the same strain, because in (1.53) all terms are products of two components of the direction, and these do not change when both change sign. So the directions with \(n_{\mathrm{z}} \ge 0\) are enough. By (1.53), \(\varepsilon(\vek n) = 2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}}\,n_{\mathrm{x}} n_{\mathrm{z}} = 0{,}001\,n_{\mathrm{x}} n_{\mathrm{z}}\). Why are the extreme values exactly in the directions of the diagonals? The square of the product is \(n_{\mathrm{x}}^2 n_{\mathrm{z}}^2 = n_{\mathrm{x}}^2\,(1 - n_{\mathrm{x}}^2) = \tfrac14 - \big(n_{\mathrm{x}}^2 - \tfrac12\big)^2\), which is never larger than \(\tfrac14\) and equals \(\tfrac14\) exactly for \(n_{\mathrm{x}}^2 = \tfrac12\). So \(|n_{\mathrm{x}} n_{\mathrm{z}}| \le \tfrac12\), and the strain is largest, \(0{,}0005\), in the direction of the diagonal \(AC\) and smallest, \(-0{,}0005\), in the direction of the diagonal \(BD\). The graph of the cube has at \(-n_{\mathrm{x}}\) the opposite value from that at \(n_{\mathrm{x}}\), because the product \(n_{\mathrm{x}} n_{\mathrm{z}}\) only changes into its negative. The direction with \(-n_{\mathrm{x}}\) is the mirror image of the direction with \(n_{\mathrm{x}}\), and a shear that lengthens one diagonal shortens the other. Near \(n_{\mathrm{x}} = \pm 1\) the graph is steep, because there \(n_{\mathrm{z}} = \sqrt{1 - n_{\mathrm{x}}^2}\) changes quickly: even a small turn of the direction away from the axis \(x\) gives a noticeable \(n_{\mathrm{z}}\). For the hanging bar at the point \(P\) take the directions in the plane \(x\)-\(y\), \(\vek n = (n_{\mathrm{x}}, n_{\mathrm{y}}, 0)\). There \(\varepsilon(\vek n) = 1{,}952 \cdot 10^{-6}\,n_{\mathrm{x}}^2 - 5{,}856 \cdot 10^{-7}\,(1 - n_{\mathrm{x}}^2)\): it is largest along the bar and smallest across it, and the fibres with \(|n_{\mathrm{x}}| = 0{,}48\) do not change their length. We calculate this number in section 1.17.4.

1.17.4 What the components mean

The formula (1.53) keeps the promise of section 1.1. The strain of a short fibre in every direction through the point \(P\) is determined by six numbers, \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\), \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}}\), \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}}\), \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}\), \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}}\) and \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yz}}\), and we need nothing else for it (SADD §2.2, PDF p. 43). What does each of them measure?

Let us start with the numbers with equal indices. For a fibre along the axis \(x\), with \(\vek n = (1, 0, 0)\), only the first term remains in (1.53), \(\varepsilon(\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}) \approx \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\). So the number \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\) is the relative change of length of a short fibre along the axis \(x\), the normal strain in the direction of the axis \(x\) (definition 1.3). In the same way \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}}\) and \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}}\) are the normal strains in the directions of the axes \(y\) and \(z\). When there are no shear strains, a small cube of material with edge \(h\) and edges along the axes becomes a box with the edges \((1 + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}})\,h\), \((1 + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}})\,h\) and \((1 + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}})\,h\) (figure 1.358). For the hanging bar, which hangs under its own weight with the axis \(x\) pointing down, on the axis \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = \partial u_{\mathrm{x}} / \partial x = 2a\,(L - x)\), which is the strain at a point from definition 1.10. So the strain at a point that we defined for the bar in section 1.4 is the component \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\) of the small strain tensor.

The axes on the left show \(x\) to the right, \(y\) back into the depth and \(z\) upwards. The blackwhite cube is a small piece of material before loading, the grey dashed edges are those that the body hides. Each edge is \(h\) long: the one at the front in the direction of the axis \(x\), the one at the side in the direction of the axis \(y\) and the one at the left edge in the direction of the axis \(z\). The point \(P\) is the bottom front left corner. The orange box is the same piece after loading, when only the normal strains are different from zero, its hidden edges are again grey dashed. The right angles stay right angles, because there are no shear strains. The edge along the axis \(x\) is \((1 + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}})\,h\) long, the edge along the axis \(y\) is \((1 + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}})\,h\) long and the edge along the axis \(z\) is \((1 + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}})\,h\) long. In the figure \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}}\) is negative, so the edge along the axis \(y\) is shorter than \(h\). The strains are greatly magnified so that the differences can be seen.

And the numbers with different indices? A fibre along a diagonal gives the answer. A fibre in the direction \(\vek n = (1, 1, 0)/\sqrt2\) has \(n_{\mathrm{x}}^2 = n_{\mathrm{y}}^2 = n_{\mathrm{x}} n_{\mathrm{y}} = \tfrac12\) and \(n_{\mathrm{z}} = 0\), so by (1.53)

\[\varepsilon\big((1, 1, 0)/\sqrt2\big) \approx \tfrac12\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} + \tfrac12\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}} ,\]

and for the other diagonal, \(\vek n = (-1, 1, 0)/\sqrt2\) with \(n_{\mathrm{x}} n_{\mathrm{y}} = -\tfrac12\),

\[\varepsilon\big((-1, 1, 0)/\sqrt2\big) \approx \tfrac12\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} + \tfrac12\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} - \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}} .\]

The axes on the left show \(x\) to the right and \(y\) upwards. The point \(P\) is the corner of the square, and the blackwhite square is a small piece of material before loading, drawn relative to \(P\). Its edges are \(h\) in the direction of the axis \(x\) and \(h\) in the direction of the axis \(y\) long. The small grey angle at \(P\) is the right angle between them. The orange rhombus is the same piece after loading, when only the shear strain \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}\) is different from zero. The grey dimensions show by how much the end points of the edges move: the end of the edge along the axis \(x\) up by \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}\,h\), the end of the edge along the axis \(y\) to the right by the same distance. So the edges tilt towards each other, and the orange angle at \(P\) is smaller than a right angle. The lengths of the edges change only by terms with the square of \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}\), so almost not at all. The first diagonal from \(P\) is grey before loading, orange after it and longer. Both lie on the same line, so the grey one is drawn wider under the orange one and is seen as an edge beside it. The second diagonal is grey before loading, orange after it and shorter. The deformation is greatly magnified.

So the number \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}\) tells by how much the first diagonal stretches more than the average of the fibres along the axes \(x\) and \(y\), and the second by as much less. The difference between the two diagonals is \(2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}\). When \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}\) is the only nonzero component, the fibres along the axes do not get longer, one diagonal gets longer and the other shorter (figure 1.359). This is the deck of cards of section 1.1.

We see the same number in the tilt of the fibres. By the columns of the matrix \(\mat F\) (figure 1.346), a short fibre along the axis \(x\) tilts towards the axis \(y\): its end moves in the direction of the axis \(y\) by \(\partial u_{\mathrm{y}} / \partial x\) times the length of the fibre. A fibre along the axis \(y\) tilts towards the axis \(x\) by \(\partial u_{\mathrm{x}} / \partial y\) times the length. Both ratios of the sideways shift of the end to the length of the fibre are numbers without a unit, and their sum is

\[\frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{y}}}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{x}}}{\partial y} = 2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}} .\]

Let us draw the left half. The point \(P\) is the common start of both fibres. The blackwhite fibres from \(P\) lie along the axes, the horizontal fibre along the axis \(x\) and the vertical one along the axis \(y\). The orange fibres are the same fibres after loading, both tilted, their lengths stay the same. The end of the fibre along the axis \(x\) has moved up, the grey dimension beside it shows this sideways shift, \(\tfrac{\partial u_{\mathrm{y}}}{\partial x}\,h\). The end of the fibre along the axis \(y\) has moved to the right, the grey dimension above it shows \(\tfrac{\partial u_{\mathrm{x}}}{\partial y}\,h\). Both ratios are positive, so the fibres tilt towards each other. The grey arc shows that the angle between them gets smaller.

The right half is drawn in the same way, with the point \(P\), the blackwhite fibres along the axis \(x\) and the axis \(y\), and the orange ones after loading. The shift beside the fibre along the axis \(x\) is again upwards and the same as before. The shift beside the fibre along the axis \(y\) is now to the left. The dimension is \(-\tfrac{\partial u_{\mathrm{x}}}{\partial y}\,h\) long, because \(\tfrac{\partial u_{\mathrm{x}}}{\partial y}\) is negative here. The ratios are equal and of opposite signs, so the fibres turn in the same sense. The grey right-angle mark says that the angle between them stays a right angle.

When both ratios are positive, the fibres tilt towards each other, and the right angle between the positive directions of the axes \(x\) and \(y\) gets smaller. The sum tells by how much. But when the ratios are equal and of opposite signs, the sum is zero. Then the fibres tilt in the same sense of turning, and the right angle stays a right angle, as for the hanging bar in section 1.7.2 (figure 1.102). The shear strain \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}\) therefore measures the part of the tilting that changes the right angle. We will know how to measure angles between vectors in chapter 2, and there we will show exactly how \(2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}\) is related to the decrease of the right angle (CM (3.5.9), PDF p. 142, SADD (2.2.3), PDF p. 43). SADD fixes the sign in the same way: the shear strain is positive when the right angle between the positive directions of the axes decreases (SADD, PDF p. 43).

Let us test both on the sheared cube (figure 1.342, right), which is glued to the table by its bottom face and whose top face moves by \(s = 10\) µm at the height \(h = 10\,000\) µm. There \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}} = 0{,}0005 = s/(2h)\), and the other components are zero. The vertical edge \(AD\) tilts in the direction of the axis \(x\) by the ratio \(\partial u_{\mathrm{x}} / \partial z = 0{,}001 = s/h\), while the bottom edge \(AB\) does not tilt, because \(\partial u_{\mathrm{z}} / \partial x = 0\). The sum of the ratios is \(0{,}001 = 2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}}\). The diagonals have the strains \(\pm\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}} = \pm 0{,}0005\), because \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\) and \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}}\) are zero. Now we see where the half came from in section 1.6.2, where the diagonals changed by half the ratio \(s/h\). The tilt \(s/h\) of the edge is the sum of both ratios, \(2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}}\), while a diagonal stretches only by \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}}\).

This half is a source of frequent mistakes. Many books and programs for structural calculations use, instead of \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}\), the sum of both ratios, the engineering shear strain (inženirska strižna deformacija)

\[\gamma_{\mathrm{xy}} = \frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{x}}}{\partial y} + \frac{\partial u_{\mathrm{y}}}{\partial x} = 2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}} ,\]

and likewise \(\gamma_{\mathrm{xz}} = 2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}}\) and \(\gamma_{\mathrm{yz}} = 2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yz}}\) (SADD (2.2.4), PDF p. 43, CM, PDF p. 141). BOWER warns that this factor of \(2\) is an endless source of confusion, and advises us to check, for every shear strain reported, which of the two is meant (BOWER §2.1.8, PDF p. 51). In this book a shear strain will always be \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}}\), because with it the formula (1.53) is a plain double sum with a symmetric matrix. For the cube \(\gamma_{\mathrm{xz}} = 0{,}001\) and \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}} = 0{,}0005\).

Let us return to the hanging bar, which hangs under its own weight, with the axis \(x\) pointing down from the centre \(O\) of the top end. From the table of partial derivatives in section 1.7.2 we get at each of its points

\[\begin{aligned} \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} &= 2a\,(L - x) , \qquad \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}} = -0{,}6\,a\,(L - x) , \\ \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}} &= \tfrac12\,(-0{,}6\,a\,y + 0{,}6\,a\,y) = 0 , \\ \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}} &= \tfrac12\,(-0{,}6\,a\,z + 0{,}6\,a\,z) = 0 , \\ \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yz}} &= \tfrac12\,(0 + 0) = 0 . \end{aligned}\]

There are no shear strains anywhere in the bar, as we predicted in words in section 1.7.2 and as CM also finds (CM Example 7.3.2, equation (3), PDF p. 305). The pairs of partial derivatives that are equal and opposite cancel in the sum. The transverse normal strains are \(-0{,}3\) times the axial one, \(-0{,}6\,a\,(L - x) = -0{,}3 \cdot 2a\,(L - x)\), which is the thinning of section 1.6. Now we also understand the fibre in the direction \(\vek n = (\tfrac13, \tfrac23, \tfrac23)\), which got shorter. By (1.53) its strain is

\[\varepsilon(\vek n) \approx 2a\,(L - x)\,\big(n_{\mathrm{x}}^2 - 0{,}3\,(n_{\mathrm{y}}^2 + n_{\mathrm{z}}^2)\big) = 2a\,(L - x)\,\big(\tfrac19 - 0{,}3 \cdot \tfrac89\big) .\]

The fibre lies mostly across the bar, \(n_{\mathrm{y}}^2 + n_{\mathrm{z}}^2 = \tfrac89\), and across the bar the bar gets thinner, as the transverse part of the fibre in figure 1.352 shows. Let us write the two terms in the brackets one below the other:

part term value
stretching along the bar \(n_{\mathrm{x}}^2\) \(\tfrac19 = 0{,}111\)
thinning across the bar \(-0{,}3\,(n_{\mathrm{y}}^2 + n_{\mathrm{z}}^2)\) \(-0{,}3 \cdot \tfrac89 = -0{,}267\)
total \(n_{\mathrm{x}}^2 - 0{,}3\,(n_{\mathrm{y}}^2 + n_{\mathrm{z}}^2)\) \(-0{,}156\)

The thinning wins over the stretching, so the fibre gets shorter, although its end moves down more than \(P\). At the point \(P\) we have \(2a\,(L - x_{\mathrm{P}}) = 1{,}952 \cdot 10^{-6}\), and

\[\varepsilon(\vek n) \approx 1{,}952 \cdot 10^{-6} \cdot (-0{,}155556) = -3{,}0364 \cdot 10^{-7} ,\]

which is the value from section 1.17.3. The fibres with \(n_{\mathrm{x}}^2 = 0{,}3\,(1 - n_{\mathrm{x}}^2)\), that is \(n_{\mathrm{x}}^2 = 0{,}3/1{,}3 = 0{,}2308\) and \(|n_{\mathrm{x}}| = 0{,}48\), do not change their length (the zeros of the graph in figure 1.357, right).

The normal strains also tell how the volume of a small piece changes. With normal strains alone, a small cube with edge \(h\) becomes a box with the volume \((1 + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}})(1 + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}})(1 + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}})\,h^3\) (figure 1.358). Multiplying out the brackets gives \(1 + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}}\) plus products of two or three strains, which we leave out for small deformations. The shear strains change only the right angles and for small deformations do not change the volume (BOWER §2.1.9, PDF p. 52), just as for the sheared cube the area of the front face did not change. The reason there is simple: the front face becomes a parallelogram with the same base \(AB\), and the top edge stays at the same height, because \(u_{\mathrm{z}} = 0\). The area of a parallelogram is base times height, so it does not change. So the fraction by which the volume of a small piece changes is about

\[\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}} = \tr\ten\varepsilon ,\]

the sum of the diagonal entries of the matrix, which we call the trace (sled) of the matrix (BOWER §2.1.9, PDF p. 51, SADD §2.4, PDF p. 49). We will derive the exact relation, which also holds for large deformations, in chapter 2. For the sheared cube the trace is zero, which agrees with the finding of section 1.6.2 that simple shear does not change the volume. For the hanging bar at the point \(P\) the trace is \(1{,}952 \cdot 10^{-6} - 2 \cdot 5{,}856 \cdot 10^{-7} = 7{,}808 \cdot 10^{-7}\), which is \((1 - 2 \cdot 0{,}3)\) times, that is \(0{,}4\) times, the axial strain. The volume grows because the bar gets thinner across by less than it gets longer. For an axial strain of \(0{,}001\) the relative change would be \(0{,}0004\), which in section 1.6 we got from \(1{,}001 \cdot 0{,}9997^2 \approx 1{,}0004\).

The graph in figure 1.357 shows one more thing. For the cube the strain is largest in the direction of the diagonal \(AC\) and smallest in the direction of the diagonal \(BD\), for the bar largest along the bar and smallest across it. Books show that for every small deformation there are three mutually perpendicular directions in which there is no shear, only stretching or compression, and that among all fibres through the point the largest and the smallest strain occur in these directions (SADD §2.4, PDF pp. 48-49, and §1.6, PDF p. 22). We already announced this in section 1.1. For the hanging bar these are the directions of the axes, because there are no shear strains. For the cube they are the directions of the two diagonals of the front face and the direction of the axis \(y\). The proof needs calculations with right angles between vectors, so we will do it in chapter 2, together with stresses (section 2.11.4).

1.17.5 The turning of the material near a point

The small strain tensor is the symmetric part of the matrix \(\mat H\). By lemma 1.103 on the split into symmetric and antisymmetric parts, \(\mat H\) is the sum of its symmetric and antisymmetric parts, and this split is unique. What does the antisymmetric part describe?

Definition 1.116 Small rotation tensor (tenzor malih zasukov)

Let \(\mat H\) be the displacement gradient at an interior point \(P\) of a body. The small rotation tensor at the point \(P\) (tenzor malih zasukov) is the matrix

\[\ten\omega = \tfrac12\big(\mat H - \mat H^\T\big) , \tag{1.54}\]

with the entries \(\omega_{\mathrm{ij}} = \tfrac12(H_{\mathrm{ij}} - H_{\mathrm{ji}})\), written out

\[\ten\omega = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & \omega_{\mathrm{xy}} & \omega_{\mathrm{xz}} \\ -\omega_{\mathrm{xy}} & 0 & \omega_{\mathrm{yz}} \\ -\omega_{\mathrm{xz}} & -\omega_{\mathrm{yz}} & 0 \end{bmatrix} ,\]

where \(\omega_{\mathrm{xy}} = \tfrac12\big(\partial u_{\mathrm{x}} / \partial y - \partial u_{\mathrm{y}} / \partial x\big)\), \(\omega_{\mathrm{xz}} = \tfrac12\big(\partial u_{\mathrm{x}} / \partial z - \partial u_{\mathrm{z}} / \partial x\big)\) and \(\omega_{\mathrm{yz}} = \tfrac12\big(\partial u_{\mathrm{y}} / \partial z - \partial u_{\mathrm{z}} / \partial y\big)\), all at the point \(P\).

Source: CM (3.5.10), (3.5.11) (PDF p. 143), where the symbol is \(\boldsymbol\Omega\), SADD (2.1.7) (PDF p. 40), BOWER §2.1.10 (PDF p. 52).

On the diagonal there are zeros, because \(\omega_{\mathrm{ii}} = \tfrac12(H_{\mathrm{ii}} - H_{\mathrm{ii}}) = 0\), and below the diagonal the opposite values of those above it, because \(\omega_{\mathrm{ji}} = -\omega_{\mathrm{ij}}\). So the matrix has only three different numbers. We have \(\mat H = \ten\varepsilon + \ten\omega\), which we check entry by entry: \(\tfrac12(H_{\mathrm{ij}} + H_{\mathrm{ji}}) + \tfrac12(H_{\mathrm{ij}} - H_{\mathrm{ji}}) = H_{\mathrm{ij}}\). By lemma 1.111 on a short fibre after loading, the difference of the displacements of the ends of a short fibre is, up to the remainders, \(\mat H\,(h\,\vek n)\), so

\[\vek u(Q) - \vek u(P) \approx h\,\ten\varepsilon\,\vek n + h\,\ten\omega\,\vek n . \tag{1.55}\]

We already know the first part: it gives the strain of the fibre. What does the second part do? Figure 1.361 shows both parts on a small square: the change by the matrix \(\mat H\) is the sum of the change by the symmetric part and the turn by the antisymmetric part. Let us show that the second part changes the length of no fibre, up to terms with squares of partial derivatives.

Let us draw the left half. The axes at the bottom left show \(x\) to the right and \(y\) upwards. The point \(P\) is the corner of a small square. The blackwhite square is the square before loading, the orange quadrilateral is the one after the change by \(\mat H\), the label below it says by which matrix. The shifts of the ends of the edges are the grey dimension at the edge along the axis \(x\) and the grey dimension at the edge along the axis \(y\). The sign \(=\) says that this change equals the sum of the changes in the middle and on the right.

In the middle is the symmetric part. It is drawn in the same way: the square, the orange quadrilateral after this part and the grey dimensions of the shifts of the ends of the edges, along the axis \(x\) and along the axis \(y\). Below it is the label \(\ten\varepsilon\). The edges get longer or shorter and tilt towards each other. The sign \(+\) adds the antisymmetric part on the right, with the same square, the orange quadrilateral, the grey dimensions of the shifts of the ends, along the axis \(x\) and along the axis \(y\), and the label \(\ten\omega\). Here the square only turns, because both edges tilt equally in the same sense of turning. The shifts of the ends of the edges on the left are the sums of the shifts in the middle and on the right. Here \(\omega_{\mathrm{xy}} = \tfrac12\big(\tfrac{\partial u_{\mathrm{x}}}{\partial y} - \tfrac{\partial u_{\mathrm{y}}}{\partial x}\big)\) is negative, because the end of the edge along the axis \(x\) moves up (\(\tfrac{\partial u_{\mathrm{y}}}{\partial x} > 0\)) and the end of the edge along the axis \(y\) to the left (\(\tfrac{\partial u_{\mathrm{x}}}{\partial y} < 0\)). The square therefore turns from the axis \(x\) towards the axis \(y\). The point \(P\) is drawn in the same place in all three (middle, right).

Let us draw why a turn does not change the length, in the \(x\)-\(y\) plane. The point \(P\) is the start of the fibre, the blackwhite arrow is the unit vector \(\vek n\). In the plane \(\ten\omega\) has a single entry \(\omega_{\mathrm{xy}} = -a\), and \(\ten\omega\,\vek n = a\,(-n_{\mathrm{y}}, n_{\mathrm{x}})\) is the vector \(\vek n\) turned by a right angle and multiplied by \(a\). It is drawn from the end of the vector \(\vek n\) sideways, in blue, with a right angle between the two. The orange arrow is the vector \(\vek n + \ten\omega\,\vek n\), the fibre after the turn. Its end lies almost on the circle of length \(1\): it is above it only by the quadratic term \(\tfrac12\,a^2\), which we leave out in the first approximation. So the length of the fibre does not change, the fibre only turns. How the computation shows this for an arbitrary \(\ten\omega\), we see in step 4.

  1. Without the remainders the fibre after loading has the vector \(h\,(\vek n + \mat H\,\vek n)\). We write the square of its length component by component as in step 3 of the proof of theorem 1.114 on the strain of a short fibre:
    \[h^2\,|\vek n + \mat H\,\vek n|^2 = h^2\Big(|\vek n|^2 + 2\sum_{\mathrm{i}} n_{\mathrm{i}}\,(\mat H\,\vek n)_{\mathrm{i}} + |\mat H\,\vek n|^2\Big) .\]
  2. The first term is \(h^2\,|\vek n|^2 = h^2\), the square of the length before loading, because \(\vek n\) is a unit vector. The last is the square of a small number. So the first-order change is the middle term, and in it \(\sum_{\mathrm{i}} n_{\mathrm{i}}\,(\mat H\,\vek n)_{\mathrm{i}} = \sum_{\mathrm{i}} \sum_{\mathrm{j}} n_{\mathrm{i}}\,H_{\mathrm{ij}}\,n_{\mathrm{j}} = \vek n^\T\mat H\,\vek n\).
  3. Since \(\mat H = \ten\varepsilon + \ten\omega\), we have \(\vek n^\T\mat H\,\vek n = \vek n^\T\ten\varepsilon\,\vek n + \vek n^\T\ten\omega\,\vek n\).
  4. In the double sum \(\vek n^\T\ten\omega\,\vek n = \sum_{\mathrm{i}} \sum_{\mathrm{j}} n_{\mathrm{i}}\,\omega_{\mathrm{ij}}\,n_{\mathrm{j}}\) the terms with \(\ix{i} = \ix{j}\) are zero, because \(\omega_{\mathrm{ii}} = 0\). Every term with \(\ix{i} \neq \ix{j}\) has a partner in the sum with the indices swapped, and \(n_{\mathrm{i}}\,\omega_{\mathrm{ij}}\,n_{\mathrm{j}} + n_{\mathrm{j}}\,\omega_{\mathrm{ji}}\,n_{\mathrm{i}} = n_{\mathrm{i}}\,n_{\mathrm{j}}\,(\omega_{\mathrm{ij}} + \omega_{\mathrm{ji}}) = 0\). So \(\vek n^\T\ten\omega\,\vek n = 0\).
  5. So the first-order change of the square of the length is \(2h^2\,\vek n^\T\ten\varepsilon\,\vek n\), and the matrix \(\ten\omega\) does not appear in it.

So the part \(h\,\ten\omega\,\vek n\) moves the end of the fibre in such a way that the length of the fibre does not change to first order: the fibre only turns. This holds for all directions at once, with the same matrix \(\ten\omega\), and more follows from it. Take two points \(Q\) and \(Q'\) near \(P\). The parts of the displacements given by \(\ten\omega\) differ at them by \(\ten\omega\) times the vector \(\overrightarrow{QQ'}\) (lemma 1.97 and item 3 of lemma 1.99). Steps 1 to 4, however, do not require a unit vector, if we write \(|\vek v|^2\) instead of \(h^2\) (for a vector \(\vek v\) the first term is \(|\vek v|^2\) and the change is still \(2\,\vek v^\T\ten\varepsilon\,\vek v\)), so they hold for every vector, also for \(\overrightarrow{QQ'}\). To first order, therefore, no distance between points near \(P\) changes, and the material near \(P\) moves as a rigid body (definition 1.11). All short fibres through \(P\) thus turn together. CM shows that a displacement given by an antisymmetric matrix that is the same at all points is a rigid turn when its entries are small (CM, PDF p. 143). Hence the name small rotation tensor. To first order, the material close to the point deforms according to \(\ten\varepsilon\) and at the same time turns according to \(\ten\omega\) (figure 1.361). SADD (2.1.8) (PDF p. 40) and BOWER (PDF p. 52) split the change in the same way.

What turn does an individual entry of the matrix \(\ten\omega\) mean? The part \(h\,\ten\omega\,\vek n\) moves the end of the fibre, and for a fibre along the axis \(\ix{j}\) this is \(h\) times the column \(\ix{j}\) of the matrix \(\ten\omega\). For a fibre along the axis \(y\) the second column is \((\omega_{\mathrm{xy}}, 0, -\omega_{\mathrm{yz}})\): the end moves in the direction of the axis \(x\) by \(\omega_{\mathrm{xy}}\,h\). For a fibre along the axis \(x\) the first column is \((0, -\omega_{\mathrm{xy}}, -\omega_{\mathrm{xz}})\): the end moves in the direction of the axis \(y\) by \(-\omega_{\mathrm{xy}}\,h\). A positive \(\omega_{\mathrm{xy}}\) therefore turns the material in the plane \(x\)-\(y\) from the axis \(y\) towards the axis \(x\), and a negative one from the axis \(x\) towards the axis \(y\). In the same way a positive \(\omega_{\mathrm{xz}}\) turns in the plane \(x\)-\(z\) from the axis \(z\) towards the axis \(x\), and a positive \(\omega_{\mathrm{yz}}\) in the plane \(y\)-\(z\) from the axis \(z\) towards the axis \(y\). The size of an entry is the ratio of the sideways shift of the end to the length of the fibre.

For the hanging bar at the point \(P\)

\[\begin{aligned} \omega_{\mathrm{xy}} &= \tfrac12\big(-4{,}685 \cdot 10^{-10} - 4{,}685 \cdot 10^{-10}\big) = -4{,}685 \cdot 10^{-10} , \\ \omega_{\mathrm{xz}} &= 0 , \qquad \omega_{\mathrm{yz}} = 0 . \end{aligned}\]

Since at the same time \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}} = 0\), the material near \(P\) only turns in the plane \(x\)-\(y\) and is not sheared. The entry \(\omega_{\mathrm{xy}}\) is negative, so the material turns from the axis \(x\) towards the axis \(y\): a fibre along the axis \(x\) tilts towards the positive axis \(y\) by the ratio \(4{,}685 \cdot 10^{-10}\). We described this in words in section 1.7.2, and figure 1.95 shows it. For the sheared cube \(\omega_{\mathrm{xz}} = \tfrac12(0{,}001 - 0) = 0{,}0005\), the same as \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xz}}\). The entry is positive, so the material turns from the axis \(z\) towards the axis \(x\): the vertical fibres tilt in the direction of the axis \(x\), and the horizontal ones along the axis \(x\) downwards, all by the ratio \(0{,}0005\). So the tilt of the vertical edge by the ratio \(0{,}001\) is half shear strain and half turn, as we saw in the split of the cube's matrix in section 1.16, where the front face turns clockwise because of the antisymmetric part.

1.17.6 When the small strain tensor fails

We obtained the small strain tensor by leaving out products of partial derivatives. For this we assumed that all partial derivatives are small, not only the strains. What happens if a body turns a lot but deforms little? Let us take the most extreme case, a body that does not deform at all.

The model is a thin square plate that lies in the plane \(x\)-\(y\) and that we turn as a whole about the axis \(z\), without deforming it. We measure lengths in centimetres, the side of the plate is \(5\), and its corners are \(O = (0, 0, 0)\), \(A = (5, 0, 0)\), \(B = (5, 5, 0)\) and \(C = (0, 5, 0)\). Let the displacement field be

\[u_{\mathrm{x}} = (c - 1)\,x - s\,y , \qquad u_{\mathrm{y}} = s\,x + (c - 1)\,y , \qquad u_{\mathrm{z}} = 0 , \qquad c = 0{,}6 , \quad s = 0{,}8 .\]

The point \((x, y, z)\) moves to the position \((x + u_{\mathrm{x}},\ y + u_{\mathrm{y}},\ z + u_{\mathrm{z}}) = (c\,x - s\,y,\ s\,x + c\,y,\ z)\). The point \((1, 0, 0)\), which is at distance \(1\) from the axis \(z\), therefore moves to \((c, s, 0)\): the numbers \(c\) and \(s\) are the coordinates \(x\) and \(y\) of its position after the turn. They are the sides of the right triangle with sides \(3\), \(4\) and \(5\), divided by \(5\), so \(c^2 + s^2 = 0{,}36 + 0{,}64 = 1\). The corner \(A\) moves to \(A_1 = (3, 4, 0)\), the corner \(C\) to \(C_1 = (-4, 3, 0)\), and the points on the axis \(z\) do not move (figure 1.363).

The axes are \(x\) to the right and \(y\) upwards, the axis \(z\) points towards the reader, because the plate lies in the plane \(x\)-\(y\). The point \(O\) is the centre of the turn. The blackwhite square is the plate before the turn, its corners are \(A\) on the axis \(x\), \(B\) and \(C\). The orange square is the same plate after the turn. It turns as a whole about \(O\), so the corners \(A\), \(B\) and \(C\) move to \(A_1\), \(B_1\) and \(C_1\). The thick blackwhite line \(OA\) is the fibre, \(5\) long, as the dimension \(5\) below it shows. After the turn the fibre \(OA_1\) is the thick orange line, which also has length \(5\), since the square does not deform. The fibre is turned, so it has a smaller component along the axis \(x\). The grey dashed vertical line from \(A_1\) drops to the axis \(x\), and the dimension \(3\) below the axis is the length of this component. So the component decreases from \(5\) to \(3\), which the small strain tensor reads as a shortening by \(40\) %.

Is this really a rigid-body displacement (definition 1.11)? Let us check that the distance between no two points changes.

  1. Let the points \(P\) and \(Q\) differ by \((\Delta x, \Delta y, \Delta z)\) before loading, for the fibre \(OA\) by \((5, 0, 0)\). We subtract the new positions coordinate by coordinate. Since each new coordinate is a sum of multiples of the old ones, the new positions differ by \((c\,\Delta x - s\,\Delta y,\ s\,\Delta x + c\,\Delta y,\ \Delta z)\).
  2. We multiply out the square of the new distance:
    \[\begin{aligned} (c\,\Delta x - s\,\Delta y)^2 + (s\,\Delta x + c\,\Delta y)^2 + \Delta z^2 &= c^2\Delta x^2 - 2cs\,\Delta x\,\Delta y + s^2\Delta y^2 \\ &\quad + s^2\Delta x^2 + 2sc\,\Delta x\,\Delta y + c^2\Delta y^2 + \Delta z^2 . \end{aligned}\]
  3. The mixed terms cancel, and we collect the others, as for the fibre \(OA_1\) from \((3, 4, 0)\) with \(3^2 + 4^2 = 5^2\): \((c^2 + s^2)(\Delta x^2 + \Delta y^2) + \Delta z^2 = \Delta x^2 + \Delta y^2 + \Delta z^2\), because \(c^2 + s^2 = 1\).

The distances stay the same, the plate does not deform. The fibre \(OA\) of length \(5\) becomes \(OA_1\) with the length \(\sqrt{3^2 + 4^2} = 5\). What do the two measures of strain say? The displacement gradient is, at every point,

\[\mat H = \begin{bmatrix} c - 1 & -s & 0 \\ s & c - 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -0{,}4 & -0{,}8 & 0 \\ 0{,}8 & -0{,}4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix} , \qquad \mat F = \begin{bmatrix} 0{,}6 & -0{,}8 & 0 \\ 0{,}8 & 0{,}6 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} .\]

The entry \((\mat F^\T\mat F)_{\mathrm{xx}}\) is \(0{,}6^2 + 0{,}8^2 + 0^2 = 1\), the entry \((\mat F^\T\mat F)_{\mathrm{xy}}\) is \(0{,}6 \cdot (-0{,}8) + 0{,}8 \cdot 0{,}6 + 0 = 0\), and in the same way we find \(\mat F^\T\mat F = \mat I\). So the Green-Lagrange tensor is exactly zero, \(\mat E = \tfrac12(\mat I - \mat I) = \mat 0\), and it correctly says that no fibre gets longer. The small strain tensor, however, is

\[\ten\varepsilon = \tfrac12\big(\mat H + \mat H^\T\big) = \begin{bmatrix} -0{,}4 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -0{,}4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix} .\]

By it every fibre in the plane \(x\)-\(y\) would get shorter by \(40\) %, which is false. Where does the error come from? The number \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = \partial u_{\mathrm{x}} / \partial x = c - 1 = -0{,}4\) measures only how the component \(x\) of a fibre along the axis \(x\) changes. The fibre \(OA\) turns into \(OA_1\), its component \(x\) decreases from \(5\) to \(3\), but its length stays \(5\) (figure 1.363). The small strain tensor mistakes the turn for a shortening, because it leaves out the term \(\tfrac12\,(\partial u_{\mathrm{y}} / \partial x)^2 = \tfrac12 \cdot 0{,}8^2 = 0{,}32\) and the term \(\tfrac12\,(\partial u_{\mathrm{x}} / \partial x)^2 = \tfrac12 \cdot 0{,}4^2 = 0{,}08\). With them, by (1.48), \(E_{\mathrm{xx}} = -0{,}4 + 0{,}08 + 0{,}32 = 0\).

Let us draw the graph. The horizontal axis is \(s\), the sine of the angle of the turn, between \(0\) and \(0{,}1\). The vertical axis is \(1 - c\), the false strain that the small strain tensor assigns to a rigid turn. The orange curve shows how the error grows with \(s\). It grows slowly for small \(s\) and faster for larger \(s\), because it is almost equal to \(s^2/2\). The grey dashed horizontal line is the level \(0{,}001\), the strain of steel. The dot at \(s = \sqrt{0{,}002} \approx 0{,}045\) is the place where the curve reaches this level. The dot at \(s = 0{,}1\) has the value \(1 - c = 0{,}0050\), five times more.

How large is the error for a small turn? Take \(s = 0{,}001\) and \(c = \sqrt{1 - s^2}\), so that again \(c^2 + s^2 = 1\) and the displacement is rigid. A point 1 m from the axis moves sideways by about 1 mm. Then \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = c - 1 = -5{,}0 \cdot 10^{-7}\). This is about \(-s^2/2\). We get the difference of the numbers \(c\) and \(1 - s^2/2\) from the difference of their squares divided by their sum, as in (1.17). Since \(c^2 = 1 - s^2\) and \((1 - s^2/2)^2 = 1 - s^2 + s^4/4\),

\[c - \Big(1 - \frac{s^2}{2}\Big) = \frac{c^2 - (1 - s^2/2)^2}{c + 1 - s^2/2} = \frac{-s^4/4}{c + 1 - s^2/2} .\]

The denominator is almost \(2\), so \(c\) differs from \(1 - s^2/2\) only by about \(s^4/8\), for \(s = 0{,}001\) by \(1{,}25 \cdot 10^{-13}\). The false strain \(c - 1\) is therefore proportional to the square of the turn. For \(s = 0{,}001\) it is small compared with the strains of steel of about \(0{,}001\). For \(s = 0{,}1\), when a point 1 m from the axis moves sideways by about 10 cm, however, \(c - 1 = -0{,}0050\). This is five times the strain at which steel already gets permanently longer (section 1.1), although the body does not deform at all.

How large a turn is still allowed? The false strain \(s^2/2\) must be small compared with the strains we calculate. For strains of about \(0{,}001\), \(s^2/2\) must therefore be much smaller than \(0{,}001\), that is \(s\) much smaller than \(\sqrt{0{,}002} \approx 0{,}045\). The turn may be larger than the strains, but not arbitrarily large: the limit is of the order of the square root of the strain. This agrees with the estimate of section 1.17.3, by which the error is at most \(4{,}5\,m^2\), where here \(m = s\).

So the small strain tensor is a good approximation only when all partial derivatives of the displacements are small, that is, when the strains and also the turns are small. In steel structures the strains are small, and when the turns of their parts are small too, this is so. When parts of a body turn a lot while the body deforms little, for example a thin ruler bent into an arc, the Green-Lagrange tensor must be used. The same holds for large strains, for example in rubber. CM warns that smallness must be checked separately in every application, and also shows the opposite example: a field for which the small strain tensor is zero but the Green-Lagrange tensor is not (CM (3.5.16)-(3.5.18), PDF pp. 143-144). The example with the turned plate is not from a source.

1.17.7 Strain relative to the shape after loading

The Green-Lagrange strain tensor and the small strain tensor measure fibres that we choose before loading. We take the point \(P\) and the direction \(\vek n\) on the unloaded body, and we compare the change of the square of the length of the fibre with the square of its length before loading, \(L_0^2\). This is how we have described a body ever since section 1.6: we name every point by the position it had before loading and assign to it its displacement. Books call this the Lagrangian or material description (Lagrangeov ali materialni opis).

Sometimes, however, we know a body mainly after loading. We draw a grid of short marks on an unloaded rubber band, stretch the band and take a photograph. On the photograph we see each mark in its position, direction and length after loading, and by these we also choose it. For a liquid flowing in a pipe, we want to know what happens at a given place in the pipe, not where the bit of liquid that is there now was before. A description in which we name points by their position after loading is the Eulerian or spatial description (Eulerjev ali prostorski opis). CM says that for solid bodies the Eulerian description is less useful, because we do not know the shape of the body after loading in advance, while for the motion of liquids it is the one usually used (CM §3.2.1-§3.2.3, PDF pp. 112-114 and 117).

Let us draw the pipe. Two walls bound the pipe, the arrow above them shows the direction in which the liquid flows. The dashed window is a given place in the pipe, marked \(\vek x\). The window is at rest, the liquid flows through it. The orange bit is the one that is now in the window. The same bit was earlier on the left, at the place \(\vek X\) (grey dashed rectangle), and the grey arrow shows its path to the window. The grey solid bit is another bit that will be in the window later. The Eulerian description asks what is in the window, and names the bit by the place \(\vek x\), not by the place \(\vek X\) where it was before.

The goal of this section is a measure of stretching that compares the change of the square of the length of a short fibre with the square of its length after loading, \(L_1^2\), and gives the direction of the fibre after loading (figure 1.366). We will find a matrix that gives this measure for every direction, and show how it is related to the Green-Lagrange tensor. Why do we need one more measure? In this book it shows when it does not matter whether we choose the fibre before loading or after it: for small partial derivatives it does not, for large deformations it does, and then we must say which measure we use.

The point \(P\) and the point \(Q\) are the end points of the fibre before loading, the blackwhite segment between them is the fibre. The grey dimension below it is its length \(L_0\). The blue arrow beside it is the unit vector \(\vek n\), the direction of the fibre before loading. The arrow is set off from the fibre so that it does not lie on it. After loading the end points move. The grey dimension \(\vek u(P)\) and the grey dimension \(\vek u(Q)\) show by how much, and lead to the point \(P_1\) and the point \(Q_1\). The orange segment between them is the fibre after loading. It is longer and turned, everything is greatly magnified. The grey dimension above it is its length \(L_1\). The blue arrow beside it is the unit vector \(\vek m\), the direction of the fibre after loading.

The physical model and both assumptions are the same as in the whole of section 1.17: the body is a continuum, its displacement field is continuously differentiable, and the point \(P\) is an interior point of the body. We add one more assumption: the deformation gradient \(\mat F\) at the point \(P\) has an inverse matrix \(\mat F^{-1}\). What this means physically we said in section 1.16.5 (figure 1.338). Matter cannot be squeezed so that a fibre disappears, and CM concludes from this that the matrix \(\mat F\) is invertible (CM §3.3.1, PDF pp. 119-120). That a matrix which sends no nonzero vector to the zero vector really has an inverse matrix, we will show only in chapter 2. Until then the existence of the matrix \(\mat F^{-1}\) is an assumption, which we check by calculation in the examples.

Let us start with the bar, where everything is a single number. A bar of length \(L_0\) gets longer, to the length \(L_1\). In section 1.1 we met the Green-Lagrange strain \((L_1^2 - L_0^2)/(2L_0^2)\). If we divide the change of the square of the length by the square of the new length, we get the quotient

\[\frac{L_1^2 - L_0^2}{2L_1^2} .\]

Let us express it with the strain of the bar \(\varepsilon = (L_1 - L_0)/L_0\).

  1. From the definition of the strain, \(L_1 = L_0\,(1 + \varepsilon)\). The square is a multiplied-out product, \(L_1^2 = L_0^2\,(1 + \varepsilon)(1 + \varepsilon) = L_0^2\,(1 + 2\varepsilon + \varepsilon^2)\), as in section 1.6.2.
  2. So the numerator is \(L_1^2 - L_0^2\) \(= L_0^2\,(2\varepsilon + \varepsilon^2)\), and the denominator is \(2L_1^2 = 2L_0^2\,(1 + \varepsilon)^2\).
  3. The factor \(L_0^2\) cancels:
    \[\frac{L_1^2 - L_0^2}{2L_1^2} = \frac{2\varepsilon + \varepsilon^2}{2\,(1 + \varepsilon)^2} . \tag{1.56}\]
  4. The quotient differs from the strain \(\varepsilon\) by
    \[\varepsilon - \frac{2\varepsilon + \varepsilon^2}{2\,(1 + \varepsilon)^2} = \frac{2\varepsilon\,(1 + \varepsilon)^2 - 2\varepsilon - \varepsilon^2}{2\,(1 + \varepsilon)^2} = \frac{\varepsilon^2\,(3 + 2\varepsilon)}{2\,(1 + \varepsilon)^2} ,\]
    which for small \(\varepsilon\) is almost \(\tfrac32\,\varepsilon^2\). We got the numerator by multiplying out \((1 + \varepsilon)^2\) as in step 1 and collecting the terms: \(2\varepsilon + 4\varepsilon^2 + 2\varepsilon^3 - 2\varepsilon - \varepsilon^2 = 3\varepsilon^2 + 2\varepsilon^3\). The Green-Lagrange strain \(\varepsilon + \tfrac12\,\varepsilon^2\), on the other hand, differs from \(\varepsilon\) by \(\tfrac12\,\varepsilon^2\).

For a steel bar with \(\varepsilon = 0{,}001\) the new quotient is \(0{,}0009985\) and the Green-Lagrange strain \(0{,}0010005\). The first differs from \(\varepsilon\) by one and a half per mille of its value, the second by half a per mille. For a rubber band stretched from 10 cm to 15 cm, \(\varepsilon = 0{,}5\), the new quotient is \((15^2 - 10^2)/(2 \cdot 15^2) = 125/450 = 0{,}278\) and the Green-Lagrange strain \(0{,}625\) (figure 1.367). In order of size they follow each other as follows:

\[\frac{L_1^2 - L_0^2}{2L_1^2} = 0{,}278 \;<\; \varepsilon = 0{,}5 \;<\; \frac{L_1^2 - L_0^2}{2L_0^2} = 0{,}625 .\]

For large strains the measures differ a lot.

Let us draw the graph. The horizontal axis is the ratio of lengths \(L_1/L_0\) from \(0{,}5\) to \(2\), the vertical axis is the value of the measure. The blackwhite straight line is the strain \(\varepsilon = L_1/L_0 - 1\). The blue curve is the Green-Lagrange strain \((L_1^2 - L_0^2)/(2L_0^2)\). The orange curve is the quotient \((L_1^2 - L_0^2)/(2L_1^2)\), which divides the change of the square of the length by the square of the length after loading. The dot at \(L_1/L_0 = 1\) is the common point of all three, where the fibre is not stretched and all three are zero. There they have the same slope, so for small strains they almost agree. For larger ratios they diverge, and the blackwhite line always lies between the curves. The three dots at \(L_1/L_0 = 1{,}5\) are the values for the rubber band stretched from 10 cm to 15 cm: \(0{,}5\), \(0{,}625\) and \(0{,}278\). The three dots at \(L_1/L_0 = 2\) are the values for a stretch to double the length: \(1\), \(1{,}5\) and \(0{,}375\).

Why is the new quotient always smaller than the Green-Lagrange one when the length changes? Both have the same numerator \(L_1^2 - L_0^2\). When the bar is stretched, \(L_1 > L_0\), so the new quotient divides a positive numerator by a larger number and is smaller. When the bar gets shorter, \(L_1 < L_0\), and the new quotient divides a negative numerator by a smaller number, so it is larger in size and again smaller. The strain \(\varepsilon\) always lies between the two. The Green-Lagrange strain is larger than it by \(\tfrac12\,\varepsilon^2\), and the new quotient is smaller by step 4, because a bar cannot disappear, so \(L_1 > 0\), \(\varepsilon > -1\) and \(3 + 2\varepsilon > 0\).

The new quotient has one more meaning. We let the stretched band of length 15 cm go back to 10 cm, and we take the length of the stretched band as the initial length. The Green-Lagrange strain of this unloading is \((10^2 - 15^2)/(2 \cdot 15^2) = -0{,}278\), the new quotient with the opposite sign. This is always so: when we swap the roles of the lengths \(L_0\) and \(L_1\), the Green-Lagrange quotient becomes \((L_0^2 - L_1^2)/(2L_1^2)\), which is the new quotient with the opposite sign. So the new quotient measures stretching with the length seen by someone who knows only the loaded body.

In space we proceed as in section 1.17.2 and first leave out the remainders, which we will justify in the theorem below. A fibre from the point \(P\) in the direction of the unit vector \(\vek n\) with length \(h > 0\) has after loading, by lemma 1.111 on a short fibre after loading and without the remainders, the vector \(\mat F\,(h\,\vek n) = h\,\mat F\vek n\) (the fibre after loading in figure 1.366).

  1. Its length after loading is \(L_1 \approx h\,|\mat F\vek n|\). The vector \(\mat F\vek n\) is not the zero vector, as we will show in the theorem below, so we may divide it by its length. We get the unit vector \(\vek m = \mat F\vek n / |\mat F\vek n|\), the direction of the fibre after loading. The vector of the fibre after loading is thus \(h\,\mat F\vek n \approx L_1\,\vek m\).
  2. We express the vector of the fibre before loading with the vector after loading. By lemma 1.97 on the linearity of the product with a matrix, item 1 of lemma 1.99 on the properties of the matrix product, (1.43) and lemma 1.106, \(\mat F^{-1}(h\,\mat F\vek n) = h\,(\mat F^{-1}\mat F)\,\vek n = h\,\vek n\). So \(h\,\vek n \approx L_1\,\mat F^{-1}\vek m\). The matrix \(\mat F^{-1}\) takes the vector of the fibre after loading back to the vector before loading, just as for the sheared cube the matrix \(\mat I - \mat K\) took back the edge \(AD\) (section 1.16.5). The matrix \(\mat K\) is the matrix of partial derivatives of the cube from section 1.16, that is, its displacement gradient \(\mat H\), which we wrote down there before we gave it a name.
  3. So the square of the length before loading is \(L_0^2 = h^2 \approx L_1^2\,|\mat F^{-1}\vek m|^2\). The same steps 2 to 5 as for \(|\mat F\vek n|^2\) in section 1.17.2, only with \(\mat F^{-1}\) instead of \(\mat F\) and \(\vek m\) instead of \(\vek n\), give
    \[|\mat F^{-1}\vek m|^2 = \vek m^\T\,(\mat F^{-1})^\T\mat F^{-1}\,\vek m .\]
  4. The vector \(\vek m\) is a unit vector, so \(1 = \vek m^\T\mat I\,\vek m\) as in step 6 there (only the terms with equal indices remain), and \(L_1^2 = L_1^2\,\vek m^\T\mat I\,\vek m\).
  5. We subtract the squares of the lengths, divide by \(2L_1^2\) and subtract the two double sums term by term:
    \[\frac{L_1^2 - L_0^2}{2L_1^2} \approx \frac{L_1^2\,\vek m^\T\mat I\,\vek m - L_1^2\,\vek m^\T(\mat F^{-1})^\T\mat F^{-1}\vek m}{2L_1^2} = \vek m^\T\,\tfrac12\big(\mat I - (\mat F^{-1})^\T\mat F^{-1}\big)\,\vek m .\]

On the right there is again a single matrix, which depends only on the displacement field at the point \(P\), and the direction appears only in the vector \(\vek m\), this time in the direction of the fibre after loading. The matrix contains the transposed matrix of the inverse matrix \(\mat F^{-1}\). Before we give the matrix a name, let us show that this is the same matrix as the inverse matrix of the matrix \(\mat F^\T\), so that we may denote both by one symbol.

Let us draw what the lemma says on the sheared cube. Top left is the matrix \(\mat F^\T\), in which \(0{,}001\) is now in row \(z\) and column \(x\). The arrow leads to its inverse matrix, in which this entry is \(-0{,}001\). Bottom left is the inverse matrix \(\mat F^{-1}\) of the cube, with \(-0{,}001\) in row \(x\) and column \(z\). The arrow leads to its transposed matrix, where \(-0{,}001\) is again in row \(z\) and column \(x\). The sign \(=\) says that the two right matrices are equal, which is what the lemma states.

Lemma 1.117 Inverse of the transposed matrix (inverzna matrika transponirane matrike)

Let a square matrix \(\mat A\) of order \(n\) have an inverse matrix \(\mat A^{-1}\). Then the transposed matrix \(\mat A^\T\) also has an inverse matrix, and it is the transposed matrix of the matrix \(\mat A^{-1}\):

\[(\mat A^\T)^{-1} = (\mat A^{-1})^\T .\]
Proof

We must show that the matrix \((\mat A^{-1})^\T\) satisfies both equalities of definition 1.107 for the matrix \(\mat A^\T\).

  1. We write \(\mat B = \mat A^{-1}\). By (1.43), \(\mat A\mat B = \mat I\) and \(\mat B\mat A = \mat I\).
  2. We transpose the first equality. By item 3 of lemma 1.101, \((\mat A\mat B)^\T = \mat B^\T\mat A^\T\), so \(\mat B^\T\mat A^\T = \mat I^\T\).
  3. The identity matrix equals its transposed matrix. The entry \((\ix{i}, \ix{j})\) of the matrix \(\mat I^\T\) is \(I_{\mathrm{ji}}\) (definition 1.100), which is \(1\) for \(\ix{j} = \ix{i}\) and \(0\) otherwise, the same as \(I_{\mathrm{ij}}\) (definition 1.105). So \(\mat B^\T\mat A^\T = \mat I\).
  4. In the same way we transpose the second equality, \(\mat B\mat A = \mat I\), and get \(\mat A^\T\mat B^\T = \mat I\).
  5. The matrices \(\mat A^\T\) and \(\mat B^\T\) are square matrices of order \(n\), and by steps 3 and 4 they satisfy both equalities (1.43) with \(\mat A^\T\) in the place of the matrix \(\mat A\). So \(\mat B^\T\) is an inverse matrix of the matrix \(\mat A^\T\). By lemma 1.108 on the uniqueness of the inverse matrix there is no other, so \((\mat A^\T)^{-1} = \mat B^\T = (\mat A^{-1})^\T\).

Source: CM §2.3.6 (PDF p. 65) states the equality without proof, KREYSZIG §7.8, problems 13 and 14 (PDF p. 335), leaves its check and proof to the reader. The proof is not from the sources.

So we write the matrix \((\mat A^{-1})^\T = (\mat A^\T)^{-1}\) more briefly as \(\mat A^{-\T}\), as CM does (CM §2.3.6, PDF p. 65). The proof used only the rule for transposing a product, the fact that the identity matrix equals its transposed matrix, and the uniqueness of the inverse matrix. For the sheared cube \(\mat F^{-1} = \mat I - \mat K\) (section 1.16.5), so by item 2 of lemma 1.101 and step 3 above, \(\mat F^{-\T} = \mat I^\T - \mat K^\T = \mat I - \mat K^\T\). This is the matrix that has a single nonzero entry off the main diagonal, \(-0{,}001\) in row \(z\) and column \(x\).

Before we define the tensor, let us compute it on the sheared cube. From \(\mat F^{-1} = \mat I - \mat K\) and \(\mat F^{-\T} = \mat I - \mat K^\T\) we get \(\mat I - \mat F^{-\T}\mat F^{-1} = \mat K + \mat K^\T - \mat K^\T\mat K\). At the top are the matrix \(\mat K^\T\) and the matrix \(\mat K\) that we multiply. Row \(z\) of the matrix \(\mat K^\T\) is \((0{,}001, 0, 0)\), column \(z\) of the matrix \(\mat K\) is the same, and their product \(10^{-6}\) is the only nonzero entry of the product \(\mat K^\T\mat K\). At the bottom is the half of the sum of three matrices: \(\mat K\), \(\mat K^\T\) and \(\mat K^\T\mat K\), which we subtract, all entry by entry. The result is the matrix \(\mat E^*\), which has \(0{,}0005\) at the entries \(xz\) and \(zx\) and \(-5 \cdot 10^{-7}\) at the entry \(zz\).

Definition 1.118 Euler-Almansi strain tensor (Euler-Almansijev tenzor deformacij)

Let \(\mat F\) be the deformation gradient at an interior point \(P\) of a body, and let \(\mat F\) have an inverse matrix. The Euler-Almansi strain tensor (Euler-Almansijev tenzor deformacij) at the point \(P\) is the matrix

\[\mat E^* = \tfrac12\big(\mat I - \mat F^{-\T}\mat F^{-1}\big) , \tag{1.57}\]

where \(\mat F^{-\T} = (\mat F^{-1})^\T\) is the inverse matrix of the matrix \(\mat F^\T\) (lemma 1.117). We denote its entry in row \(\ix{i}\) and column \(\ix{j}\) by \(E^*_{\mathrm{ij}}\).

Source: CM (3.4.24) (PDF p. 133), BOWER §2.1.6 (PDF p. 49).

What kind of object is \(\mat E^*\)? Like \(\mat E\), it is a \(3 \times 3\) matrix, calculated from the deformation gradient at one point. It is symmetric (definition 1.102). By items 3 and 1 of lemma 1.101, \((\mat F^{-\T}\mat F^{-1})^\T = (\mat F^{-1})^\T(\mat F^{-\T})^\T = \mat F^{-\T}\mat F^{-1}\), and the identity matrix equals its transposed matrix, so by item 2 of the same lemma \((\mat E^*)^\T = \mat E^*\). The matrix \(\mat E^*\) therefore has at most six different entries. We calculate it from the partial derivatives of the displacements at the point \(P\), but its numbers describe the fibres that pass through the point \(P_1\) after loading, in their directions after loading. The symbol \(\mat E^*\) is used by BOWER, while CM writes the same matrix with a small bold \(\mathbf e\).

CM calls this tensor the Almansi-Hamel or Euler strain tensor (Almansi-Hamelov ali Eulerjev tenzor deformacij), and in its examples the Almansi strain tensor (CM, PDF pp. 133-134). BOWER calls it the Eulerian strain tensor (Eulerjev tenzor deformacij) and denotes it by \(\mat E^*\) (BOWER §2.1.6, PDF p. 49). The name in this book joins the two names. CM also writes it with partial derivatives of the displacements with respect to the coordinates of the points after loading, and there the quadratic part has the opposite sign to that of the Green-Lagrange tensor (CM (3.4.25) and (3.4.27), PDF p. 133). We will not use such derivatives, because we name the points of a body by their position before loading.

Both matrices, \(\mat E\) and \(\mat E^*\), are calculated from the same matrix \(\mat F\). How do we get one from the other?

Let us draw the diagram. In the top row, on the left, is the blackwhite arrow \(\vek n\), the direction of the fibre before loading. On the right is the orange arrow \(\vek m\), the direction of the same fibre after loading. The upper blue arrow \(\mat F\) in the top row leads from \(\vek n\) to \(\vek m\), because the matrix \(\mat F\) sends the vector of the fibre before loading to the vector after it, which we turn into \(\vek m\) by dividing by its length. The lower arrow \(\mat F^{-1}\) in the top row leads back. In the bottom row, on the left, is the blackwhite rectangle with \(\mat E\), the Green-Lagrange measure, and on the right the orange rectangle with \(\mat E^*\), the Euler-Almansi measure. The colours follow the top row: blackwhite before loading, orange after it. The upper arrow in the bottom row says that from \(\mat E\) we get \(\mat E^*\) with the matrices \(\mat F^{-\T}\) from the left and \(\mat F^{-1}\) from the right. The lower arrow in the bottom row leads back, with \(\mat F^\T\) from the left and \(\mat F\) from the right. Under the rectangles are the numbers of the same fibre: \(G = \vek n^\T\mat E\,\vek n\) for the Green-Lagrange measure and \(A = \vek m^\T\mat E^*\,\vek m\) for the Euler-Almansi one.

Let us draw how the factors combine. Each matrix is a box. In the first row are the first term \(\mat F^\T\mat I\,\mat F\) and the second term \(\mat F^\T\mat F^{-\T}\mat F^{-1}\mat F\) of the expression \(\mat F^\T\mat E^*\,\mat F\), once we insert the definition of \(\mat E^*\). In the second row the identity matrix drops out of the first term, because multiplying by it changes nothing, and \(\mat F^\T\mat F\) remains. In the third row the first two factors of the second term combine into \(\mat I\), because \(\mat F^{-\T}\) is the inverse matrix of \(\mat F^\T\), and so do the last two, because \(\mat F^{-1}\) is the inverse matrix of \(\mat F\). What remains is \(\mat I\mat I = \mat I\). In the fourth row the half of the difference \(\mat F^\T\mat F - \mat I\) is the matrix \(\mat E\). In the last row, at the second equality, there are \(\mat F^{-\T}\) in front of \(\mat F^\T\) and \(\mat F\) in front of \(\mat F^{-1}\), both pairs are \(\mat I\), and \(\mat E^*\) remains.

Lemma 1.119 Relation between the Euler-Almansi and the Green-Lagrange strain tensor (zveza med Euler-Almansijevim in Green-Lagrangeovim tenzorjem)

Let the deformation gradient \(\mat F\) at an interior point \(P\) of a body have an inverse matrix, and let \(\mat E\) be the Green-Lagrange and \(\mat E^*\) the Euler-Almansi strain tensor at \(P\). Then

\[\mat F^\T\mat E^*\,\mat F = \mat E \qquad \text{and} \qquad \mat E^* = \mat F^{-\T}\mat E\,\mat F^{-1} . \tag{1.58}\]
Proof

We must show both equalities. We use the properties of the matrix product (lemma 1.99) and the fact that \(\mat F^{-\T}\) is the inverse matrix of the matrix \(\mat F^\T\) (lemma 1.117).

The first equality.

  1. We substitute (1.57). By item 3 of lemma 1.99, used for multiplication from the left and from the right, \(\mat F^\T\mat E^*\,\mat F = \tfrac12\big(\mat F^\T\mat I\,\mat F - \mat F^\T\mat F^{-\T}\mat F^{-1}\mat F\big)\).
  2. By lemma 1.106, \(\mat F^\T\mat I\,\mat F = \mat F^\T\mat F\).
  3. By item 2 of lemma 1.99, \(\mat F^\T\mat F^{-\T}\mat F^{-1}\mat F = (\mat F^\T\mat F^{-\T})(\mat F^{-1}\mat F)\). By (1.43) both brackets equal \(\mat I\), the first because \(\mat F^{-\T}\) is the inverse matrix of the matrix \(\mat F^\T\). By lemma 1.106, \(\mat I\mat I = \mat I\).
  4. So \(\mat F^\T\mat E^*\,\mat F = \tfrac12(\mat F^\T\mat F - \mat I)\), which by (1.47) is the matrix \(\mat E\).

The second equality.

  1. We multiply the first equality from the left by \(\mat F^{-\T}\) and from the right by \(\mat F^{-1}\): \(\mat F^{-\T}\mat E\,\mat F^{-1} = \mat F^{-\T}\mat F^\T\mat E^*\,\mat F\mat F^{-1}\).
  2. By item 2 of lemma 1.99 the right side equals \((\mat F^{-\T}\mat F^\T)\,\mat E^*\,(\mat F\mat F^{-1})\). By (1.43) both brackets equal \(\mat I\), and by lemma 1.106, \(\mat I\,\mat E^*\,\mat I = \mat E^*\).

Source: The definitions of the two tensors are CM (3.4.10) (PDF p. 129) and (3.4.24) (PDF p. 133). The proof is not from the sources.

So we get \(\mat E^*\) from \(\mat E\) by multiplying \(\mat E\) from the left by \(\mat F^{-\T}\) and from the right by \(\mat F^{-1}\), and \(\mat E\) from \(\mat E^*\) with the matrices \(\mat F^\T\) and \(\mat F\). When \(\mat E = \mat 0\), therefore also \(\mat E^* = \mat 0\), because every entry of a product with the zero matrix is a sum of products with zero, and the other way round. The proof used only the grouping of factors and the fact that the product of a matrix with its inverse matrix gives the identity matrix.

So far we have left out the remainders. As for the Green-Lagrange tensor, let us show that this is justified for ever shorter fibres. We will not need a new calculation with remainders, because the new quotient is expressed through the Green-Lagrange one.

Let us draw the left half. The point \(P\) is the common start of all three vectors. The blackwhite arrow \(\vek n\) is the unit vector of the fibre before loading. The blue arrow \(\mat F\,\vek n\) is the vector to which \(\mat F\) sends it. For the figure \(G = 0{,}48\) is chosen, so \(|\mat F\,\vek n| = \sqrt{1 + 2G} = 1{,}4\), a length longer than \(1\). The orange arrow \(\vek m\) lies on the first part of \(\mat F\,\vek n\) and has length \(1\), since it is the unit vector in the direction of \(\mat F\,\vek n\). So the orange arrow turns into the blue one.

On the right we compare the squares of the lengths of the fibre at \(h = 1\) on one line. The grey dashed horizontal line is this line. The upper dimension \(L_1^2\) is the square of the length after loading, \(1{,}96\), and the dimension \(L_0^2\) below it is the square of the length before it, \(1\). The grey vertical lines carry the ends of the dimensions to the line, so that the difference between them can be seen. The orange dimension at the bottom is the difference \(L_1^2 - L_0^2 = 2G = 0{,}96\). Below it are the quotients that divide this same difference by different numbers: \(G\) by \(2L_0^2\) and \(A\) by \(2L_1^2\), so \(A = 0{,}48/1{,}96 \approx 0{,}245\).

Let us draw why \(\mat F\vek n\) is not the zero vector. Suppose it is. The vector \(\vek n\) of length \(1\) goes by the matrix \(\mat F\) (blue arrow) to the zero vector. By the matrix \(\mat F^{-1}\) we send it on and again get the zero vector. But the two matrices in a row are \(\mat F^{-1}\mat F = \mat I\) (lower arrow) and return the vector \(\vek n\) of length \(1\). Zero and a vector of length \(1\) are not equal, which is a contradiction.

Let us draw the two bands that we will need for the limit, with the number \(c = 2\) for the picture. At the top is the band of the number \(1 + 2g(h)\) around \(c\), of half-width \(c/2\), because \(1 + 2g(h) = c + 2\big(g(h) - G\big)\) and \(|g(h) - G| < c/4\). The left edge of the band, \(c/2\), is a lower bound for the number \(1 + 2g(h)\). At the bottom is the band for \(g(h) - G\) with half-width \(\eta c^2/2\). The factor \(2/c^2\) carries it to the band for \(a(h) - G/c\) with half-width \(\eta\), which for \(c = 2\) is half as wide.

Theorem 1.120 Strain of a short fibre relative to its length after loading (deformacija kratkega vlakna glede na dolžino po obremenitvi)

Let the displacement field of a body be continuously differentiable, \(P\) an interior point of the body, \(r > 0\) a number such that all points closer to \(P\) than \(r\) are interior points of the body (such an \(r\) exists by lemma 1.89 on the neighbourhood of an interior point), \(\mat F\) the deformation gradient at \(P\), which has an inverse matrix, \(\mat E\) the Green-Lagrange and \(\mat E^*\) the Euler-Almansi strain tensor at \(P\), and \(\vek n\) a unit vector. For a number \(h\) with \(0 < |h| < r\) let a fibre reach from \(P\) to the point \(Q\) with \(\overrightarrow{PQ} = h\,\vek n\). Its length before loading is \(L_0 = |h|\), and after loading \(L_1 = |\overrightarrow{P_1 Q_1}|\). Then \(\mat F\vek n\) is not the zero vector, and for the unit vector \(\vek m = \mat F\vek n / |\mat F\vek n|\):

  1. the quotient \((L_1^2 - L_0^2)/(2L_1^2)\) is defined for all small enough \(|h|\) and approaches the number \(\vek m^\T\mat E^*\,\vek m\),
    \[\lim_{\mathrm{h} \to 0} \frac{L_1^2 - L_0^2}{2L_1^2} = \vek m^\T\mat E^*\,\vek m , \tag{1.59}\]
  2. the two measures are related by the equality
    \[\vek m^\T\mat E^*\,\vek m = \frac{\vek n^\T\mat E\,\vek n}{1 + 2\,\vek n^\T\mat E\,\vek n} . \tag{1.60}\]
Proof

First we show that \(\mat F\vek n\) is not the zero vector, then item 2, and from it item 1.

The vector \(\mat F\vek n\).

  1. Suppose that \(\mat F\vek n = \vek 0\).
  2. Then by item 1 of lemma 1.99, \((\mat F^{-1}\mat F)\,\vek n = \mat F^{-1}(\mat F\vek n) = \mat F^{-1}\vek 0\), and every entry of the product \(\mat F^{-1}\vek 0\) is a sum of products with zero, so it is zero.
  3. By (1.43) and lemma 1.106, however, \((\mat F^{-1}\mat F)\,\vek n = \mat I\vek n = \vek n\), which is not the zero vector, because its length is \(1\). This contradicts step 2.
  4. So \(\mat F\vek n \neq \vek 0\), and its length \(|\mat F\vek n|\) is positive. Every component of the vector \(\vek m\) is a component of the vector \(\mat F\vek n\) divided by \(|\mat F\vek n|\), so by (1.10) \(|\vek m|^2 = |\mat F\vek n|^2/|\mat F\vek n|^2 = 1\), and \(\vek m\) is a unit vector.

2. The relation between the two measures.

  1. We write \(G = \vek n^\T\mat E\,\vek n\). By step 4 of the proof of theorem 1.114 on the strain of a short fibre, \(|\mat F\vek n|^2 = \vek n^\T\mat F^\T\mat F\,\vek n\) and \(G = \tfrac12\big(|\mat F\vek n|^2 - 1\big)\). So \(|\mat F\vek n|^2 = 1 + 2G\), and by step 4 above this number is positive.
  2. By lemma 1.119, \(\mat E = \mat F^\T\mat E^*\,\mat F\), so \(G = \vek n^\T\mat F^\T\mat E^*\,\mat F\,\vek n\).
  3. By item 3 of lemma 1.101, \(\vek n^\T\mat F^\T = (\mat F\vek n)^\T\), and by item 2 of lemma 1.99 we may group the factors as we like. So \(G = (\mat F\vek n)^\T\,\mat E^*\,(\mat F\vek n)\).
  4. We substitute \(\mat F\vek n = |\mat F\vek n|\,\vek m\). By item 2 of lemma 1.101, \((|\mat F\vek n|\,\vek m)^\T = |\mat F\vek n|\,\vek m^\T\), and by item 3 of lemma 1.99 we take the number out of each product. We get \(G = |\mat F\vek n|^2\,\vek m^\T\mat E^*\,\vek m = (1 + 2G)\,\vek m^\T\mat E^*\,\vek m\).
  5. We divide by the positive number \(1 + 2G\) and get (1.60).

1. The limit.

  1. We write \(g(h) = (L_1^2 - L_0^2)/(2L_0^2)\) and \(c = 1 + 2G\), where \(G = \vek n^\T\mat E\,\vek n\) as above. By item 1 of theorem 1.114 on the strain of a short fibre, \(\lim_{\mathrm{h} \to 0} g(h) = G\), and by step 1 of item 2, \(c = |\mat F\vek n|^2 > 0\).
  2. From the definition of the function \(g\) we get \(L_1^2/L_0^2 = 1 + 2g(h)\), when we multiply the equality \(g(h) = \tfrac12\big(L_1^2/L_0^2 - 1\big)\) by \(2\) and add \(1\).
  3. We use the definition of the limit 1.5 with the error \(c/4\): there is a \(\delta_1 > 0\) such that \(|g(h) - G| < c/4\) for every \(h\) with \(0 < |h| < \delta_1\). We may always narrow the band, as we said after the definition of the limit, so we take \(\delta_1 \le r\), and \(g(h)\) is defined for all these \(h\). For such \(h\), \(1 + 2g(h) = c + 2\big(g(h) - G\big) > c - c/2 = c/2\). So \(L_1^2 = L_0^2\,\big(1 + 2g(h)\big) > 0\), hence \(L_1 > 0\), and the quotient \(a(h) = (L_1^2 - L_0^2)/(2L_1^2)\) is defined. So we may apply the definition of the limit to the function \(a\), with \(\delta_1\) in the role of the number \(r\).
  4. For these \(h\) we divide the numerator and the denominator of the quotient \(a(h)\) by \(L_0^2\) and use step 2:
    \[a(h) = \frac{(L_1^2 - L_0^2)/L_0^2}{2L_1^2/L_0^2} = \frac{2g(h)}{2\,\big(1 + 2g(h)\big)} = \frac{g(h)}{1 + 2g(h)} .\]
  5. By item 2, \(\vek m^\T\mat E^*\,\vek m = G/(1 + 2G) = G/c\). We bring the two fractions to a common denominator:
    \[a(h) - \frac{G}{c} = \frac{g(h)\,(1 + 2G) - G\,\big(1 + 2g(h)\big)}{\big(1 + 2g(h)\big)\,c} = \frac{g(h) - G}{\big(1 + 2g(h)\big)\,c} ,\]
    because the terms \(2\,g(h)\,G\) in the numerator cancel.
  6. By step 3 the denominator is larger than \((c/2) \cdot c = c^2/2\), so \(|a(h) - G/c| < 2\,|g(h) - G|/c^2\).
  7. We choose any error \(\eta > 0\). By the definition of the limit there is a \(\delta_2 > 0\) such that \(|g(h) - G| < \eta\,c^2/2\) for every \(h\) with \(0 < |h| < \delta_2\). For \(\delta\) we take the smaller of the numbers \(\delta_1\) and \(\delta_2\). For every \(h\) with \(0 < |h| < \delta\), by step 6, \(|a(h) - G/c| < \eta\). We chose the error \(\eta\) arbitrarily, so the limit of the quotient \(a(h)\) is \(G/c = \vek m^\T\mat E^*\,\vek m\).

Source: BOWER §2.1.6 (PDF p. 49) writes item 1 for an infinitesimally short fibre, with the unit vector along the fibre after loading and without a limit, and leaves the proof to the reader. CM (3.4.23) (PDF p. 133) writes \((ds)^2 - (dS)^2 = 2\,d\vek x\cdot\mat E^*\cdot d\vek x\). The proof is not from the sources.

The theorem is the version in space of the quotient for the bar. The Euler-Almansi tensor gives, for every direction \(\vek m\) after loading, how much a short fibre has been stretched, measured with its length after loading. The vector \(\vek m\) is the direction of the fibre after loading up to the remainders, since by lemma 1.111 on a short fibre after loading the vector of the fibre after loading is \(h\,\mat F\vek n\) plus the remainders. For negative \(h\) the fibre points in the direction \(-\vek m\), which does not change the double sum, because each of its terms is a product of two components of the direction. The proof showed why the theorem holds. The new quotient is exactly the Green-Lagrange quotient \(g\) divided by \(1 + 2g = L_1^2/L_0^2\), so we got its limit from theorem 1.114 on the strain of a short fibre, and item 2 is the same relation in the limit.

Item 2 relates the two measures of the same fibre. We write \(G = \vek n^\T\mat E\,\vek n\) and \(A = \vek m^\T\mat E^*\,\vek m\). From (1.60),

\[G - A = G - \frac{G}{1 + 2G} = \frac{G\,(1 + 2G) - G}{1 + 2G} = \frac{2G^2}{1 + 2G} = 2\,G\,A .\]

So the two measures of the same fibre differ by exactly twice their product. When \(|G| \le 0{,}001\), the difference is at most \(0{,}002\,|A|\) in size, two thousandths of the value \(A\). For small strains it therefore does not matter which of the two measures we use. With the strain of the fibre \(\varepsilon(\vek n)\) of section 1.17.3 the relation is even simpler. By item 2 of theorem 1.114 on the strain of a short fibre, \(1 + 2G = \big(1 + \varepsilon(\vek n)\big)^2\), so \(G = \varepsilon(\vek n) + \tfrac12\,\varepsilon(\vek n)^2\) and \(A = G/\big(1 + \varepsilon(\vek n)\big)^2\), which is exactly the formula (1.56) with \(\varepsilon = \varepsilon(\vek n)\). So the curves of figure 1.367 hold for every short fibre, not only for the bar.

Let us test everything on the sheared cube, which is glued to the table by its bottom face and whose top face we pushed sideways by \(s = 10\) µm at the height \(h = 10\,000\) µm. The axis \(x\) points in the direction of the push, the axis \(z\) upward. The deformation gradient is \(\mat F = \mat I + \mat K\), where \(\mat K\) is the displacement gradient \(\mat H\) of the cube, with the only nonzero entry \(0{,}001\) in row \(x\) and column \(z\). Above we found \(\mat F^{-1} = \mat I - \mat K\) and \(\mat F^{-\T} = \mat I - \mat K^\T\).

  1. We multiply out the brackets term by term by item 3 of lemma 1.99 and lemma 1.106: \(\mat F^{-\T}\mat F^{-1} = (\mat I - \mat K^\T)(\mat I - \mat K) = \mat I - \mat K - \mat K^\T + \mat K^\T\mat K\), where \(\mat K\), \(\mat K^\T\) and \(\mat K^\T\mat K\) are the matrices in the figure.
  2. In the product \(\mat K^\T\mat K\) only the entry in row \(z\) and column \(z\) is nonzero. Row \(z\) of the matrix \(\mat K^\T\) is \((0{,}001, 0, 0)\), column \(z\) of the matrix \(\mat K\) is also \((0{,}001, 0, 0)\), and their product is \(0{,}001^2 = 10^{-6}\). The other rows of the matrix \(\mat K^\T\) and the other columns of the matrix \(\mat K\) are zero.
  3. By (1.57), therefore, the half of the sum of three matrices, the matrix \(\mat E^*\), is
    \[\mat E^* = \tfrac12\big(\mat K + \mat K^\T - \mat K^\T\mat K\big) = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 & 0{,}0005 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0{,}0005 & 0 & -0{,}0000005 \end{bmatrix} .\]

Let us compare it with the Green-Lagrange tensor of the cube from section 1.17.2,

\[\mat E = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 & 0{,}0005 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0{,}0005 & 0 & 0{,}0000005 \end{bmatrix} .\]

The matrices differ only in the entry in row \(z\) and column \(z\), which has the opposite sign. How can \(E_{\mathrm{zz}}\) be positive and \(E^*_{\mathrm{zz}}\) negative? By theorem 1.114 on the strain of a short fibre, the entry \(E_{\mathrm{zz}}\) is the measure of the fibre that is vertical before loading (\(\vek n = \vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\)), and by theorem 1.120 the entry \(E^*_{\mathrm{zz}}\) is the measure of the fibre that is vertical after loading (\(\vek m = \vek e_{\mathrm{z}}\)). These are two different fibres (figure 1.375).

Let us draw the left half. The axes show \(x\) to the right and \(z\) upwards. The hatched line is the table to which the cube is glued. The thin blackwhite square is the front face before loading, the thin orange parallelogram after it, since we push the top edge by \(s\) to the right. The ratio \(s/h = 0{,}001\) is magnified in the figure to \(0{,}25\) so that the difference can be seen. The corners \(B\), \(C\) and \(C_1\) are labelled at the sides. The thick blackwhite line is the fibre \(AD\), which is vertical before loading, and the thick orange line from \(A\) to \(D_1\) is the same fibre after it: it leans and gets longer. The dimension \(h\) is the height of the cube, the dimension \(s\) is the shift of the top edge. This fibre belongs to the entry \(E_{\mathrm{zz}}\) of the Green-Lagrange tensor.

The right half shows the same faces. The table, the blackwhite square, the orange parallelogram and the corners are as before. Now we choose another fibre. The thick blackwhite line from \(B\) to \(T\) is the fibre before loading, which is leaning. The point \(T\) is on the top edge, \(s\) to the left of \(C\). After loading \(T\) moves by \(s\) to the right to \(T_1\), which is the position where the corner \(C\) was before loading. So the thick orange line from \(B\) to \(T_1\) is vertical and shorter. This fibre belongs to the entry \(E^*_{\mathrm{zz}}\) of the Euler-Almansi tensor. The dimension \(h\) and the dimension \(s\) are drawn again on the right half, for the same quantities.

The vertical edge \(AD\) leans and gets longer from \(h\) to \(\sqrt{h^2 + s^2} = 10\,000{,}005\) µm. The fibre \(BT\) with coordinates \(B = (10\,000, 0, 0)\), \(T = (9\,990, 0, 10\,000)\) and \(T_1 = (10\,000, 0, 10\,000)\) in µm stands upright and gets shorter from \(\sqrt{h^2 + s^2} = 10\,000{,}005\) µm to \(h = 10\,000\) µm. Its quotient is

\[\frac{L_1^2 - L_0^2}{2L_1^2} = \frac{h^2 - (h^2 + s^2)}{2h^2} = -\frac{s^2}{2h^2} = -5 \cdot 10^{-7} ,\]

exactly \(E^*_{\mathrm{zz}}\). The shear that makes a vertical fibre lean and get longer makes a leaning fibre stand upright and get shorter.

The field of the cube is linear, so there are no remainders, and the equalities of theorem 1.120 hold for every fibre of the cube without a limit, as we saw for the Green-Lagrange tensor in section 1.17.2. Let us calculate both quotients for the fibres of the front face from section 1.6.2 and for the fibre \(BT\), from the lengths in micrometres.

fibre \(L_0\) \(L_1\) \((L_1^2 - L_0^2)/(2L_0^2)\) \((L_1^2 - L_0^2)/(2L_1^2)\)
bottom edge \(AB\) \(10\,000\) \(10\,000\) \(0\) \(0\)
vertical edge \(AD\) \(10\,000\) \(10\,000{,}005\) \(5{,}000000 \cdot 10^{-7}\) \(4{,}999995 \cdot 10^{-7}\)
diagonal \(AC\) \(14\,142{,}136\) \(14\,149{,}208\) \(5{,}0025 \cdot 10^{-4}\) \(4{,}9975 \cdot 10^{-4}\)
diagonal \(BD\) \(14\,142{,}136\) \(14\,135{,}066\) \(-4{,}9975 \cdot 10^{-4}\) \(-5{,}0025 \cdot 10^{-4}\)
fibre \(BT\) \(10\,000{,}005\) \(10\,000\) \(-4{,}999995 \cdot 10^{-7}\) \(-5{,}000000 \cdot 10^{-7}\)

The two columns differ by \(2GA\), as the relation above says. For the diagonals this is \(2 \cdot 5{,}0025 \cdot 10^{-4} \cdot 4{,}9975 \cdot 10^{-4} = 5{,}0 \cdot 10^{-7}\), which is exactly the difference \(5{,}0025 \cdot 10^{-4} - 4{,}9975 \cdot 10^{-4}\). For the edge \(AD\) and the fibre \(BT\) it is only \(2 \cdot (5 \cdot 10^{-7})^2 = 5 \cdot 10^{-13}\), so the columns differ only by a millionth of the value. We also get the last column from the matrix \(\mat E^*\) when we put in the direction of the fibre after loading. For the diagonal \(AC\) the vector after loading is \((10\,010, 0, 10\,000)\) with the length \(14\,149{,}208\) µm, so \(\vek m = (0{,}70746, 0, 0{,}70675)\). Only the terms with the indices \(x\) and \(z\) remain in the double sum:

\[\begin{aligned} \vek m^\T\mat E^*\,\vek m &= 2E^*_{\mathrm{xz}}\,m_{\mathrm{x}} m_{\mathrm{z}} + E^*_{\mathrm{zz}}\,m_{\mathrm{z}}^2 = 2 \cdot 0{,}0005 \cdot 0{,}70746 \cdot 0{,}70675 - 5 \cdot 10^{-7} \cdot 0{,}70675^2 \\ &= 5{,}0000 \cdot 10^{-4} - 2{,}4975 \cdot 10^{-7} = 4{,}9975 \cdot 10^{-4} , \end{aligned}\]

as in the table.

For the plate that in section 1.17.6 we turned as a whole about the axis \(z\) with the numbers \(c = 0{,}6\) and \(s = 0{,}8\), \(\mat F^\T\mat F = \mat I\). Also \(\mat F\mat F^\T = \mat I\). The entry \((\mat F\mat F^\T)_{\mathrm{xx}}\) is row \(x\) of the matrix \(\mat F\), \((0{,}6, -0{,}8, 0)\), multiplied by column \(x\) of the matrix \(\mat F^\T\), which is the same triple, so \(0{,}36 + 0{,}64 = 1\). The entry \((\mat F\mat F^\T)_{\mathrm{xy}}\) is \(0{,}6 \cdot 0{,}8 + (-0{,}8) \cdot 0{,}6 + 0 = 0\), and we get the others in the same way. So by definition 1.107 the matrix \(\mat F^\T\) is an inverse matrix of the matrix \(\mat F\), and by lemma 1.108 on the uniqueness of the inverse matrix, \(\mat F^{-1} = \mat F^\T\). Transposing twice gives back the original matrix (lemma 1.101, item 1), so \(\mat F^{-\T} = (\mat F^\T)^\T = \mat F\). Then \(\mat F^{-\T}\mat F^{-1} = \mat F\mat F^\T = \mat I\) and \(\mat E^* = \tfrac12(\mat I - \mat I) = \mat 0\). Like the Green-Lagrange tensor, the Euler-Almansi tensor correctly says that no fibre gets longer, while the small strain tensor wrongly predicts a shortening by \(40\) %. The same follows from lemma 1.119, since \(\mat E = \mat 0\) gives \(\mat E^* = \mat F^{-\T}\,\mat 0\,\mat F^{-1} = \mat 0\).

For the hanging bar all partial derivatives are small. A steel bar 10 m long hangs under its own weight and is fixed only at the point \(O\), the centre of its upper end, the axis \(x\) points vertically down, and the point \(P\) with \(x_{\mathrm{P}} = 5\) m, \(y_{\mathrm{P}} = 4\) mm and \(z_{\mathrm{P}} = 0\) lies 5 m below \(O\) and 4 mm from the axis of the bar. We calculate the inverse matrix of the deformation gradient at \(P\) with a computer, and how to calculate it by hand we will see in chapter 2. That it really is the inverse we check by multiplication, \(\mat F\mat F^{-1} = \mat F^{-1}\mat F = \mat I\). By (1.57) we get

\[\mat E^* = \begin{bmatrix} 1{,}951994 \cdot 10^{-6} & 5{,}94 \cdot 10^{-16} & 0 \\ 5{,}94 \cdot 10^{-16} & -5{,}856005 \cdot 10^{-7} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -5{,}856005 \cdot 10^{-7} \end{bmatrix} .\]

The Green-Lagrange tensor at \(P\) has \(1{,}952002 \cdot 10^{-6}\) and twice \(-5{,}855998 \cdot 10^{-7}\) on the diagonal, the small strain tensor \(1{,}952 \cdot 10^{-6}\) and twice \(-5{,}856 \cdot 10^{-7}\) (sections 1.17.2 and 1.17.3). Rounded to five significant digits, the diagonal entries of all three matrices are equal, and the entries off the diagonal differ by at most \(1{,}2 \cdot 10^{-15}\). The largest difference, between \(E_{\mathrm{xx}}\) and \(E^*_{\mathrm{xx}}\), is \(7{,}6 \cdot 10^{-12}\), about four millionths of the entry.

The differences on the diagonal have a simple pattern. For the entry \(xx\), \(E_{\mathrm{xx}} - \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = 1{,}905 \cdot 10^{-12} = \tfrac12\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}^2\) and \(E^*_{\mathrm{xx}} - \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = -5{,}715 \cdot 10^{-12} = -\tfrac32\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}^2\), and for the entry \(yy\) likewise \(\tfrac12\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}}^2 = 1{,}71 \cdot 10^{-13}\) and \(-\tfrac32\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}}^2 = -5{,}14 \cdot 10^{-13}\). Why?
