A short fibre along the axis \(x\) leans only by the ratio \(4{,}7 \cdot 10^{-10}\), so it lies almost along the axis \(x\) both before and after loading, and the formulas for the bar hold for it, as the curves near \(L_1/L_0 = 1\) show. The Green-Lagrange strain is \(\varepsilon + \tfrac12\,\varepsilon^2\), and the new quotient, by step 4 of the derivation of the formula (1.56), almost \(\varepsilon - \tfrac32\,\varepsilon^2\). So we check the entry \(E^*_{\mathrm{xx}}\) also without a computer:

\[\begin{aligned} \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} - \tfrac32\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}^2 &= 1{,}952 \cdot 10^{-6} - \tfrac32\,(1{,}952 \cdot 10^{-6})^2 \\ &= 1{,}952 \cdot 10^{-6} - 5{,}715 \cdot 10^{-12} \\ &= 1{,}951994 \cdot 10^{-6} , \end{aligned}\]

which, on the digits shown, is the entry from the computer. The entries \(E_{\mathrm{xy}} = -5{,}94 \cdot 10^{-16}\) and \(E^*_{\mathrm{xy}} = 5{,}94 \cdot 10^{-16}\) even have opposite signs. Since \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xy}} = 0\), both consist only of products of partial derivatives of the size \(10^{-16}\) to \(10^{-15}\), and these products enter \(\mat E^*\) with other coefficients than \(\mat E\), as \(\tfrac12\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}^2\) and \(-\tfrac32\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}^2\) do on the diagonal.

Let us also test theorem 1.120 on the bar. For the fibre in the direction \(\vek n = (\tfrac13, \tfrac23, \tfrac23)\) of section 1.17.2, \(A = \vek m^\T\mat E^*\,\vek m = -3{,}036443 \cdot 10^{-7}\), less than \(G = -3{,}036441 \cdot 10^{-7}\) by \(2GA = 1{,}84 \cdot 10^{-13}\). The quotient \((L_1^2 - L_0^2)/(2L_1^2)\), calculated exactly from the field (1.18), comes within \(1{,}01 \cdot 10^{-11}\) and \(1{,}01 \cdot 10^{-12}\) of the value \(A\) for fibres of length 1 mm and 0.1 mm, as the theorem says.

For small partial derivatives the matrices \(\mat E^*\), \(\mat E\) and \(\ten\varepsilon\) therefore differ only by terms with products of partial derivatives, and then we need not distinguish whether we give points and directions of fibres before loading or after it (CM §3.5.1, PDF p. 141, BOWER §2.1.7, PDF p. 50). For a single fibre we showed this exactly with the relation \(G - A = 2GA\). For all entries of the matrices at once we still need a bound for the entries of the matrix \(\mat F^{-1}\).

How close is \(\mat F^{-1}\) to the matrix \(\mat I - \mat H\)? For the sheared cube \(\mat F^{-1} = \mat I - \mat K\) exactly, because \(\mat K\mat K = \mat 0\) (section 1.16.5, figure 1.338, top). For the hanging bar the matrix \(\mat F^{-1}\), which we computed with a computer, differs from the matrix \(\mat I - \mat H\) by at most \(3{,}81 \cdot 10^{-12}\), in the entry \(xx\). This is the square of the largest partial derivative, \((1{,}952 \cdot 10^{-6})^2 = 3{,}81 \cdot 10^{-12}\). Why? We can express the difference \(\mat B = \mat I - \mat F^{-1}\) from the equation \(\mat F\mat F^{-1} = \mat I\), and we get \(\mat B = \mat H - \mat H\mat B\). If \(\mat B\) is small, then \(\mat H\mat B\) is a product of two small matrices, and \(\mat B\) is almost \(\mat H\). The difference \(\mat F^{-1} - (\mat I - \mat H) = \mat H - \mat B = \mat H\mat B\) is therefore almost \(\mat H\mat H\), whose entry \(xx\) we calculate by hand:

\[H_{\mathrm{xx}}^2 + H_{\mathrm{xy}}\,H_{\mathrm{yx}} + H_{\mathrm{xz}}\,H_{\mathrm{zx}} = 3{,}810 \cdot 10^{-12} - 2{,}2 \cdot 10^{-19} + 0 = 3{,}81 \cdot 10^{-12} .\]

This is the number from the computer. That \(\mat B\) really is small, the same equation tells us when we read it as an inequality for the largest entry of the matrix \(\mat B\). As in section 1.17.3, let \(m\) be a number that no partial derivative of the displacement at the point exceeds in absolute value. The lemma also requires \(m \le \tfrac16\). We need this condition in step 7 of the proof, where we divide by the number \(1 - 3m\), which must be positive and not too small: for \(m \le \tfrac16\) it is at least \(\tfrac12\).

Let us draw the graph. The horizontal axis is the number \(m\), the marks \(\tfrac16\) and \(\tfrac13\) are the important ones. The vertical axis is the value \(1/(1 - 3m)\). The number \(\mu\) is the largest in absolute value among the entries of the matrix \(\mat B = \mat I - \mat F^{-1}\), which we will bound in the lemma below. In step 7 of its proof we get \(\mu \le m/(1 - 3m)\), so the ratio \(\mu/m\) is at most \(1/(1 - 3m)\). The orange curve shows this value. It grows because the denominator \(1 - 3m\) gets smaller as \(m\) grows. The dot at \(m = \tfrac16\) has the value \(2\), which the grey horizontal line also shows. For a smaller \(m\) the value is smaller than \(2\), so for \(m \le \tfrac16\) we divide by a number that is at least \(\tfrac12\). The grey vertical line at \(m = \tfrac13\) is the place where the denominator becomes zero, that is, where the value is no longer bounded.

Let us draw the estimates. At the top are the nine numbers \(|B_{\mathrm{ij}}|\), each at most \(\mu\), and one of them equals \(\mu\), because \(\mu\) is the largest. At the bottom is the entry \((y, z)\) of the product \(\mat H\mat B\). Row \(y\) of the matrix \(\mat H\) is multiplied by column \(z\) of the matrix \(\mat B\). Each of the three products is at most \(m\mu\) in absolute value, because \(|H_{\mathrm{ik}}| \le m\) and \(|B_{\mathrm{kj}}| \le \mu\). The sum therefore has absolute value at most \(3m\mu\).

Lemma 1.121 Estimate of the inverse matrix (ocena inverzne matrike)

Let \(\mat H\) be a \(3 \times 3\) matrix and \(m\) a number with \(0 < m \le \tfrac16\) such that \(|H_{\mathrm{ij}}| \le m\) for all indices \(i\) and \(j\). Let the matrix \(\mat F = \mat I + \mat H\) have an inverse matrix \(\mat F^{-1}\), and let \(\mat B = \mat I - \mat F^{-1}\). Then

\[\mat B = \mat H - \mat H\mat B , \qquad \mat F^{-1} = \mat I - \mat H + \mat H\mat B , \tag{1.61}\]

and for all \(i\) and \(j\) we have \(|B_{\mathrm{ij}}| \le 2m\) and \(|(\mat H\mat B)_{\mathrm{ij}}| \le 6m^2\).

Proof

We must show both equalities and both estimates. We get the equalities from the definition of the inverse matrix, the estimate for \(\mat B\) from the first equality, read as an inequality, and the estimate for \(\mat H\mat B\) from the estimate for \(\mat B\).

  1. By definition 1.107 of the inverse matrix, \(\mat F\mat F^{-1} = \mat I\). We substitute \(\mat F = \mat I + \mat H\) and \(\mat F^{-1} = \mat I - \mat B\). By item 3 of lemma 1.99 on the properties of the matrix product and by lemma 1.106 on multiplication by the identity matrix, \((\mat I + \mat H)(\mat I - \mat B) = \mat I - \mat B + \mat H - \mat H\mat B\).
  2. This matrix is \(\mat I\), so by the calculation rules for matrices (lemma 1.95) \(\mat H - \mat B - \mat H\mat B = \mat 0\), hence \(\mat B = \mat H - \mat H\mat B\). This is the first equality.
  3. From \(\mat F^{-1} = \mat I - \mat B\) and the first equality it follows that \(\mat F^{-1} = \mat I - \mat H + \mat H\mat B\), the second equality.
  4. Let \(\mu\) be the largest of the nine numbers \(|B_{\mathrm{ij}}|\). Among finitely many numbers one is the largest.
  5. By the first equality, \(B_{\mathrm{ij}} = H_{\mathrm{ij}} - \sum_{\mathrm{k}} H_{\mathrm{ik}}\,B_{\mathrm{kj}}\). By the triangle inequality for numbers and the rule for the absolute value of a product (lemma 1.6), \(|B_{\mathrm{ij}}| \le |H_{\mathrm{ij}}| + \sum_{\mathrm{k}} |H_{\mathrm{ik}}|\,|B_{\mathrm{kj}}| \le m + 3m\mu\), because the sum has three terms and each is at most \(m\mu\).
  6. The inequality from step 5 holds for all entries, also for the entry with \(|B_{\mathrm{ij}}| = \mu\). So \(\mu \le m + 3m\mu\), hence \((1 - 3m)\,\mu \le m\).
  7. Since \(m \le \tfrac16\), we have \(1 - 3m \ge \tfrac12\), so \(1/(1 - 3m) \le 2\), as the dot shows. When we divide the inequality by the positive number \(1 - 3m\), we get \(\mu \le m/(1 - 3m) \le 2m\). So \(|B_{\mathrm{ij}}| \le 2m\) for all \(i\) and \(j\).
  8. The entry \((i, j)\) of the matrix \(\mat H\mat B\) is \(\sum_{\mathrm{k}} H_{\mathrm{ik}}\,B_{\mathrm{kj}}\), a sum of three terms, of which each is at most \(m \cdot 2m\) in absolute value, because \(\mu \le 2m\) in the estimate in the figure. By the triangle inequality for numbers, therefore, \(|(\mat H\mat B)_{\mathrm{ij}}| \le 6m^2\).

Source: LEBL2 prop. 8.2.6 (PDF pp. 23-24) proves the related statement that a matrix close enough to an invertible matrix is invertible too. The lemma and the proof are not from the source.

The lemma says that \(\mat F^{-1}\) equals \(\mat I - \mat H\) up to the matrix \(\mat H\mat B\), whose entries are at most \(6m^2\). The proof used the equation \(\mat B = \mat H - \mat H\mat B\) twice: first as an inequality that bounds the largest entry of \(\mat B\), then to estimate the correction \(\mat H\mat B\). We needed the condition \(m \le \tfrac16\) in step 7, so that the number \(1 - 3m\) is positive and not too small (it is at least \(\tfrac12\), so \(1/(1 - 3m) \le 2\)). The lemma does not prove that \(\mat F^{-1}\) exists but assumes it, like this whole section. For the cube \(m = 0{,}001\), \(\mat B = \mat K\) and \(\mat H\mat B = \mat K\mat K = \mat 0\). For the hanging bar \(m = 1{,}952 \cdot 10^{-6}\), the largest entry of \(\mat B\) is \(1{,}951996 \cdot 10^{-6}\), less than \(2m\), and the largest entry of \(\mat H\mat B\) is \(3{,}81 \cdot 10^{-12}\), below the bound \(6m^2 = 2{,}29 \cdot 10^{-11}\). Now we can compare all three measures.

The figure has three panels, each with its own horizontal axis, on which every gap between powers is a factor of \(10\) (a logarithmic scale). Each has three rows for the differences between the measures: \(E - \varepsilon\), \(E^* - \varepsilon\) and \(E^* - E\). Every row is built in the same way. The blackwhite dot is the true difference, that is, the largest entry of the difference of the two measures. The blue dash is the bound from corollary 1.122. The dot always lies to the left of the dash or on it, because the true difference does not exceed the bound. The grey dimension between them is the gap to the bound.

The top panel is the sheared cube with \(m = 0{,}001\), the middle one is the hanging bar at the point \(P\) with \(m = 1{,}952 \cdot 10^{-6}\). Each panel has its own powers on the axis: the axis of the bar and the axis of the last panel have different ones, because the differences for the bar are much smaller, and for the last panel much larger. For the cube the largest entries of the differences, \(zz\), are taken, for the bar \(xx\). The last panel is the matrix with all nine entries \(-\tfrac16\) at \(m = \tfrac16\). For it all three differences equal the bounds, so there are no grey dimensions and the dots lie on the dashes.

Corollary 1.122 Three strain measures for small partial derivatives (tri mere deformacije pri majhnih parcialnih odvodih)

Let \(\mat H\) be the displacement gradient at an interior point of a body and \(m\) a number with \(0 < m \le \tfrac16\) such that \(|H_{\mathrm{ij}}| \le m\) for all \(i\) and \(j\), and let the deformation gradient \(\mat F = \mat I + \mat H\) have an inverse matrix. Let \(\mat E\), \(\mat E^*\) and \(\ten\varepsilon\) be the Green-Lagrange strain tensor, the Euler-Almansi strain tensor and the small strain tensor at this point. Then for all \(i\) and \(j\) we have

\[\begin{aligned} |E_{\mathrm{ij}} - \varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}| &\le \tfrac32\,m^2 , \\ |E^*_{\mathrm{ij}} - \varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}| &\le 12\,m^2 , \\ |E^*_{\mathrm{ij}} - E_{\mathrm{ij}}| &\le \tfrac{27}{2}\,m^2 . \end{aligned} \tag{1.62}\]
Proof

We must show three estimates. We write each difference with products of matrices and bound it with lemma 1.121 on the estimate of the inverse matrix.

  1. By lemma 1.113 on the Green-Lagrange strain from the displacement gradient, \(\mat E = \tfrac12(\mat H + \mat H^\T + \mat H^\T\mat H)\), and by (1.51), \(\ten\varepsilon = \tfrac12(\mat H + \mat H^\T)\). So \(\mat E - \ten\varepsilon = \tfrac12\,\mat H^\T\mat H\).
  2. The entry \((i, j)\) of the matrix \(\mat H^\T\mat H\) is \(\sum_{\mathrm{k}} H_{\mathrm{ki}}\,H_{\mathrm{kj}}\), a sum of three products, each at most \(m^2\) in absolute value. By the triangle inequality for numbers (lemma 1.6), therefore, \(|E_{\mathrm{ij}} - \varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}| \le \tfrac12 \cdot 3m^2 = \tfrac32\,m^2\).
  3. Let \(\mat B = \mat I - \mat F^{-1}\) as in lemma 1.121. By item 2 of lemma 1.101 on transposing a sum, a multiple and a product, and since the identity matrix equals its transpose, \(\mat F^{-\T} = (\mat I - \mat B)^\T = \mat I - \mat B^\T\).
  4. By item 3 of lemma 1.99 on the properties of the matrix product and lemma 1.106 on multiplication by the identity matrix, \(\mat F^{-\T}\mat F^{-1} = (\mat I - \mat B^\T)(\mat I - \mat B) = \mat I - \mat B - \mat B^\T + \mat B^\T\mat B\). By (1.57), therefore, \(\mat E^* = \tfrac12(\mat B + \mat B^\T - \mat B^\T\mat B)\), as for the cube, where \(\mat B = \mat K\).
  5. By lemma 1.121, \(\mat B = \mat H - \mat H\mat B\), and by item 2 of lemma 1.101, \(\mat B^\T = \mat H^\T - (\mat H\mat B)^\T\). Inserting this into step 4 and subtracting \(\ten\varepsilon = \tfrac12(\mat H + \mat H^\T)\) gives
    \[\mat E^* - \ten\varepsilon = -\tfrac12\big(\mat H\mat B + (\mat H\mat B)^\T + \mat B^\T\mat B\big) .\]
  6. By lemma 1.121 every entry of the matrices \(\mat H\mat B\) and \((\mat H\mat B)^\T\) is at most \(6m^2\) in absolute value. The entry \((i, j)\) of the matrix \(\mat B^\T\mat B\) is \(\sum_{\mathrm{k}} B_{\mathrm{ki}}\,B_{\mathrm{kj}}\), a sum of three products, each at most \(2m \cdot 2m = 4m^2\) by the same lemma, so it is at most \(12m^2\). By the triangle inequality for numbers, \(|E^*_{\mathrm{ij}} - \varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}| \le \tfrac12\,(6m^2 + 6m^2 + 12m^2) = 12m^2\).
  7. We write the difference as \(E^*_{\mathrm{ij}} - E_{\mathrm{ij}} = (E^*_{\mathrm{ij}} - \varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}}) + (\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ij}} - E_{\mathrm{ij}})\). By the triangle inequality for numbers and steps 6 and 2, \(|E^*_{\mathrm{ij}} - E_{\mathrm{ij}}| \le 12m^2 + \tfrac32\,m^2 = \tfrac{27}{2}\,m^2\).

Source: CM §3.5.1 (PDF pp. 140-141) says that for small partial derivatives, when terms of the order of the square are dropped, the Green-Lagrange and the Eulerian strain tensor need not be distinguished. BOWER §2.1.7 (PDF p. 50) says that the infinitesimal strain approximates the Lagrange strain, and the Eulerian strain with the same accuracy, and leaves the latter to the reader. The estimates with fixed numbers and the proof are not from the sources.

The corollary says exactly what we saw on the numbers. For small partial derivatives the entries of all three matrices differ by at most a fixed number times the square of the largest partial derivative. For steel, where \(m\) is of the order \(0{,}001\), the differences are at most of the order \(10^{-5}\), a hundred times less than the partial derivatives themselves. The numbers \(\tfrac32\), \(12\) and \(\tfrac{27}{2}\) are the bounds that the proof gives, and with the same assumptions they cannot be made smaller. This is shown by the matrix \(\mat H\) with all nine entries equal to \(-\tfrac16\), at \(m = \tfrac16\). Its \(\mat F^{-1}\) has \(\tfrac43\) on the diagonal and \(\tfrac13\) off it, which we check by multiplying \(\mat F\mat F^{-1} = \mat I\). All the matrices of lemma 1.121 on the estimate of the inverse matrix and of the corollary then have nine equal entries:

matrix each of its entries bound
\(\mat B\) \(-\tfrac13\) \(2m = \tfrac13\)
\(\mat H\mat B\) \(\tfrac16\) \(6m^2 = \tfrac16\)
\(\mat E - \ten\varepsilon\) \(\tfrac1{24}\) \(\tfrac32\,m^2 = \tfrac1{24}\)
\(\mat E^* - \ten\varepsilon\) \(-\tfrac13\) \(12\,m^2 = \tfrac13\)
\(\mat E^* - \mat E\) \(-\tfrac38\) \(\tfrac{27}{2}\,m^2 = \tfrac38\)

All three bounds are attained exactly at the matrix with all entries \(-\tfrac16\), which we also checked with SymPy: its dots lie on the blue dashes. The first bound is attained for every \(m\): if all nine entries of the matrix \(\mat H\) equal \(m\), every entry of the matrix \(\tfrac12\,\mat H^\T\mat H\) equals \(\tfrac12 \cdot 3m^2 = \tfrac32\,m^2\). In both examples below the actual differences are smaller than the bounds, about three times for the first estimate and at least six times for the other two.

  • The sheared cube, \(m = 0{,}001\): the bounds are \(1{,}5 \cdot 10^{-6}\), \(1{,}2 \cdot 10^{-5}\) and \(1{,}35 \cdot 10^{-5}\). The largest differences are in the entry \(zz\), \(E_{\mathrm{zz}} - \varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}} = 5 \cdot 10^{-7}\), \(E^*_{\mathrm{zz}} - \varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}} = -5 \cdot 10^{-7}\) and \(E^*_{\mathrm{zz}} - E_{\mathrm{zz}} = -10^{-6}\).
  • The hanging bar at the point \(P\), \(m = 1{,}952 \cdot 10^{-6}\): the bounds are \(5{,}7 \cdot 10^{-12}\), \(4{,}6 \cdot 10^{-11}\) and \(5{,}1 \cdot 10^{-11}\). The largest differences are in the entry \(xx\), \(1{,}905 \cdot 10^{-12}\), \(-5{,}715 \cdot 10^{-12}\) and \(-7{,}6 \cdot 10^{-12}\).

But what if the partial derivatives are not small? Then we must not use the corollary, and the three measures are no longer almost equal. Let us stretch the bar to twice its length along the axis \(x\), and later we will compress it to a fifth of its length.

Let us draw the bars at a wall, so that only the change of length is seen. The hatched line is the wall from which we measure. The blackwhite bar is before loading, its length is \(L_0\). The orange bar, twice as long, is stretched to the length \(L_1 = 2L_0\). The lower orange bar is compressed to a fifth, its length is \(L_1 = L_0/5\). All three are drawn to the same scale.

For the double length we have \(\mat F = \mathrm{diag}(2, 1, 1)\), the displacement gradient is \(\mat H = \mathrm{diag}(1, 0, 0)\) and the largest element is \(m = 1 > \tfrac16\). The matrix \(\mat F\) has the inverse matrix \(\mathrm{diag}(\tfrac12, 1, 1)\), so the other assumptions of the corollary are satisfied. The small strain tensor has \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = H_{\mathrm{xx}} = 1\). By lemma 1.113 the Green-Lagrange tensor has \(E_{\mathrm{xx}} = \tfrac12\,(2 H_{\mathrm{xx}} + H_{\mathrm{xx}}^2) = \tfrac12\,(2^2 - 1) = 1{,}5\), because \(2^2\) is the square of the length ratio \(2\) along \(x\). By (1.57) the Euler-Almansi tensor is \(E^*_{\mathrm{xx}} = \tfrac12\,(1 - 1/2^2) = 0{,}375\). In figure 1.367 these are the dots at \(L_1/L_0 = 2\). The measures differ: \(E_{\mathrm{xx}}\) is larger than \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\) by a factor of \(1{,}5\) and larger than \(E^*_{\mathrm{xx}}\) by a factor of \(4\). For a stretch along the axis \(x\) we have \(E_{\mathrm{xx}} - \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = \tfrac12 H_{\mathrm{xx}}^2\). Here this is \(0{,}5\), half of the strain itself, while for \(H_{\mathrm{xx}} = 0{,}001\) it is \(5 \cdot 10^{-7}\), two thousand times less than the strain. The reason is in the denominator. Both measures divide the difference of the squares of lengths, \(l^2 - L^2\), with the length \(L\) before loading and \(l\) after it, by \(2L^2\) and \(2l^2\): \(E_{\mathrm{xx}} = (l^2 - L^2)/(2L^2)\) and \(E^*_{\mathrm{xx}} = (l^2 - L^2)/(2l^2)\). For \(l = 2L\) the second denominator is four times the first, while for \(l\) barely larger than \(L\) the two denominators are almost equal. Here \(m = 1 > \tfrac16\), so the corollary says nothing about this case. Only the first estimate does not need the condition \(m \le \tfrac16\), because steps 1 and 2 of the proof do not use it, and indeed \(|E_{\mathrm{xx}} - \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}| = 0{,}5 \le \tfrac32\,m^2 = 1{,}5\). But this bound is larger than the strain itself, \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = 1\), so it does not say that the measures are almost equal.

Would the other two estimates hold for a larger \(m\) as well? We have not proved this, and in general they do not hold. Let us compress the bar to a fifth of its length. Then \(\mat F = \mathrm{diag}(\tfrac15, 1, 1)\), \(\mat H = \mathrm{diag}(-\tfrac45, 0, 0)\) and \(m = \tfrac45\), and the matrix \(\mat F\) has the inverse matrix \(\mathrm{diag}(5, 1, 1)\). In the entry \(xx\) we have

\[\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = -0{,}8 , \qquad E_{\mathrm{xx}} = \tfrac12\big((\tfrac15)^2 - 1\big) = -0{,}48 , \qquad E^*_{\mathrm{xx}} = \tfrac12\,(1 - 5^2) = -12 .\]

The first estimate holds, \(|E_{\mathrm{xx}} - \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}| = 0{,}32 \le \tfrac32\,m^2 = 0{,}96\). The second does not: \(|E^*_{\mathrm{xx}} - \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}| = 11{,}2\), while the bound is \(12\,m^2 = 7{,}68\). The third does not either: \(|E^*_{\mathrm{xx}} - E_{\mathrm{xx}}| = 11{,}52\), while the bound is \(\tfrac{27}{2}\,m^2 = 8{,}64\). Without a condition on \(m\) the corollary therefore does not hold. Whether \(\tfrac16\) is the largest bound at which it still holds, we have not investigated. We chose the condition so that the proof in step 7 of lemma 1.121 works. Rubber can be stretched to twice its length, so for it the choice of the measure is not a matter of indifference.

Both examples in an overview, with the bounds from the corollary. The bound \(\tfrac32\,m^2\) may be used for every \(m\). The bound \(12\,m^2\) is guaranteed by the corollary only for \(m \le \tfrac16\), which neither of the two examples satisfies, so it is in the last column only for comparison:

| length ratio \(L_1/L_0\) | \(m\) | \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\) | \(E_{\mathrm{xx}}\) | \(E^*_{\mathrm{xx}}\) | \(\lvert E_{\mathrm{xx}} - \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\rvert\), bound \(\tfrac32\,m^2\) | \(\lvert E^*_{\mathrm{xx}} - \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\rvert\), bound \(12\,m^2\) | |---|---|---|---|---|---| | \(2\) | \(1\) | \(1\) | \(1{,}5\) | \(0{,}375\) | \(0{,}5 \le 1{,}5\) | \(0{,}625 \le 12\) | | \(\tfrac15\) | \(\tfrac45\) | \(-0{,}8\) | \(-0{,}48\) | \(-12\) | \(0{,}32 \le 0{,}96\) | \(11{,}2 > 7{,}68\) |

So in steel structures we use the small strain tensor, where the measures almost agree, while for large strains, for example in rubber, we must say which measure we use and whether the direction of the fibre is given before loading or after it.

Three measures together:

measure the fibre is given the change of the square of the length is divided by
Green-Lagrange tensor \(\mat E\) before loading, by the direction \(\vek n\) \(2L_0^2\)
Euler-Almansi tensor \(\mat E^*\) after loading, by the direction \(\vek m\) \(2L_1^2\)
small strain tensor \(\ten\varepsilon\) before or after loading \(2L_0^2 \approx 2L_1^2\)

We can now calculate from the displacement field the strain at every interior point and in every direction. The Green-Lagrange tensor gives it exactly when we give the direction of the fibre before loading, and the Euler-Almansi tensor when we give it after loading, while for small partial derivatives the small strain tensor is enough. The path went from displacements to strains. Often we must go the other way: we know the six components of strain and look for the displacements. Is this always possible? We calculate six components from only three components of the displacement, so they cannot be arbitrary. Which conditions they must satisfy, we look at in the next section.
